meta.author: Pseudo-Orpheus
meta.translation_method: Chunk-based semantic translation with philological notes
meta.subject: Magical and medicinal properties of stones and gems
meta.description: Scholarly edition with line-by-line Greek-English translation and philological commentary

lines.gr: Δῶρον ἀλεξικάκοιο Διὸς θνητοῖσιν ὀπάσσαι
lines.en: To bestow upon mortals a gift from Zeus Alexikakos,
lines.note: ἀλεξικάκοιο (“averter of evil”) preserves the cult epithet Alexikakos of Zeus; ὀπάσσαι is the aorist infinitive of ὀπάζω, “to bestow, grant.”

lines.gr: κεκλόμενος Μαίης ἐριούνιος ἦλθε κομίζων
lines.en: called Eriounios, of Maia, he came bearing,
lines.note: ἐριούνιος is the traditional epithet of Hermes; Maia is his mother. κεκλόμενος means “being called.” The genitive Μαίης is enjambed with υἱός in the next line (“of Maia … the son”).

lines.gr: υἱός, ὅπως ἂν ἔχοιμεν ὀϊζύος ἀτρεκὲς ἄλκαρ.
lines.en: the son, so that we might have a sure ward against woe.
lines.note: ἀτρεκές ἄλκαρ = “sure/unfailing defence, ward”; ὀϊζύς = “woe, misery.” ὅπως ἄν + optative expresses purpose (“so that we might have”).

lines.gr: γηθόσυνοι δέχνυσθε βροτοί, πινυτοῖσιν ἐνίσπω,
lines.en: Be glad and receive, mortals; I declare to the prudent,
lines.note: δέχνυσθε is an epic/poetic variant of δέχεσθε “receive”; γηθόσυνοι functions adverbially (“joyfully”). ἐνίσπω = “I declare/tell”; the direct object (“my words/teaching”) is understood. πινυτοῖσιν = “to the prudent/wise.”

lines.gr: οἷς ἀγαθὴ κραδίη, καὶ πείθεται ἀθανάτοισι·
lines.en: to those whose heart is good and yields to the Deathless Ones.
lines.note: κραδίη (sing.) and πείθεται (sing.) with plural οἷς show Homeric-style concord: “those whose heart is good and [whose heart] obeys.” ἀθανάτοισι (epic dative) = “the Deathless Ones,” i.e., the gods.

lines.gr: νηπυτίοισι δ' ὄνειαρ ἀκήρατον οὐ θέμις εὑρεῖν.
lines.en: but for the witless it is not lawful to find the undefiled boon.
lines.note: νηπύτιος = “childish, witless,” often of the unwise/uninitiated. ὄνειαρ = “boon, benefit”; ἀκήρατον = “undefiled, pure” (with ritual overtones). οὐ θέμις = “it is not sanctioned/right,” invoking divine law rather than mere custom.

lines.gr: τῷ δ' αὐτῷ καὶ πρόσθεν ἀγαλλομένους ἐπὶ δώρῳ
lines.en: and too beforetime, exulting in this same gift,
lines.note: The accusative participle ἀγαλλομένους (“exulting”) anticipates and agrees with the two accusative objects named in lines 8–10 (the son and Herakles); τῷ δ’ αὐτῷ (‘with this same [gift]’) refers back to the previously mentioned gift/stone.

lines.gr: υἷά τε Λητοΐδης ἀκεσίμβροτον ἀθανάτοισιν
lines.en: the Letoid led his son, the healer of mortals, to the deathless ones,
lines.note: Λητοΐδης (‘the Letoid’) = Apollon. ἀκεσίμβροτον is a compound (‘healer‑of‑mortals’), identifying the son as Asklepios. ἀθανατοῖσιν = ‘to the immortals.’

lines.gr: ἷξεν ἄγων ἐς Ὄλυμπον ἀγάννιφον, ἠδὲ σαόφρων
lines.en: he came leading to snow‑rich Olympos, and prudent
lines.note: ἀγάννιφον = ‘very snowy/snow‑rich,’ a standard epithet of Olympos; ἷξεν ἄγων = ‘came, leading.’

lines.gr: Παλλὰς Ἀθηναίη λαοσσόον Ἡρακλῆα·
lines.en: Pallas Athenaia led Herakles, savior of the people;
lines.note: λαοσσόον literally ‘people‑saving/people‑guarding.’ The verb ‘led’ is supplied from the previous line’s construction.

lines.gr: ἆλτο δὲ καὶ Κρονίδης ταναὴν ὑπὲρ αἰθέρα Χείρων,
lines.en: and the Kronid Cheiron too leapt over the lofty aither,
lines.note: Κρονίδης Χείρων = ‘the Kronid Cheiron,’ i.e., Cheiron as son of Kronos (not Zeus here). ταναὴν ὑπὲρ αἰθέρα = ‘over the lofty aither,’ a hyperbolic description of his upward leap.

lines.gr: σευάμενος πρὸς Ὄλυμπον, ἐπεὶ μάθεν ἄμβροτα δῶρα.
lines.en: hastening toward Olympos, when he learned of the immortal gifts.
lines.note: σευάμενος = ‘hastening, rushing.’ ἄμβροτα δῶρα (‘immortal gifts’) likely refers to the same divine gift(s) mentioned earlier.

lines.gr: ἀλλ' ἤτοι κείνους μὲν ἀμώμητοι Διὸς οἶκοι
lines.en: But indeed those men the blameless halls of Zeus—
lines.note: “Blameless halls of Zeus” is a Homeric-style periphrasis for the divine abode (Olympus); the verb is enjambed into the next line, hence the dash in translation.

lines.gr: χαίροντες δέξαντο, θεηγενέων ὄχ' ἀρίστους·
lines.en: —received with rejoicing, by far the best of the god-born.
lines.note: ὄχ’ ἀρίστους is the epic formula “by far the best”; θεηγενέων (“of the god-born”) denotes divinely descended heroes/demigods.

lines.gr: ἡμῖν δ' ἐν γαίῃ κέλεται Χρυσόρραπις ὄλβῳ
lines.en: But for us on earth the Golden‑wanded bids us to live in prosperity,
lines.note: Χρυσόρραπις is the epic epithet “Golden‑wanded,” used of Hermes; κέλεται is a deponent with active sense “bids”; ὄλβῳ is a dative of manner (“in/with prosperity”).

lines.gr: ζώειν τερπομένοισιν ἀπειρήτοις κακότητος.
lines.en: taking delight, unacquainted with wickedness.
lines.note: ἀπειρήτοις κακότητος = “untried/unacquainted with evil,” a dative agreeing with ἡμῖν; τερπομένοις is a dative participle of attendant circumstance (“taking delight”).

lines.gr: ὃν δέ κεν ἀνθρώπων πεπνυμένον ἦτορ ἀνώγῃ
lines.en: And whomsoever among men his prudent heart should bid
lines.note: pepnymenon hētor (“prudent/wise heart”) is a Homeric expression; the construction means “the man whom his own wise heart bids.”

lines.gr: ἐς πολυήρατον ἄντρον ἐσελθέμεν Ἑρμείαο,
lines.en: to enter the much‑beloved cave of Hermês,
lines.note: Hermēíao is the epic genitive “of Hermês”; poluēratos = “much‑beloved, much‑desired.”

lines.gr: ἔνθ' ὅγε παντοίων ἀγαθῶν κατέθηκεν ὅμιλον,
lines.en: where he has laid down a multitude of goods of every sort,
lines.note: The pronoun ho ge (“he indeed”) refers to Hermês; homilos here = “throng/heap/assemblage” of goods.

lines.gr: αἶψά κεν ἀμφοτέρῃσιν ὀνείατα πολλὰ κομίζων
lines.en: straightway he would go, bearing many provisions in both hands,
lines.note: amphoterēisin is the epic dual dative “with both (hands)”; oneiata = “provisions, victuals.”

lines.gr: οἴκαδ' ἀποστείχοι, προφυγὼν πολύδακρυν ὀϊζύν·
lines.en: homeward, having escaped tear‑wet distress;
lines.note: polydakryn oizyn = “tear‑wet distress/woe,” a poetic compound.

lines.gr: οὐδέ ἑ νοῦσος ἄκικυς ἐνὶ μεγάροισι δαμάσσει,
lines.en: nor would an incurable disease subdue him in his halls,
lines.note: ákikus is rare and problematic; generally taken as “incurable” (cf. ἀκήκεστος), hence “a disease without remedy.”

lines.gr: οὐδ' ὕγε δυσμενέων ποθ' ὑποτρέσσας μένος αἰνὸν
lines.en: nor would he ever, cowering at the dread might of enemies,
lines.note: The transmitted ὕγε is doubtful; many take it as a corruption related to φύγε/φυγή (“flight”). Sense: he will not retreat by cowering before enemies. hypotrēssas = “shrinking back, cowering.”

lines.gr: ἂψ ἀναχωρήσει, προλιπὼν ἐριγηθέα νίκην·
lines.en: withdraw back again, leaving exultant victory;
lines.note: erigēthea = “exultant, thrilling (with joy),” of victory; a Homeric epithet.

lines.gr: οὐδέ οἱ ἀθλητῆρι κονισσαμένῳ ἐν ἀγῶνι
lines.en: nor, as an athlete dust‑covered in the contest,
lines.note: athlētēri (dative) “as/for an athlete”; konissamenos = “dust‑covered,” a regular image of wrestlers in the agōn.

lines.gr: ἀντιβίην τινὰ θυμὸς ἐφορμήσει μενεαίνειν,
lines.en: would his spirit impel him to lust for any counter‑violence,
lines.note: antibiēn tina = “(meet) force with counter‑force, any opposing violence”; meneainein = “to be eager/rage for,” of aggressive impulse.

lines.gr: οὐδ' εἰ χάλκεα γυῖα καὶ ἄγναμπτον σθένος ἀνὴρ
lines.en: not even if a man with brazen limbs and unbending strength
lines.note: “Brazen limbs” (chalkea guia) and “unyielding (agnamptos) strength” are hyperbolic epic epithets of a formidable opponent.

lines.gr: ἄντικρυ στεφάνοιο πόθῳ κομίσας ἐριδαίνοι.
lines.en: should confront him outright, eager to carry off the wreath.
lines.note: antikry = “straight on, face‑to‑face”; stephanoio pothōi = “from desire for the wreath”; komisas is used of “carrying off (as a prize).”

lines.gr: ναί μιν καὶ θήρεσσιν ὀρεσκῴοισι λέοντα
lines.en: Aye, him too a lion to the mountain‑haunting beasts,
lines.note: μιν (“him/it”) is an enclitic accusative; its referent is contextually the person empowered by the stone. ὀρεσκώοισι (“mountain‑haunting”) is a Homeric epithet; θήρεσσιν is a dative of respect/advantage: “a lion to/for the beasts.”

lines.gr: δεινὸν καὶ λαοῖσιν ἐοικότα δαίμονι τεύξω.
lines.en: dread, and to the peoples, like a daimon, will I fashion.
lines.note: ἐοικότα (acc. masc. sg.) modifies λέοντα: “resembling a daimon.” δεινόν takes the dative (θήρεσσιν, λαοῖσιν) “dread to [them].” τεύξω is “I will fashion/make,” a common epic verb.

lines.gr: καί οἱ καὶ βασιλεῦσι διοτρεφέεσσιν ὀπάσσω
lines.en: and it also bestows on him, even among Zeus-nurtured kings,
lines.note: ὀπάσσω is transmitted as 1st singular (“I bestow”), but many take the sense as 3rd singular (“it bestows”), sc. the stone; some editors print ὀπάσσει. διοτρεφέεσσιν is the Homeric epithet “Zeus-nurtured,” used of kings; the datives mark the sphere “among” which the honor is granted.

lines.gr: ῥεῖα καὶ ἀλλοδαποῖσι μετ' ἀνθρώποισι τίεσθαι.
lines.en: to be held in honor with ease among foreign men.
lines.note: μετ’ ἀνθρώποισι with ἀλλοδαποῖσι yields “among foreign men.” ῥεῖα modifies τιέσθαι (“to be honored” in the middle/passive). The sense is that the bearer is readily honored even outside his own people.

lines.gr: τὸν δὲ καὶ ἠΐθεοι τερενόχροες ἱμερτῇσιν
lines.en: And him even beardless, tender‑skinned youths, with lovely hands,
lines.note: ἠΐθεοι = unmarried/beardless youths; τερενόχροες = tender‑skinned. ἱμερτῇσιν is best taken with παλάμῃσι (“with lovely hands”), not as a dative of manner (“with desire”).

lines.gr: αἰὲν ἐφορμήσουσι περιπτύσσειν παλάμῃσι,
lines.en: will ever rush to clasp with their palms,
lines.note: Enjambment from the previous line; ἐφορμήσουσι + infinitive expresses “be eager/make a rush to do.” Περιπτύσσειν = “to enfold, embrace, clasp.”

lines.gr: καὶ μαλακὴ χρύσειον ἐπὶ λέχος αἰὲν ἐρύσσει
lines.en: and a soft maiden ever draws him to the golden bed,
lines.note: Μαλακή modifies κούρη (supplied explicitly in the next line). Ἐρύσσει (“draws/drags”) is idiomatic in erotic contexts. Χρύσειον λέχος (“golden bed”) is an epic formula for the luxurious/bridal bed. The understood object “him” refers to the man empowered by the stone.

lines.gr: ἄλληκτον κούρη ἐπιϊεμένη φιλότητος.
lines.en: an unwearied maiden, eager for love.
lines.note: Ἄλληκτον = “unceasing, unwearied” (often “relentless/insatiate” in erotic contexts). Ἐπιϊεμένη (from ἐπιίημι/ἐπείγομαι sense) means “pressing on toward, eager for” love; hence “eager for love.”

lines.gr: εὐχομένου τε πρὸς οὔατ' ἀφίξεται αἰὲν ἐόντων
lines.en: and, as he prays, it will reach the ears of the Ever-Existing Ones,
lines.note: “αἰὲν ἐόντων” (ever-existing) is a Homeric epithet for the gods; εὐχομένου is a genitive absolute, with εὐχή (“prayer”) supplied as the subject in the next line.

lines.gr: εὐχή· καὶ πόντοιο κυκωμένου οὐκ ἀλεγίζων
lines.en: the prayer; and, though the sea is being churned, giving it no heed,
lines.note: εὐχή resumes the subject of ἀφίξεται; πόντοιο κυκωμένου is a genitive absolute (“while the sea is being churned”); οὐκ ἀλεγίζων (“not heeding”) modifies the implied agent who benefits from the stone’s power.

lines.gr: βήσετ' ἐπὶ τραφερὴν χθόν' ἀκυμάντοισι πόδεσσι.
lines.en: he will step upon the dry land with wave-untroubled feet.
lines.note: τραφερὴν χθόνα = “dry/firm land”; ἀκυμάντοισι (from κύμα, “wave”) means “not wave-tossed,” hence “wave-untroubled” feet, expressing safe, unwetted landing.

lines.gr: τὸν καὶ ληϊστῆρες ἀνάρσιοι οἶον ἐόντα
lines.en: Even raiders, savage men, will flee him, though he is alone.
lines.note: τὸν = the bearer/possessor of the stone (from prior context). ληϊστῆρες is the Homeric “raiders/pirates” (from ληίς, “booty”). ἀνάρσιοι = “hard to deal with, unapproachable,” rendered here as “savage.” οἶον ἐόντα is concessive: “though he is alone.”

lines.gr: φεύξονται· καὶ δμῶες ὀϊόμενοι πατέρ' εἶναι
lines.en: and the slaves, supposing him to be their father,
lines.note: δμῶες is Homeric for “household slaves/servants.” ὀϊόμενοι = “supposing.” πατέρ’ εἶναι has apocope for πατέρα εἶναι; the object “him” is understood from context.

lines.gr: τίσουσιν, καὶ οἶκον ἑοῦ στέρξουσιν ἄνακτος.
lines.en: will do him honor, and will love the house of their own lord.
lines.note: τίσουσιν is future of τίω “honor” (not τίνω “pay”), hence “do him honor.” στέργω with οἶκον = “to be fond of, love (one’s) house.” ἑοῦ ἄνακτος = “of their own lord,” i.e., their master.

lines.gr: ἴδμεναι αἴκ' ἐθέλῃσι, δαήσεται, ὅσσα τε φῶτες
lines.en: If he should wish to know, he will learn whatever things men

lines.gr: κρυπτάδια σφετέρῃσιν ἐνὶ φρεσὶ μηχανόωνται,
lines.en: devise in secret within their own minds,
lines.note: κρυπτάδια is a neuter plural used adverbially (“in secret”); μηχανόω “devise, contrive” with φρένες “mind/heart.”

lines.gr: ὅσσα τε κεκλήγασι μετά σφισιν ἠεροφοῖται,
lines.en: and whatever the mist-wanderers have cried out among themselves,
lines.note: ἠεροφοῖται (“mist-/gloom-wanderers”) can in epic denote shades, but here it anticipates οἰωνοί in line 47 and is best taken of birds roaming the murky air; κεκλήγασι (perf.) suggests their cries as an ongoing sign-source.

lines.gr: ἀνθρώποις ἄφραστον ἰακχάζοντες ἀοιδήν,
lines.en: shrieking to mortals a song that may not be uttered,
lines.note: ἰακχάζειν is “to cry/shout,” with possible Bacchic/Mystery resonance (Iacchos); ἄφραστος “unspeakable, ineffable,” often of mysteries, marking birdsong as requiring interpretation.

lines.gr: οἰωνοί, μεγάλοιο Διὸς κραιπνοὶ ὑποφῆται.
lines.en: the birds of omen, swift interpreters of great Dios.
lines.note: οἰωνοί are birds as omens; ὑποφῆται “interpreters/expounders (spokesmen)” of a god; κραιπνοί “swift, nimble.” Διός is transliterated “Dios” per instruction.

lines.gr: ῥοῖζόν τε στῆσαι χαμαὶ ἐρχομένοιο δράκοντος
lines.en: and to still the hiss of a serpent coming along the ground,
lines.note: ῥοῖζον = the hissing/whizzing sound; στῆσαι “to make stand, stop” gives “to still” a noise. χαμαὶ ἐρχομένοιο = “coming along the ground.” δράκων here means a (large) serpent rather than a mythical “dragon.”

lines.gr: εἴσεται, ἠδ' ὄφεων ἰὸν σβέσαι ἑρπυστήρων.
lines.en: he will know, and to quench the venom of creeping serpents.
lines.note: εἴσεται governs both infinitives (στῆσαι, σβέσαι). ἰόν = “venom, poison”; σβέσαι “to quench” is a conventional metaphor for neutralizing poison. ἑρπυστήρων = “crawlers,” here appositional to ὄφεων, i.e., “creeping serpents.”

lines.gr: δώσω οἱ καὶ φῶτα χόλῳ πίπτοντα σελήνης
lines.en: I will grant him also a man falling under Selene’s wrath
lines.note: δώσω οἱ = “I will grant to him” (dative of advantage, scil. the bearer of the stone). φῶτα = epic “man.” χόλῳ σελήνης is best taken as “the wrath of Selene,” i.e., a moon-induced seizure (“falling sickness”).

lines.gr: ῥύσασθαι, καὶ νοῦσον ἀταρτηρὴν ἐλέφαντος·
lines.en: to rescue, and [to free him] from the baneful disease of elephantiasis;
lines.note: ῥύσασθαι is middle “to rescue/deliver,” with the object (the man) carried over from the previous line. νοῦσον ἀταρτηρὴν ἐλέφαντος = “the baneful disease of the elephant,” i.e., elephantiasis (genitive of specification).

lines.gr: καὶ ψυχὴν ἐλάσαι τεθνηότος, ἥ κεν ἐρεμνοῦ
lines.en: and to drive off the soul of a dead man, which, coming forth from murky
lines.note: ἐλάσαι (aor. inf. of ἐλαύνω) = “to drive off.” ψυχὴν τεθνηότος = “the soul of a dead man.” ἐρεμνός = “murky, dark,” modifying Aidēs; προμολοῦσα = “coming forth (up) from.”

lines.gr: ἐξ Ἄϊδος προμολοῦσα ποτιχρίμπτηται ἑκάστῳ.
lines.en: Aidēs, might draw near to each man.
lines.note: ποτιχρίμπτηται is an epic form “might draw near to, press close to” (ποτί + χρίμπτομαι), with potential κεν; Aidēs transliterates Ἄϊδος.

lines.gr: ἄλλαι ἀπειρέσιοι πολυμήτιος Ἑρμείαο
lines.en: Other countless gifts of Hermes of many counsels
lines.note: ἀπειρέσιοι = “countless, boundless” (Homeric). Ἑρμείαο is the epic genitive “of Hermes.” The epithet “of many counsels” renders polymētis, preserving the traditional epic coloring; ἄλλαι (“other”) signals further items in a list.

lines.gr: δωτῖναι κομίσαντος ἐνὶ σπήλυγγι κέονται,
lines.en: are laid away, brought within a cavern,
lines.note: δωτῖναι (“gifts, donations”) is epic-poetic; κέονται is the epic form of κεῖνται “are laid/lie.” κομίσαντος is a genitive participle dependent on Ἑρμείαο, “of Hermes (having) brought [them],” i.e., “brought by Hermes.” σπήλυγξ (dat. σπήλυγγι) is a poetic word for “cavern.”

lines.gr: ἄμβροτοι, ἀτρεκέες, ῥίμφα πρήσσουσαι ἕκαστα·
lines.en: deathless, unerring, swiftly accomplishing each thing;
lines.note: ἄμβροτοι literally “deathless” (often of gods/ambrosia), here of the gifts’ imperishable, divine quality; ἀτρεκέες “exact, unerring.” ῥίμφα “swiftly, nimbly”; πρήσσουσαι “accomplishing, effecting.”

lines.gr: τάων ἡμίθεός τε καὶ ὄλβιος ὅς κ' ἐφίκηται.
lines.en: of these, a demigod and blessed is whoever attains any of them.
lines.note: τάων is a partitive genitive “of these (gifts).” ἐφίκηται (middle subjunctive) with genitive = “reach, obtain.” ἡμίθεος = “demigod,” marking semidivine status for the possessor; ὄλβιος “blessed, fortunate.”

lines.gr: τὰς ἐμὲ κηρύσσειν λαοσσόος Ἀργειφόντης
lines.en: those things for me to proclaim, people‑stirring Argeiphontes
lines.note: τὰς (fem. acc. pl.) likely refers to previously mentioned “powers/virtues” (aretai) of stones; λαοσσόος (“people‑stirring”) is an epithet more common of Ares, here transferred to Hermes (Argeiphontes). ἐμὲ κηρύσσειν is an acc.+inf. construction, fitting Hermes’ role as herald/proclaimer.

lines.gr: ἀνθρώποισιν ὄρινε, μελιγλώσσοιο κελεύσας
lines.en: stirred among mortals, bidding me
lines.note: ἀνθρώποισιν is epic dative “among/for mortals.” ὄρινε (“he stirred/set in motion”) takes its object implicitly from ἐμέ in the previous line. μελιγλώσσοιο modifies φθόγγον in the next line.

lines.gr: φθόγγον ἀπὸ στήθεσφιν ἀοιδῆς γηρύσασθαι.
lines.en: to sound forth from my breast the honey‑tongued voice of song.
lines.note: ἀπὸ στήθεσφιν is epic “from (my) breast(s)” with dative plural; γηρύσασθαι “to voice/utter.” φθόγγον ἀοιδῆς = “the voice/sound of song.”

lines.gr: - Ἀλλ' οὐ πάγχυ βροτοῖσι σαοφροσύνης ἀλεγίζειν
lines.en: But not altogether do mortals have a desire to take thought for sound‑mindedness.
lines.note: “σαοφροσύνης” is the epic form of σωφροσύνης (sōphrosynê, ‘self‑control, prudence’); “ἀλεγίζειν” = ‘to take heed of, care for.’

lines.gr: ἵμερος, αἶψα δέ, πρέσβα, σ' ἀλιτροσύναις ἀτίουσι·
lines.en: Rather, straightway, presba, they dishonor you with transgressions;
lines.note: “πρέσβα” (presba) is vocative ‘aged/ancient one,’ here personifying Sōphrosynê; “ἀλιτροσύναις” (‘transgressions, sins’) and “ἀτιόω” (‘to dishonor’) yield ‘dishonor you with transgressions.’

lines.gr: μητέρα δ' ἡρώων ἀρετὴν ἀπάτερθε κλύοντες
lines.en: and, hearing from their fathers of Arete, mother of heroes,
lines.note: “ἀπάτερθε” is taken as ‘from (one’s) fathers’/‘on the paternal side’; hence ‘hearing from their fathers.’ “Arete, mother of heroes” personifies Virtue as the begetter of heroic status.

lines.gr: προτροπάδην φεύγουσιν, ἀοσσητῆρα δὲ μόχθον,
lines.en: they flee headlong, and unhelping toil,
lines.note: “προτροπάδην” = ‘headlong, precipitately.’ “ἀοσσητῆρα” = ‘unhelping, ineffectual’ (cf. Hesych. ἀοσσήτωρ = ἀβοήθητος). The object of ‘flee’ is both Arete (understood) and ‘toil.’

lines.gr: μόχθον ἀοσσητῆρα βίου μάλα πεφρίκασιν.
lines.en: the unhelping toil of life they greatly shudder at.
lines.note: Perfect πεφρίκασιν (‘they have shuddered’) conveys abiding dread; “βίου” is a subjective/possessive genitive: ‘the unhelping toil of life.’ The repetition of μόχθον ἀοσσητῆρα is emphatic.

lines.gr: οὐδέ σφι κρείων ἐνὶ δώμασιν ὄλβος ὁμιλεῖ,
lines.en: Nor does lordly prosperity keep company with them in their halls,
lines.note: κρείων modifies ὄλβος (“lordly prosperity”). ὁμιλεῖ takes the dative σφι (“with them”) and the locative phrase ἐνὶ δώμασιν (“in their halls”); ὄλβος is “prosperity, blessed fortune,” often personified in epic diction.

lines.gr: οὐδέ τις οἶδε θεοῖς ὀαριζέμεν ἀθανάτοισιν.
lines.en: nor does anyone know to hold intimate converse with the immortal gods.
lines.note: ὀαριζέμεν is the epic infinitive of ὀαρίζω, “to chat, hold intimate talk” (often of lovers); hence “intimate converse.” οἶδε + infinitive = “knows how to …”; θεοῖς ἀθανάτοισιν is the dative plural, “with the immortal gods.”

lines.gr: ἐκ δ' οἵγε πτολίων τε καὶ ἀγρῶν ἤλασαν ἐσθλὴν
lines.en: And they, indeed, drove forth from cities and from fields the noble—
lines.note: οἵγε adds emphatic force (“they indeed”). ἤλασαν (aorist of ἐλαύνω) = “drove out/banished.” ἐσθλὴν modifies σοφίην, which is enjambed into the next line.

lines.gr: ‑ ἆ δειλοί ‑ σοφίην, Ἐριούνιον ὑβρίζοντες.
lines.en: —ah, wretches!—wisdom, committing outrage against Eriounios.
lines.note: ἆ δειλοί is an exclamatory apostrophe (“ah, wretches!”). Ἐριούνιον is the accusative of the Hermes epithet Eriounios; ὑβρίζοντες = “committing hubris/doing outrage” against him. The dashes mark the parenthetical interjection.

lines.gr: ὤλετο δὲ προτέροις πεπονημένον ἡμιθέοισιν
lines.en: And the work wrought by the earlier demigods perished.
lines.note: προτέροις ἡμιθέοισιν: “earlier demigods” evokes the mythic age of heroes; πεπονημένον ἔργον = “work wrought/toiled at,” a common epic collocation. ὤλετο = “has perished/was destroyed,” elevated and formulaic.

lines.gr: ἔργον· ὃ δ' ἀργαλέος καὶ ἀπεχθὴς αὐτίκα πᾶσιν,
lines.en: But he is grievous and hateful straightway to all,
lines.note: ἀργαλέος (“hard to bear, grievous”) and ἀπεχθής (“odious, hateful”) are strong evaluatives suited to didactic invective. The relative construction here is loose; the masculine predicates suggest a human referent.

lines.gr: ᾧ κεν ἐπωνυμίην λαοὶ τεύξωσι μάγοιο.
lines.en: to whom the peoples are wont to confer the by-name of ‘magos’.
lines.note: ἐπωνυμίην (“by-name, epithet, sobriquet”) with τεύξωσι (“fashion, contrive”) and modal κεν expresses customary potential (“are wont to assign”). μάγοιο is the epic genitive of μάγος (“magus, magician”); in Greek usage it often carries a pejorative sense of sorcerer, fitting the characterization as hateful to all. The dative ᾧ (“to whom”) resumes the implied person of line 71.

lines.gr: καί ῥ' ὃ μὲν ἐν κονίῃσιν ὑπ' ἄορι κρατὸς ἀμερθεὶς
lines.en: And he, in the dust, his head cut off beneath the blade,
lines.note: κρατὸς ἀμερθείς = “deprived of the head,” a vivid Homeric-type idiom; ἄορι is “blade/sword,” here instrumental; κονίῃσιν evokes battlefield dust.

lines.gr: λευγαλέῳ θανάτῳ δῖος φὼς ἐκτετάνυσται·
lines.en: lies stretched in baneful death—a godlike man;
lines.note: λευγαλέος means “baneful, deadly” (not ‘white’ like λευκός). δῖος φώς is the epic formula “godlike man.”

lines.gr: οἳ δ' ἴκελοι θήρεσσιν, ἀΐδριες ἠδ' ἀδίδακτοι
lines.en: but others, like beasts, unknowing and untaught,
lines.note: ἴκελοι θήρεσσιν is a conventional simile for brutishness; ἀΐδριες (“unaware”) and ἀδίδακτοι (“untaught”) form a privative pair.

lines.gr: χήτεϊ δαιμονίοιο νοήματος, οὔθ' ὑπ' ἀρωγὴν
lines.en: bereft of daemonic understanding, neither by divine aid
lines.note: χήτει (dative of lack) = “in want/bereft of.” δαιμόνιος here “daemonic” (superhuman, not necessarily ‘divine’ in the theistic sense). ἀρωγή = “aid, succor.”

lines.gr: θεσπεσίην φυγέτην ὀλεσιμβρότου ἐκ κακότητος,
lines.en: know the escape from man‑destroying wickedness,
lines.note: φυγέτην is difficult; many editors prefer φυγήν (“escape”), which suits the syntax with ἴσασι. I translate the sense “escape from man‑destroying wickedness.” ὀλεσιμβρότος = “man‑destroying.”

lines.gr: οὔτε τι θέσκελον ἔργον, ὅ κεν μάλα θαυμάζοιτο,
lines.en: nor any wonder‑work that would be much admired;
lines.note: θέσκελον ἔργον = “wonder‑work,” with connotations of marvel or magical feat in didactic/mantic contexts; ὅ κεν μάλα θαυμάζοιτο = potential, “that would be much marveled at.”

lines.gr: ἴσασ'· ἀλλά σφιν νεφέλη πραπίδεσσι κελαινὴ
lines.en: rather, a black cloud about their wits,
lines.note: πραπίδες = “wits, midriff,” seat of thought; νεφέλη κελαινή is a Homeric image for mental obscuration/delusion.

lines.gr: ἀμφιπεριπλεχθεῖσα βαδιζέμεν ἀνθεμόεντα
lines.en: having twined itself all around, begrudges them the going to the flowery
lines.note: ἀμφιπεριπλεχθεῖσα = “having twined itself all around.” The construction continues to the next line; I render μεγαίρει with an English periphrasis (“begrudges them the going”) to keep the sense.

lines.gr: εἰς ἀρετῆς λειμῶνα πολυστεφάνοιο μεγαίρει.
lines.en: meadow of Virtue, many‑wreathed.
lines.note: μεγαίρειν usually “begrudge, deny.” Here it effectively “bars” them from reaching the “meadow of Virtue.” πολυστεφάνοιο = “many‑wreathed/garlanded,” suiting the ἀνθεμόεις (“flowery”) meadow and evoking moral/allegorical topoi.

lines.gr: ἀλλ' ἐμέθεν στεῦμαι κειμήλια πειθομένοισιν
lines.en: But on my part I solemnly vow treasures to those who hearken
lines.note: στεῦμαι is a solemn epic pledge; κειμήλια are “treasures/heirlooms,” here the valuable lore on stones; πειθομένοις means “those who heed/obey” the instruction.

lines.gr: ἀφνειοῦ χρυσοῖο πολὺ προφερέστερα δείξειν·
lines.en: to show, far more preeminent than rich gold;
lines.note: πολύ προφερέστερα is “far more excellent/preeminent than”; ἀφνειοῦ χρυσοῖο = “rich/opulent gold.” δείξειν depends on στεῦμαι (“I vow to show”).

lines.gr: φῶτα δὲ δίζημαι ταλακάρδιον, ὅς κεν ἑκάστου
lines.en: and I seek a stout‑hearted man, who of each one
lines.note: φῶτα is epic for “man”; ταλακάρδιον = “stalwart-/hardy‑hearted.” ἑκάστου has an understood object (sc. “stone”), supplied by the broader Lithica context. ὅς κεν introduces a potential relative clause.

lines.gr: ἐμμεμαὼς πειρῷτο, μενοινήσαι τε, κάμοι τε,
lines.en: would eagerly make trial, be intent on it, and labor,
lines.note: ἐμμεμαώς (“eager/zealous,” from μέμαα), πειρῷτο (“make trial”), μενοινήσαι (“be intent, eagerly desire”), κάμοι (“labor, toil”) pile up the ideal pupil’s experimental zeal.

lines.gr: ὅς τε διδάσκηται, καὶ ὃς εἰδότας ἐξερεείνῃ.
lines.en: who is teachable, and who would question those who know.
lines.note: ὅς τε … καὶ ὃς … is correlative (“both … and …”): the desired man is both teachable and inquisitive. διδάσκηται and ἐξερεείνῃ (epic ‘question closely’) show some mood variation in the sequence but convey the general requirement.

lines.gr: οὐ γὰρ ἄτερ καμάτοιο τέλος μύθοισι καὶ ἔργοις
lines.en: For not without toil an end to words and to deeds
lines.note: telos here means ‘fulfilment/consummation’; muthois kai ergois is the traditional pairing ‘words and deeds’ (utterance and practice) in didactic style.

lines.gr: εὐρύοπα Κρονίδης ἐθέλει δόμεν· ἀλλὰ καὶ αὐτὸν
lines.en: is the wide-seeing Kronides minded to grant; but even him,
lines.note: Euryopa (‘wide-seeing’) is a conventional epithet of Zeus; Kronides = ‘son of Kronos’ (Zeus). The verb ethelei domen = ‘is willing/minded to grant.’ The object resumed by “auton” is clarified appositively in the next lines.

lines.gr: ἐς δύσιν ἀσθμαίνοντες ἀν' αἰθέρα λαμπετόωσαν
lines.en: toward the west, panting, through the blazing aether,
lines.note: The phrase an’ aithera lampe‑ is formulaic (‘through the gleaming/blazing aether’). The transmitted lampe-toōsan is difficult; many editors take it with aither (‘blazing’) or emend toward lampe-toenta (sc. of Helios). I translate the sense ‘through the blazing aether.’

lines.gr: Ἠέλιον φαέθοντα σὺν ἅρματι πῶλοι ἄγουσι.
lines.en: the colts lead—shining Helios—together with his chariot.
lines.note: Pōloi (‘colts’) are the Sun’s steeds; agousi ‘lead/draw.’ Hēelion phae-thonta = ‘shining Helios’ (phaethon as an epithet). The pronoun in the previous line is resolved by the apposition here.

lines.en: [lacuna]
lines.note: The verse is not extant: editors print an ellipsis (. . . .) to mark a gap in the tradition at this point, and no secure reconstruction can be offered.

lines.gr: Μᾶλλον ἐγὼ πινυτοῖο παραίφασιν ἀνέρος εὑρὼν
lines.en: I shall take greater delight, on finding the counsel of a prudent man,
lines.note: paráiphasis (παραίφασιν) is an epic term for “advice/counsel” (often a whispered prompting or admonition); pinytoios anēr (πινυτοῖο ἀνέρος) conveys Homeric “prudent, sensible” rather than merely “clever.” The participle heurōn (εὑρών) is temporal (“on finding”).

lines.gr: τέρψομαι, ἤπερ χρυσὸν ἁπάντων κοίρανον ἀνδρῶν.
lines.en: than in gold, the lord of all men.
lines.note: Koíranos (κοίρανος) is a Homeric “lord/chieftain”; applied appositively to gold it personifies gold as ruler over all men, a gnomic hyperbole. The comparative structure μᾶλλον … ἤπερ spans the two lines (“more … than”).

lines.gr: Ἠελίῳ γὰρ ἄγων ἱερήιον ἀντεβόλησα
lines.en: For I came face to face with him as he was leading a sacrificial victim for Hêlios,
lines.note: ἱερήιον = “sacrificial victim/beast”; Hêlios is transliterated as requested. ἀντεβόλησα = “I met/encountered,” epic-poetic.

lines.gr: ἀγρόθεν ἄστυδ' ἰόντι περίφρονι Θειοδάμαντι·
lines.en: going from the countryside to the city, Theiodamas the shrewd;
lines.note: περίφρων = a standard epic epithet, “shrewd, very prudent.” ἀγρόθεν ἄστυδε = “from country to city.”

lines.gr: καί μιν ἑλὼν χερὶ χεῖρα προσηύδων ὧδ' ἐπέεσσιν·
lines.en: and, taking his hand in mine, I addressed him with these words:
lines.note: Homeric formula: “taking his hand in mine” (χερὶ χεῖρα ἑλών).

lines.gr: - Ἐς πόλιν, εἰ μὴ πάμπαν ἐπισπέρχωσιν ἀνάγκαι,
lines.en: “To the city—unless urgent necessities press you utterly—
lines.note: πάμπαν intensifies “utterly, completely”; ἐπισπέρχωσιν = “press hard, drive urgently.”

lines.gr: ῥηιδίως σοι, ἑταῖρε, καὶ αὔριον ἔσσεθ' ἱκέσθαι·
lines.en: it will be easy for you, comrade, to arrive even tomorrow;
lines.note: ἔσσεθ’ = ἔσσεται with elision before ἱκέσθαι: “it will be [easy] for you to arrive.” ἑταῖρε = “comrade.”

lines.gr: νῦν δέ σέ μοι στείχοντι μετ' εἰλαπίνην θεὸς αὐτὸς
lines.en: but now, as I am going on my way to a banquet, a god himself
lines.note: μετ’ εἰλαπίνην with acc. = “in pursuit of, on the way to a banquet,” not “after” temporally here. θεὸς αὐτὸς ὦρσεν = “a god himself has stirred [you].”

lines.gr: ὦρσεν ὑπαντιάσαι· τῷ μοι πρόφρων ἐπίνευσον
lines.en: has stirred you to come meet me; to this kindly nod assent,
lines.note: πρόφρων = “willing, gracious”; ἐπίνευσον = “nod assent, agree.”

lines.gr: ἕσπεσθαι. θυσίαι δ' ἱεροπρεπέες τελέθουσιν,
lines.en: to follow. And sacrifices befitting the sacred are underway,
lines.note: τελέθουσιν = “are afoot/underway, come to pass.” ἱεροπρεπέες = “befitting the sacred/holy.”

lines.gr: ἃς ἀγαθοὶ ῥέζουσι βροτοί· γάνυται δὲ φίλον κῆρ
lines.en: which good mortals perform; and the dear heart rejoices
lines.note: ῥέζουσι = epic for “perform (sacrifice/rites).” γάνυται φίλον κῆρ = Homeric “the dear heart rejoices.”

lines.gr: ἀθανάτων, εὖτ' ἄν σφι χοροὺς ἀνάγωσιν ἄριστοι.
lines.en: of the Immortals, whenever the best lead choruses for them.”
lines.note: ἀθανάτων = “of the Immortals” (the gods). χοροὺς ἀνάγωσιν = “lead/set the choruses in motion”; σφι = “for them,” i.e., for the gods.

lines.gr: ἄξω δ' οὐ μακρὴν ἐς ἀταρπιτόν· εἰσοράᾳς γὰρ
lines.en: I shall lead you by no long bypath; for you see
lines.note: ἀταρπιτόν: a problematic form; likely the epic/Ionic variant of ἀτραπός/ἀταρπός (“bypath, short-cut”). Hence “no long bypath” = “a short way.” ἄξω is future of ἄγω (“I shall lead”), with the object (you) understood; εἰσορᾷς = “you see.”

lines.gr: ἡμετέρων με κιόντα πρὸς ἀγρῶν ἀκρώρειαν.
lines.en: me going toward the ridge of our fields.
lines.note: με κιόντα is the object plus participle construction after εἰσορᾷς: “you see me going.” ἀκρώρεια denotes a ridge or upland, here “the ridge of our fields.”

lines.gr: ἔνθα νεογνὸς ἐὼν ἔτλην ποτὲ μοῦνος ἀνελθεῖν,
lines.en: There, being newborn, once I dared to go up alone,
lines.note: νεογνός can shade “new‑hatched,” suiting the avian scene; ἀνελθεῖν = “go up/approach.”

lines.gr: λαιψηρὼ πέρδικε μετασπόμενος προφυγόντε·
lines.en: following after the two nimble partridges that had fled ahead;
lines.note: λαιψηρὼ πέρδικε and προφυγόντε are dual forms (“two nimble partridges,” “the two having fled ahead”); μετασπόμενος = “following after (in pursuit).”

lines.gr: οἳ δ' ἤτοι εἵως μὲν ἀκούων οὔνομ' ἕκαστος
lines.en: and they—indeed, so long as each, on hearing its name,
lines.note: εἵως is an epic form of ἕως (“so long as”); “name” implies trained/accustomed birds responding to calls.

lines.gr: ἱστάμενος μίμνασκεν, ὀρεξάμενον δὲ δοκεύσας,
lines.en: standing, would keep waiting; but, having spied me reaching out,
lines.note: δοκεύσας (“having watched/spied”) takes ὀρεξάμενον (“[me] reaching out,” sc. the hand) as its object; the subject is each bird.

lines.gr: πρὶν μάρψαι χείρεσσιν, ἀλυσκάζων προφύγεσκεν.
lines.en: before I could snatch with my hands, dodging, it would keep escaping ahead.
lines.note: μάρψαι = “seize/snatch”; ἀλυσκάζων = “dodging/shunning.” The -σκ- in μίμνασκεν and προφυγέσκεν marks iterative/habitual action.

lines.gr: αὐτὰρ ἐγὼ σπουδῇ κεν ἐπὶ στόμα κάππεσον ἐλθών·
lines.en: But I, in haste, would fall upon its mouth when I came near;
lines.note: κάππεσον is an epic form for κατέπεσον (“I fell upon”); κεν marks a potential (“would”). ἐπὶ στόμα (“upon the mouth”) hints at a kiss; in the magnet/iron context of the Lithica, the speaking “I” is the iron personified, rushing to the Μαγνῆτις λίθος as to a beloved.

lines.gr: ἂψ δ' αὖτις γαίηθεν ἀναΐξας ἐδίωκον.
lines.en: and back again, springing up from the earth, I kept pursuing.
lines.note: ἂψ δ’ αὖτις is a formulaic “back again, once more.” γαίηθεν is the epic ablatival “from the earth,” and ἀναΐξας means “leaping/springing up.” The imperfect ἐδίωκον conveys repeated pursuit.

lines.gr: ἀλλ' ὅτε δὴ κορυφήνδε μετασπόμενος κίον ἄκρην,
lines.en: But when indeed, pressing on toward the ridge, he went to the topmost peak,
lines.note: μετασπόμενος (from metaspomai) can mean “following after, pursuing”; the participle is used adverbially. κίον is the epic aorist of kiō (“he went”).

lines.gr: οἳ μὲν ἄρ' ἐξαπίνης ἰαχὴν ὀξεῖαν ὀρόντε
lines.en: then they, all of a sudden, raised a shrill shout,
lines.note: ὀρόντε is difficult; it is best taken as a participle of ὄρνυμι (“to raise”), i.e., “raising a cry.” Some have taken it as ὁρῶντες (“seeing”), which yields the strained “seeing a cry.” ἐξαπίνης = “suddenly.”

lines.gr: αἰγανέης ἔσσυντο θοώτερον ἠὲ βελέμνου
lines.en: and they rushed swifter than a boar-spear or a dart
lines.note: αἰγανέη is a boar-spear (with a crossbar); βέλεμνον is a dart/javelin. ἔσσυντο = “they sped/rushed.”

lines.gr: ὑψίκομον ποτὶ φηγὸν, ἐπεσσύμενον προϊδόντε
lines.en: toward the lofty-leaved oak, having seen beforehand a dread serpent charging against it,
lines.note: ὑψίκομος (“high-tressed”) is a standard tree-epithet meaning thick- or high-foliaged. φηγός is rendered “oak” (epic usage), though sometimes “beech.” προϊδόντες = “having seen beforehand”; ἐπεσσύμενον = “charging (against).”

lines.gr: αἰνὸν ὄφιν πετάσαντα γένυν πλείην θανάτοιο.
lines.en: its jaw flung wide, full of death.
lines.note: πετάσαντα γένυν = “having spread/flung (its) jaw.” πλείην θανάτοιο (“full of death”) is a traditional epic phrase meaning deadly.

lines.gr: τὸν δ' ἐγὼ ἐγχριμφθεὶς ὑπεναντίον ἀΐξαντα
lines.en: But I, having drawn near, did not see him as he darted head-on against me;
lines.note: ἐγχριμφθείς is the aorist passive participle of ἐγχρίμπτω “to draw near, approach”; ὑπεναντίον is adverbial “straight against, head‑on”; ἀΐξαντα is the aorist participle of ἀΐσσω “to dart, rush.” The object (τὸν) is the hostile creature previously in view (likely a serpent).

lines.gr: οὐκ ἴδον· ὀφθαλμοὶ δέ μοι ὀρνίθων λελίηντο·
lines.en: my eyes had been turned aside by the birds;
lines.note: λελίηντο is best taken as a rare/perfect middle of λιάζω “to turn aside,” hence “my eyes were averted/distracted”; the genitive ὀρνίθων is a genitive of cause/object of attention (“by/toward the birds”). The form is unusual and has prompted emendation in some discussions, but the sense “were turned aside” suits the context.

lines.gr: πρίν περ ἀναστήσαντος ἀπὸ χθονὸς αὐχένα δεινὸν
lines.en: until, when he had lifted from the earth his dread neck,
lines.note: πρίν περ with the genitive absolute (ἀναστήσαντος …) after a negation (“I did not see …”) conveys “not until.” δεινὸν αὐχένα evokes a rearing, dangerous neck (serpentine imagery).

lines.gr: ἐφρασάμην ἤδη τε δέμας μεμαῶτα λαφύξαι.
lines.en: I realized his frame already eager to snatch its prey.
lines.note: ἐφρασάμην (middle) “I perceived/realized”; δέμας “body, frame”; μεμαῶτα (perf. part. of μέμαα) “eager, impetuous”; λαφύξαι (aor. inf. of λαφύσσω) “to snatch as spoil,” here idiomatically “to seize its prey.”

lines.gr: ἔνθ' εἴ τις σπεύδοντα παλίσσυτον εἰσενόησεν,
lines.en: There, if anyone observed me rushing back,
lines.note: παλίσσυτον (literally “rushing back/again”) is used adverbially with σπεύδοντα; it can suggest a backward or repeated motion (“back and forth”). εἰσενόησεν = “noticed, perceived.”

lines.gr: οὔτε με περδίκεσσιν ἀελλοπόδεσσιν ἕπεσθαι,
lines.en: neither that I was following after the storm‑footed partridges,
lines.note: ἕπομαι governs the dative (περδίκεσσιν); ἀελλοπόδεσσιν (“storm‑footed,” lit. “gale‑footed”) is an epic epithet transferred here to partridges, marking swift movement.

lines.gr: οὔτε με νηπιάχοισιν ὀΐσατο ποσσὶ φέρεσθαι.
lines.en: nor did he suppose that I was being borne on childish feet.
lines.note: ὀΐσατο = aorist of οἴομαι (“suppose, think”). φέρεσθαι ποσσί is an idiom “to be borne on the feet” = “to run.” νηπιάχοισιν (“childish, infant‑like”) emphasizes that the motion is not that of a child.

lines.gr: κέκλετο γάρ μοι δεῖμα τανύπτερον αἰετὸν εἶναι,
lines.en: For I had taken the fearful sign to be a long‑winged eagle,
lines.note: Line 125: κέκλετο is the pluperfect middle/passive of καλέω (“be called/named”), used with a dative of agent (μοι); rendering as “I had taken … to be” conveys the quasi‑active sense. δεῖμα can denote a terrifying apparition or portent. τανύπτερος is an epic epithet meaning “long‑winged,” here of the eagle (αἰετός).

lines.gr: καὶ πνοιὴν ἀνέμου, παρὰ γὰρ ποσσὶν κακὸν ἦεν.
lines.en: and a breath of wind as well; for there was a bane at my feet.
lines.note: Line 126: πνοιὴ ἀνέμου is literally “breath of wind,” i.e., a gust. παρὰ ποσσίν is “at (one’s) feet,” the possessive understood from context; ἦεν is the epic form of ἦν (“was”).

lines.gr: πολλάκι δ' εἵματος ἄκρου ἐπιψαύεσκεν ἀκωκαῖς·
lines.en: and often it kept grazing the hem of my cloak with its points;
lines.note: ἐπιψαύεσκεν is iterative (“kept touching/grazing”); εἵματος ἄκρου is the garment’s edge/hem. ἀκωκαῖς (“points, sharp tips”) is instrumental; in context it can suggest teeth or claws without specifying which.

lines.gr: καί κεν ὑπὲρ μοῖράν με πελώριος ἀμφέχανεν θήρ,
lines.en: and a monstrous beast would have gaped over me beyond my destined lot,
lines.note: κεν with the imperfect gives a past potential (“would have”); ὑπὲρ μοῖραν is an idiom “beyond/contrary to fate,” i.e., before one’s time. ἀμφέχανεν means “opened (its jaws) over, gaped over.”

lines.gr: εἰ μή μοι νόος ὦρτο θοῶς ἐπὶ βωμὸν ὀροῦσαι,
lines.en: had not my mind swiftly arisen, rushing toward the altar,
lines.note: νόος ὦρτο = “my mind arose/was roused.” The participle ὀροῦσαι (“rushing”) is problematic in form; many take it as adverbial (“rushing toward the altar”) and some emend to ὀρούσῃ to smooth agreement.

lines.gr: τόν ῥα παλαιότεροι Φαεσιμβρότῳ ἱδρύσαντο.
lines.en: the one which the men of old established for Phaesimbrotos.
lines.note: Φαεσιμβρότῳ (“Phaesimbrotos,” ‘light-bringing-to-mortals’) is treated as a theonym/epithet; likely refers to Helios (or occasionally Apollo) in Orphic diction. ἱδρύσαντο (mid.) “set up, established” of founding an altar.

lines.gr: τῷ δ' ἄρ' ἔπι τρύφος αὖον ἐλαϊνέης ἐλέλειπτο
lines.en: And upon it there had been left a dry scurf from an olive-wood splinter,
lines.note: τρύφος is rare; many emend to τύφος (“soot, smoke”). I render “scurf”/“residue” to suit either reading. ἐλαϊνέης σχίζης = “of an olive-wood splinter.”

lines.gr: σχίζης, ἥν τε μαρανθὲν ἀδηφάγον ἐξέλιπεν πῦρ.
lines.en: which the all-devouring fire, once quenched, abandoned.
lines.note: μαρανθέν is neut. nom. sg. agreeing with πῦρ (“once the fire was quenched”). ἐξέλιπεν is transitive here (“abandoned/left behind”), with ἥν referring to σχίζην. The deliberate echo with ἐλέλειπτο (“had been left”) preserves the Greek’s diction.

lines.gr: τὴν ἐγὼ ἁρπάξας ὀλοοῦ κατένωπα δράκοντος
lines.en: Having snatched it, I turned to face the baneful serpent.
lines.note: ‘τὴν’ likely refers to the stone at issue in the Lithica; κατένωπα is an adverb, ‘face to face, opposite’; ὀλοοῦ = ‘baneful, deadly’; δράκων = ‘serpent/dragon.’

lines.gr: ἐστρέφθην. μαίμησε δ' ὀρεσκῴου μένος αἰνὸν
lines.en: And the terrible might of the mountain-roamer raged to fight, seeing me eager.
lines.note: μαίμησε is the epic aorist of μαιμάω (‘be eager, rage for’); μένος (‘might’) is the grammatical subject. ὀρεσκῴος = ‘mountain-roaming/dwelling’ (elsewhere an epithet of Pan), here transferred to the serpent’s ‘might.’ μεμαῶτα (‘eager’) is the object-complement: ‘seeing me eager.’

lines.gr: μάρνασθαι, μεμαῶτα ἰδών. εἱλεῖτο δὲ πυκνῶς,
lines.en: It kept coiling tightly,
lines.note: εἱλεῖτο is middle (‘coiled itself’); πυκνῶς = ‘closely/tightly.’

lines.gr: γνάμπτων εὐκύκλως ταναὴν ῥάχιν· αὐτὰρ ἐπ' ἄλλῳ
lines.en: bending its long back in well-rounded curves; but upon one [coil] another,
lines.note: γνάμπτων ‘bending/curving’; εὐκύκλως ‘in fair/well-rounded circles’; ταναὴν ῥάχιν ‘long back.’ The understood object of ἐπ’ ἄλλῳ ἄλλος is ‘[coil] upon [coil],’ supplied in translation.

lines.gr: ἄλλος, ἔπειτα δέ τ' ἄλλος ἑλισσομένου τροχὸς ἦεν·
lines.en: and then yet another—like the whirling of a rolling wheel;
lines.note: ἑλισσομένου τροχὸς ἦεν is an elliptical simile: literally ‘it was a wheel in its whirling/rolling,’ i.e., ‘like a wheel whirling.’

lines.gr: ἠδ' ἔτι καὶ βωμοῦ ὕπερ αὐχένας ἠέρταζε
lines.en: and even above the altar it was lifting its neck(s) aloft,
lines.note: ἠέρταζε is a rare epic verb ‘was lifting/brandishing aloft.’ αὐχένας in the plural may be a poetic plural for the serpent’s neck or for multiple arched loops; ὕπερ βωμοῦ underscores a cultic/ritual setting.

lines.gr: συρίζων βοόωντος ἐμῆς πολὺ μεῖζον ἀϋτῆς.
lines.en: hissing far louder than my own shouting.
lines.note: συρίζων (‘hissing,’ lit. ‘piping’) is onomatopoetic. πολὺ μεῖζον with the genitive ἐμῆς ἀϋτῆς (‘of my shout’) expresses comparison; βοόωντος is a participle agreeing with ἀϋτῆς (‘my shouting’).

lines.gr: καὶ τύπτων ἄρρηκτον ὀρεσκῴοιο κάρηνον
lines.en: and, striking the unbreakable brow of the mountain‑dwelling crag,
lines.note: ὀρεσκῴοιο (gen. of ὀρεσκώιος, “mountain‑haunting/ranging”) is taken with κάρηνον (“brow, crest”) to mean the brow of a crag or rocky outcrop; ἄρρηκτον = “unbreakable, very hard.” The participle τύπτων suggests quarrying/striking the rock.

lines.gr: ἀμφ' αὐτῷ θραύεσκον ὑπέκπυρον ὄζον ἄκικυν·
lines.en: about it they would keep breaking off the calcined nodule of Akikē (agate);
lines.note: θραύεσκον is iterative (“they kept shattering”); ὑπέκπυρον = “fired from beneath/calcined,” a mining technique for fracturing rock. ὄζος here = “nodule/lump.” ἄκικυν is a lapidary term for agate (Akikē), likely from Semitic/Arabic ʿaqīq; many editors compare/replace with ἀχάτην (“agate”).

lines.gr: οὐδ' ἄρα μόρσιμος ἦα δαφοινῷ θηρὶ δαμῆναι.
lines.en: nor then was he fated to be subdued by the tawny beast.
lines.note: ἦα is epic for ἦν (“was”); the subject is generic (“he/one” using the stone). δαφοινός = “tawny/blood‑red,” a conventional epithet of the lion; θήρ = “beast.” The line attributes protective power against a lion to the Akikē stone.

lines.gr: τοὔνεκεν αἰπολίοισιν ἀπόπροθι βοσκομένοισιν
lines.en: Therefore, while the goatherds were pasturing at a distance,
lines.note: αἰπολίοισιν … βοσκομένοισιν is an epic dative of attendant circumstance (“while the goatherds were pasturing”); ἀπόπροθι functions adverbially “at a distance.”

lines.gr: ἑσπομένω δύο πατρὸς ἐμοῦ κύνε κεκλήγοντα
lines.en: two dogs of my father, barking as they followed after me,
lines.note: κύνε is dual nominative/accusative of κύων (“dogs”), and ἐπεδραμέτην (line 145) is dual aorist (“the two … ran up”). ἑσπομένω is the dative singular participle of ἕπομαι (“follow”), which governs the dative of the person followed; the understood object is “me,” hence “as they followed after me.” κεκλήγοντα (perf. part. of κλάζω) is used of loud animal cries here “barking.”

lines.gr: γνόντες ἐπεδραμέτην· μάλα γάρ σφισι μείλιχος ἔσκον.
lines.en: having recognized me, ran up; for I was very gentle to them.
lines.note: γνόντες (“having recognized”) has an implied object (“me”). μείλιχος means “gentle/soothing,” a term with appeasing connotations; ἔσκον is the epic iterative/imperfect (“I was/used to be”). σφισι = “to them.”

lines.gr: οἳ μὲν ἄρ' ὑλάσσοντες ἐπέδραμον· αὐτὰρ ὅγ' αἶψα
lines.en: They, baying, rushed upon him; but he straightway
lines.note: ὑλάσσειν (“to bay”) marks them as hounds; ἐπέδραμον = “charged, rushed upon.”

lines.gr: ἀντίον ἔσσυτο τοῖϊν· ἐγὼ δ' ἐς γαῖαν ὀρούσας
lines.en: sped to face the pair; and I, leaping to the earth
lines.note: τοῖϊν is the dative dual, “the pair,” highlighting two attackers singled out; ἔσσυτο = “rushed.”

lines.gr: προτροπάδην, ὥς τίς τε Διὸς γαμψώνυχα φεύγων
lines.en: headlong, as when some hare, fleeing the hook‑clawed Eagle of Zeus,
lines.note: γαμψώνυχα (“hook‑clawed”) is an epic epithet; Διὸς αἰετός = “Eagle of Zeus.”

lines.gr: αἰετὸν ἐν πυκινοῖσι λάθῃ θάμνοισι λαγωός,
lines.en: hides in the dense thickets, a hare,
lines.note: λαθῇ is aorist subjunctive in a vivid generalizing simile; λαγωός is the poetic form for “hare.”

lines.gr: τῷ ἴκελος μήλοισι μιγεὶς ὀλοοῦ ἀπὸ θηρὸς
lines.en: even so, like him, mingling with the flocks, away from the deadly beast,
lines.note: μήλοισι = “flocks” (sheep/goats), not “apples”; ἴκελος = “like to”; ὀλοός = “baneful, deadly.”

lines.gr: ἐκρύφθην, μέσσοισιν ἐνὶ πτήξας ἐρίφοισιν.
lines.en: I hid, cowering in the midst among the kids.
lines.note: πτήσσω = “to cower, crouch” (esp. of prey); ἐρίφοι = “kids” (young goats).

lines.gr: ὄφρα μὲν οὖν ἀκάκητα πατὴρ ἐμέθεν ζώεσκεν,
lines.en: So long then as my father lived, unscathed,
lines.note: ἀκάκητα is adverbial (“without harm, unscathed”); ἐμέθεν is epic for “of me,” i.e., “my”; ζώεσκεν is iterative (“was wont to live”).

lines.gr: αἰεὶ μόσχον ἄγεσκεν ἐμὸν πρὸς ἀμύντορα βωμόν,
lines.en: ever would he bring my calf to the warding altar,
lines.note: ἄγεσκεν is iterative (“would bring habitually”); ἀμύντορα (“warding, defending”) marks the altar as apotropaic; ἐμὸν modifies μόσχον (“my calf”).

lines.gr: τίνων Ἠελίῳ ζωάγρια παιδὸς ἑοῖο·
lines.en: paying to Hēlios the life‑ransom for his own child;
lines.note: τίνων is the participle of τίνω (“pay”), not an interrogative: “paying life‑ransom”; ζωάγρια are propitiatory offerings given “for the saving of life”; Hēlios is the recipient.

lines.gr: αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ μοῖραί μιν ἀπήγαγον ἠελίοιο,
lines.en: but when the Moirai led him away from the sun,
lines.note: A set phrase: the Moirai “led him away from the sun” (ἀπ’ ἠελίοιο) = “to death.”

lines.gr: αὐτὸς ἐγὼν ἀγέληθεν ἐλάσσας πίονα μόσχον
lines.en: I myself, driving from the herd a fat calf,
lines.note: ἀγέληθεν (“from the herd”) with the ablatival suffix ‑θεν; πίονα (“fat, rich”).

lines.gr: εἰαρινόν, θαλέθοντα νεήνιδος οὔθατι μητρός,
lines.en: spring‑born, thriving at the udder of its youthful mother,
lines.note: εἰαρινόν (“spring‑born”); θαλέθοντα (“flourishing”); οὔθατι is the dative of οὖθαρ (“udder”); νεήνιδος (“of a youthful [mother]”), here of a heifer.

lines.gr: ἔρχομ' ἐς ἀκρώρειαν, ἄγων χορὸν ἡδὺν ἑταίρων·
lines.en: I go to the ridge‑top, leading a sweet chorus of companions;
lines.note: ἀκρώρεια (“mountain ridge, height”); χορὸν ἡδύν suggests a festive, processional “chorus/band.”

lines.gr: σὺν δέ σφιν καὶ τώδε δρακοντοφόνω κύνε βήτην
lines.en: and with them went likewise these two serpent‑slaying dogs
lines.note: Dual forms: τώδε … βήτην (= “these two … went”); κύνες here functions as dual; δρακοντοφόνος = “serpent‑slaying.”

lines.gr: αὐτομάτω· γλυκερὴ δὲ πέλει περὶ βωμὸν ἄνακτος
lines.en: of their own accord; and sweet delight abides about the lord’s altar,
lines.note: αὐτομάτω (“of their own accord,” dual/adverbial); ἄναξ (“lord”) likely refers to Hēlios; τερπωλή = “delight, festivity”;πέλει = archaic “is.”

lines.gr: τερπωλή, χλοερόν τε πέδον, μαλακαί τ' ἔπι ποῖαι,
lines.en: delight—the ground is green, and soft grasses upon it,
lines.note: χλοερὸν πἐδον = “green sward”; the clause continues the scene of festal pleasantness around the altar.

lines.gr: καὶ λασίαις πτελέῃσιν ὕπο σκιή· ἄγχι δ' ἄρ' αὐτῶν
lines.en: and shade beneath shaggy elms; and close by them
lines.note: λασίαις (“shaggy, densely leafed”) of trees; πτελέαι = elms; note pastoral shading of the sacred site.

lines.gr: ὕδωρ ἀέναον λισσῆς ὑπὸ πυθμένι πέτρης
lines.en: water ever‑flowing, beneath the base of a smooth rock,
lines.note: ἀέναον (“ever‑flowing”); λισσῆς (“smooth, polished”); πυθμήν (“base, foot”) of the rock.

lines.gr: λευκὸν ἀναβλύζον κελαρύζεται εἴκελον ᾠδῇ.
lines.en: gushing up white, it babbles, like to a song.
lines.note: κελαρύζεται (“babbles, gurgles,” onomatopoetic); λευκὸν ἀναβλύζον (“spouting up white”); εἴκελον ᾠδῇ (“like to a song”).

lines.gr: ἴομεν· οὔτοι δαῖτα θεῶν θέμις ἀρνήσασθαι.
lines.en: Let us go; for it is by no means right to refuse the gods’ feast.
lines.note: ἴομεν is hortatory (“let us go”); οὔτοι adds emphatic denial (“by no means”). θέμις is the impersonal epic idiom for what is divinely sanctioned (“right, lawful”), not the goddess Themis here. δαῖτα θεῶν (“the gods’ feast”) is a formulaic epic phrase referring to a sacrificial banquet; ἀρνήσασθαι is the aorist middle infinitive “to refuse.”

lines.gr: - Ὣς ἐφάμην. ὃ δέ μ' ὧδε προσηύδα δαιμόνιος φώς·
lines.en: Thus I spoke; and the daemonic man addressed me thus:
lines.note: δαιμόνιος φώς: literally “daemonic/man of the daimon,” Homeric φώς = ‘man, person’; the phrase suggests a numinous/uncanny figure rather than a mere mortal.

lines.gr: Ἀλλά σε μὲν κρείων Φαεσίμβροτος ἐξ ἀλεγεινῆς
lines.en: But as for you, may lord Phaesímbrotos ever lead you out of grievous misery,
lines.note: κρείων = ‘lord’; Φαεσίμβροτος (‘Bringer-of-light-to-mortals’) is likely an epithet used as a theonym for Hēlios. ἄγοι is benedictive optative (“may he lead”). ἀλεγεινῆς κακότητος = ‘painful/grievous misery.’

lines.gr: αἰὲν ἄγοι κακότητος, ἀδακρύτοιό τε πέμποι
lines.en: and may he send you,
lines.note: ἀδακρύτοιό is genitive and modifies ὄλβου in the next line (“of tearless wealth”); πέμποι is another benedictive optative (“may he send”).

lines.gr: ὄλβου πρὸς μέγα δῶμα φιλοφροσύνης ἕνεκα σφῆς.
lines.en: to the great house of tearless wealth, for the sake of his own goodwill.
lines.note: ὄλβου πρὸς μέγα δῶμα = “to the great house of wealth,” i.e., to a household of prosperity (the genitive is descriptive). σφῆς is Homeric reflexive genitive = “his own.” φιλοφροσύνη = ‘kindly disposition, goodwill.’

lines.gr: οὐδὲ μὲν οὐδέ σ' ἐγώ περ ἀμοιβῆς αὐτὸς ἀμέρσω·
lines.en: Nor indeed will I myself deprive you of recompense.
lines.note: ἀμέρσω is the future of ἀμέρδω “deprive,” governing the genitive ἀμοιβῆς (“recompense, return”); the clustering of particles (οὐδὲ μὲν οὐδέ … περ … αὐτός) heightens the speaker’s emphatic assurance.

lines.gr: ἀλλ' ἐπεὶ οὖν ἄξων ἱερήϊον εἰσαναβαίνεις,
lines.en: But since, then, you go up to lead in a sacrificial victim,
lines.note: ἄξων is the future participle of ἄγω (“about to lead”), not the noun ἄξων (“axle”); ἱερήϊον is the epic form of ἱερεῖον (“sacrificial victim”); εἰσαναβαίνειν suggests ascending into the sanctuary (the place is implicit).

lines.gr: ὄφρα τοι εὐχομένοιο κλύοι θεός, ἐγγυαλίξω.
lines.en: so that, as you pray, the god may hear, I will put it into your hand.
lines.note: ὄφρα + optative (κλύοι) expresses desired purpose (“so that … may hear”); εὐχομένου is genitive absolute (“as you pray”); ἐγγυαλίζω literally “to put in the palm,” here figuratively “to impart/provide (the needed means/instruction).”

lines.gr: - Κρύσταλλον φαέθοντα διαυγέα λάζεο χερσὶ
lines.en: Take up in your hands the crystal, the radiant, transparent stone,
lines.note: κρύσταλλον = rock crystal; λάζεο (middle imperative) “take for yourself.” φαέθοντα/διαυγέα emphasize brilliance and clarity befitting crystal.

lines.gr: λᾶαν, ἀπόρροιαν πυριφεγγέος ἀμβρότου αἴγλης·
lines.en: a stone, an emanation of fire-bright, immortal radiance.
lines.note: ἀπόρροια (“emanation, efflux”) evokes physical theories of effluences; πυριφεγγέος = “fire-bright” (pyr + pheggos). ἀμβρότου αἴγλης = “immortal/divine radiance.”

lines.gr: αἴθεϊ δ' ἀθανάτων μέγα τέρπεται ἄφθιτον ἦτορ·
lines.en: and in the aether of the Deathless the imperishable heart rejoices greatly;
lines.note: αἴθεϊ ἀθανάντων = “in the aether of the gods.” The subject ἄφθιτον ἦτορ (“imperishable heart”) is generic/collective; sense: the gods’ heart delights (at this stone).

lines.gr: τόν κ' εἴπερ μετὰ χεῖρας ἔχων παρὰ νηὸν ἵκηαι,
lines.en: this one, if indeed, holding it in your hands, you come to the temple,
lines.note: τόν refers back to the crystal; μετὰ χεῖρας ἔχων = “holding it in your hands.” παρὰ νηόν = “to/by the temple.”

lines.gr: οὔτις τοι μακάρων ἀρνήσεται εὐχωλῇσι.
lines.en: none of the Blessed will refuse your prayers.
lines.note: μακάρων = “the Blessed (Ones),” i.e., the gods. εὐχωλαί = vows/prayers; ἀρνήσεται = “will refuse.”

lines.gr: κέκλυθι δ' ὄφρα μάθοις μένος ἀργεννοῖο λίθοιο.
lines.en: But hearken, that you may learn the potency of the silvery stone.
lines.note: κεκλυθι is a formal imperative (“hearken”) typical of didactic hexameter; μένος here denotes a stone’s efficacy/power; ἀργεννός means “bright/silvery-white,” hence “silvery,” and may indicate color rather than composition (not necessarily ‘of silver’). Identification of the specific stone is uncertain.

lines.gr: εἰ γὰρ ἄτερ κρατεροῦ ἐθέλοις πυρὸς ἐκ φλόγας ὄρσαι,
lines.en: For if you should wish, without mighty fire, to kindle the flames of fire,
lines.note: ἐκ φλόγας is a pleonastic-sounding expression (“flames of fire”); ἄτερ κρατεροῦ πυρός = “without strong/mighty fire.” ὄρσαι = “rouse, kindle.”

lines.gr: κέκλομαι αὐαλέων μιν ὑπὲρ δαΐδων καταθεῖναι·
lines.en: I enjoin you to set it above dry torches;
lines.note: αὐαλέων is taken as “dry, parched” (gen. pl.), hence “dry torches.” Some have proposed αὐλέων (“of halls”), but the context favors torches used as kindling. κέκλομαι = “I enjoin/charge,” and μιν refers to the stone previously described.

lines.gr: αὐτὰρ ὅγ' ἠελίου κατεναντίον αὐγάζοντος
lines.en: but it, when facing Helios as he beams,
lines.note: κατεναντίον ἠελίου αὐγάζοντος = “facing the beaming Helios.” The subject throughout is the stone.

lines.gr: αὐτίχ' ὑπὲρ δαΐδων ὀλίγην ἀκτῖνα τανύσσει.
lines.en: straightway stretches a slight ray over the torches.
lines.note: ὑπὲρ δαΐδων is spatial (“over/above the torches”). ὀλίγην ἀκτῖνα τανύσσει describes a concentrated beam; the passage alludes to using a stone (like crystal) as a burning-glass to ignite kindling by sunlight.

lines.gr: ἣ δ' ὅτε καρφαλέης τε θίγῃ καὶ πίονος ὕλης,
lines.en: But when it touches dry and resin‑rich wood,
lines.note: karphalēs = “parched, withered, dry”; píos hylē = “rich/fat wood,” i.e., resinous, pitch‑rich timber used as good fuel.

lines.gr: καπνόν, ἔπειτα δὲ πῦρ ὀλίγον, μετὰ δὲ φλόγα πολλὴν
lines.en: it will raise smoke, then a little fire, and after that a great flame;
lines.note: Orsei (“will stir up/raise”) governs the sequence kapnon → pyr → phloga, marking stages of ignition.

lines.gr: ὄρσει· τὴν δ' ἄρα φασὶ παλαιγενέες ἱερὸν πῦρ.
lines.en: and that flame, they say, men of old called the sacred fire.
lines.note: Palai-genes (“men of old”) is a poetic plural for “the ancients”; “sacred fire” (hieron pyr) likely alludes to cultic/perpetual fire, a term later associated with asbestos-wicked lamps.

lines.gr: τάων οὐχ ἑτέρης μᾶλλον φλογὸς ἔλπομ' ἔγωγε
lines.en: From none of the others do I, for my part, look for a stronger flame,
lines.note: τάων is the epic/genitive plural feminine (“of them”), referring back to a previously named feminine plural (likely stones). The syntax is compressed: ἔλπομ’ takes the infinitive καίειν in the next line; οὐχ ἑτέρης … φλογὸς μᾶλλον conveys “not from another of them [do I expect] more of a flame,” i.e., “no stronger flame from any other.” The genitive φλογός is partitive with the comparative sense implied by μᾶλλον.

lines.gr: ἀθανάτοις οὕτω κεχαρισμένα μηρία καίειν.
lines.en: to burn thus the thigh-bones, pleasing to the Immortals.
lines.note: μηρία are the thigh-bones burned to the gods in epic-sacrificial practice; κεχαρισμένα means “acceptable/pleasing,” and ἀθάνατοι (“the Immortals”) is the standard epithet for the gods. οὕτω (“thus”) points to the correct ritual manner previously described.

lines.gr: πρὸς δ' ἔτι τοι καὶ τοῦτο, φίλος, μέγα θαῦμα πιφαύσκω·
lines.en: And besides this too, friend, I make known to you a great marvel:
lines.note: πιφαύσκω = “make clear, reveal,” a marked epic/didactic verb; τοι is an ethic dative (“I tell you”).

lines.gr: αὐτὸν ὅτις πέλεται φλογὸς αἴτιος, αἴκε μάλ' ὦκα
lines.en: the very stone that is the cause of flame—if very swiftly
lines.note: The subject (“stone”) is implied from context. “Cause of flame” (φλογὸς αἴτιος) points to a fire‑making or fiery stone (often taken as pyrites or a ‘carbuncle’/anthrax in lapidary lore), but identifications vary.

lines.gr: ἐκ πυρὸς ἁρπάξῃς, ψυχρὸς πέλει ἀμφαφάασθαι,
lines.en: you snatch it from the fire, it is cold to the touch,
lines.note: ἀμφαφάασθαι is an epic verb “to be handled/touched all around”; hence “cold to the touch.” The paradox of a ‘fiery’ stone that feels cold is a standard lapidary marvel.

lines.gr: ἀμφὶ δὲ καὶ νεφροῖσι δεθεὶς κάμνοντα σαώσει.
lines.en: and, bound about the kidneys, it will save the sufferer.
lines.note: δεθεὶς ἀμφὶ νεφροῖσι refers to amuletic binding around the loins/kidney area; “will save” (σαώσει) = ‘heal/cure’ a sufferer from kidney trouble.

lines.gr: - Δεύτερον εὐχομένῳ τοι ἀρηγόνα λᾶαν ὀπάσσω,
lines.en: Secondly, to you as you pray I bestow a succoring stone,
lines.note: “ἀρηγόνα” = help‑bringing, succoring; “εὐχομένῳ τοι” addresses the supplicant directly (“to you as you pray”).

lines.gr: θεσπεσίοιο γάλακτος ἐνίπλεον, ἠΰτε μαζὸν
lines.en: brimful of wondrous milk, like a breast
lines.note: “θεσπέσιοιο” can be “divine” or “wondrous”; the description anticipates the so‑called galaktites (“milk‑stone”), famed in antiquity for promoting lactation. “ἐνίπλεον” = brimful.

lines.gr: πρωτοτόκου νύμφης ἢ μηκάδος οὐθατοέσσης·
lines.en: of a first-delivered bride or a rich‑uddered bleating she‑goat;
lines.note: “πρωτοτόκου νύμφης” = a bride/newly married woman who has borne her first child; “μηκάς” is a she‑goat; “οὐθατοέσσης” (from οὖθαρ, udder) = rich‑uddered, udder‑swollen.

lines.gr: τόν ῥα παλαιγενέες μὲν ἀνακτίτην ἀδάμαντα
lines.en: this one the ancient‑born called Adamas the Subduer,
lines.note: “Adamas” here is the generic ancient term for the hardest substance (not necessarily diamond); “ἀνακτίτην” is taken as “subduer/ruler‑making,” fitting the following causal clause.

lines.gr: κλεῖον, ὅτι γνάμπτει μακάρων νόον, ὄφρα θυηλὰς
lines.en: because it bends the mind of the Blessed, so that
lines.note: “μακάρων” = the Blessed (the gods). “γνάμπτει” = bends, inclines (persuades) the mind.

lines.gr: ἁζόμενοι ἐθέλωσιν ἐπιχθονίους ἐλεαίρειν·
lines.en: in reverence for the burnt‑offerings they wish to pity the earth‑dwellers;
lines.note: “θυήλας” = sacrificial victims/offerings; “ἁζόμενοι” = in holy awe/reverence. “ἐπιχθονίους” = earth‑dwellers (mortals).

lines.gr: οἳ δ' ἄρα μιν λήθαιον ἐφήμισαν, οὕνεκεν αἰεὶ
lines.en: while others named it Lēthaios, since always

lines.gr: μεμνῆσθαι κακότητος ὀϊζυρῆς ἀπερύκει
lines.en: it keeps mortals and immortals from remembering wretched misery;
lines.note: “Λήθαιον” = the Forgetfulness‑stone; “ἐφήμισαν” = they styled/named.

lines.gr: θνητοὺς ἀθανάτους τε· νόον δ' ἐριούνιον εἶναι
lines.en: and it makes the mind Eriounios,
lines.note: “ἀπερύκει μεμνῆσθαι” = keeps from remembering; “κακότητος ὀϊζυρῆς” is a hendiadys for wretched misfortune.

lines.gr: θέλγει ἐποτρύνων ἀγανὰ φρεσὶ βουλεύεσθαι.
lines.en: charming it, urging it to take gentle counsel in its wits.
lines.note: “ἐριούνιος” is the epithet of Hermes (Eriounios, ‘beneficent/helpful’); used adjectivally of the mind here. Retained in transliteration with the connotation ‘gracious/propitious’.

lines.gr: ἄλλοι δ' ἐσκέψαντο γαλακτίδα φέρτερον εἶναι
lines.en: But others have judged “Galaktis” to be the better
lines.note: γαλακτίς (Galaktis) is the lapidary name “Milk-stone” (galactite). The construction with ἐσκέψαντο … φέρτερον εἶναι is completed by the infinitive κικλῆσκειν in the next line.

lines.gr: κικλήσκειν πέτρην, ὅτι τοι τρίψαντι γάλακτος
lines.en: name to give the stone, since indeed, when it is rubbed,
lines.note: κικλῆσκειν is a poetic form of “to call/name”; πέτρη here = “stone.” The particle τοι is asseverative (“indeed”). The dative τρίψαντι is generic (“when one rubs it/when it is rubbed”).

lines.gr: ἐκπρορέει λευκοῖο πανείκελος ἔνδοθεν ἰχώρ.
lines.en: there exudes from within an ichor wholly like white milk.
lines.note: ἰχώρ is the Homeric term for “ichor,” here meaning a fluid/exudate rather than divine blood. πανείκελος = “wholly like, entirely resembling.” ἐκπρορέει ἔνδοθεν conveys the idea of the stone “exuding from within,” a property attributed to galactite in ancient lapidaries.

lines.gr: πεῖρα δέ τοι καὶ τοῦδε παρέσσεται, αἴκ' ἐθέλησθα.
lines.en: And a proof of this too will be at hand for you, if you are willing.
lines.note: πεῖρα = “proof, test (experiment)” in didactic context; παρέσσεται = “will be present/at hand” (future of πάρειμι); αἴκ’ = εἴ κε “if”; ἐθέλησθα is the epic 2nd sg subjunctive of ἐθέλω, hence “if you are willing/if you wish.”

lines.gr: οὔθατα γὰρ μήλων ὅτε κεν μινύθοντα ἴδηαι,
lines.en: For when you see the udders of the flocks dwindling,
lines.note: οὔθατα = ‘udders’; μήλων here ‘flocks’ (sheep/goats collectively). μινύθοντα ‘dwindling, shrinking’ suggests reduced milk.

lines.gr: πῶς ἔρξεις, φίλε τέκνον, ἐπὴν ἐρίφοισι τεοῖσιν,
lines.en: what will you do, dear child, when it concerns your kids,
lines.note: ἐπὴν = ἐπεί ἄν ‘whenever/when(ever)’. ἐρίφοις = ‘kids’ (young goats).

lines.gr: οὕς ποτε θῆρα πέλωρον ὑπεκπροφυγὼν ἱκέτευσας,
lines.en: whom once, having slipped away from a monstrous wild beast, you implored,
lines.note: ἱκέτευσας takes a content clause supplied by the optative in the next line; θῆρα πέλωρον ‘monstrous wild beast’. ὑπεκπροφυγών ‘having escaped from under/away’.

lines.gr: τοῖσι παρασταίης τετληόσιν, οἳ δ' ἐνὶ σηκῷ
lines.en: that you might stand beside them, steadfast—while they in the pen
lines.note: παρασταίης (aor. opt.) functions as the object of ἱκέτευσας (‘you implored that you might stand by them’); τετληόσιν ‘steadfast/dauntless’. The syntax is compressed; some take the request as for protective assistance to the kids.

lines.gr: ἀμφί σε λεπταλέοι γοερὸν περιμηκήσωνται;
lines.en: delicate as they are, shall bleat piteously all around you?
lines.note: περιμηκήσωνται is a rare form built on μηκάομαι ‘to bleat’ (here ‘bleat all around/loudly’); λεπταλέοι ‘delicate, tender’ suits kids in the pen (σηκός).

lines.gr: τῶν μὲν ἀκηχεμένας ἐπιτέλλεο μητέρας αἶψα
lines.en: Of these, bid their sorrowing mothers straightway
lines.note: τῶν refers back to the kids; their ‘mothers’ are the she‑goats. ἀκηχεμένας ‘grieved, distressed’.

lines.gr: λούειν πηγάων κυαναυγέσιν ἐν δίνῃσι·
lines.en: to bathe in the dark-gleaming eddies of the springs;
lines.note: κυαναυγέσιν ‘dark‑gleaming’ is a poetic compound; πηγάων is genitive with δίναι ‘eddies (of springs)’.

lines.gr: στήσας δ' ἠελίου κατεναντίον ἀντέλλοντος,
lines.en: and, taking your stand opposite Helios as he rises,
lines.note: Helios is named rather than generic ‘sun’, marking ritual orientation at sunrise (ἀντέλλοντος).

lines.gr: ἁγνίζειν μὲν πρῶτον ἐποιχόμενος περὶ πάσας,
lines.en: purify first, going around them all;
lines.note: ἁγνίζειν ‘to purify’ signals a ritual act; ἐποιχόμενος ‘going around’ implies circumambulation.

lines.gr: ἅλμην δ' ἐν κρητῆρι καὶ ἄλφιτα λεπτὰ λίθοιο
lines.en: and, after pouring brine in a mixing-bowl and fine stone‑ground barley‑meal,
lines.note: ἅλμη ‘brine’ used as lustral liquid; ἄλφιτα λεπτὰ λίθοιο = ‘fine barley‑groats ground on a stone (mill)’ (genitive of material). Some have queried whether λίθοιο modifies ἄλφιτα or the vessel; ‘stone‑ground’ suits context.

lines.gr: χευάμενος, διὰ πῶϋ καὶ αἰγῶν ἔρχευ ὅμιλον,
lines.en: go through the flock and the band of goats,
lines.note: πῶϋ is an epic/pastoral term for a sheep‑flock; ὅμιλος ‘throng, band’ used of animals.

lines.gr: ῥαίνων καρποφόρῳ λάσιον κατὰ νῶτον ἑκάστης
lines.en: sprinkling along the shaggy back of each with a fruit-bearing twig;
lines.note: καρποφόρῳ θάλλῳ ‘fruit‑bearing twig’, probably an olive sprig; ῥαίνειν ‘sprinkle’ the brine‑and‑barley mixture as a lustral asperging.

lines.gr: θαλλῷ· ταὶ δ' ἄρα πᾶσαι ἰαινόμεναι περὶ σηκοὺς
lines.en: and they, all of them, being warmed/cheered, about the folds
lines.note: ἰαίνεσθαι ‘be warmed/cheered/comforted’ of animals soothed after the rite; σηκοί ‘folds, pens’.

lines.gr: ἐξαπίνης μετὰ τέκνα φερεγλαγέες στιχόωνται.
lines.en: suddenly, with their young, rich in milk, will form their ranks in order.
lines.note: φερεγλαγέες is a rare adjective ‘milk‑bearing/rich in milk’ (from γάλα); στιχόωνται ‘form up in rows/array themselves’, denoting orderly, settled behavior after the ritual.

lines.gr: οἳ δ' ἄρ' ὑπαὶ μαζοῖσι κορεσσάμενοι γαλαθηνοὶ
lines.en: and those who, milk-fed, having had their fill beneath the breasts,
lines.note: ὑπαὶ μαζοῖσι (“beneath the breasts”) is an epic idiom for suckling at the breast; κορεσσάμενοι is the aorist middle participle of κορέννυμι (“to sate, fill”); γαλαθηνοί = “milk-fed,” i.e., sucklings.

lines.gr: σκιρτηθμῶν ἐξαῦτις ἀναμνήσοντ' ἀγέρωχοι.
lines.en: will once more, high-spirited, remember their leapings.
lines.note: σκιρτηθμῶν is likely a corrupt or dialectal form for σκιρτημῶν (“leapings, gambols”); ἀναμνήσοντ' = ἀναμνήσονται with elision before ἀγέρωχοι; “remember their leapings” idiomatically implies “resume their gambols”; ἀγέρωχοι = “high-spirited, lordly.”

lines.gr: σὴν δὲ μελικρήτοιο μετὰ γλυκεροῖο μιγέντα
lines.en: and your [stone], when mixed together with sweet mead,
lines.note: μελικρήτοιο μετὰ γλυκεροῖο = “with sweet mead” (μελικρήτος ‘honey‑mixture, mead’). There is a grammatical hitch: σὴν (fem. acc.) sits awkwardly with μιγέντα (masc. acc.). Many editors emend σὴν to σόν (‘your’ masc./neut.), or take σὴν with νύμφην in the next line; I adopt the latter, understanding the drink/potion as the object implied by μιγέντα.

lines.gr: ὄρνυε πινέμεναι νύμφην, ἵνα νήπιον υἷα
lines.en: urge the Nymph to drink it, so that an infant son
lines.note: ὄρνυε is causative ‘rouse, urge, set in motion’; πινέμεναι is the epic infinitive ‘to drink.’

lines.gr: μαστοῖσιν μεθύοντα παρ' ἀενάοισι κομίζῃ.
lines.en: she may nurse, drunken at her breasts, beside the ever‑flowing springs.
lines.note: μαστοῖσιν μεθύοντα ‘drunken at the breasts’ evokes a suckling infant. παρ’ ἀενάοισι is taken locatively, ‘beside the ever‑flowing springs,’ a typical Nymph‑locus; less likely is construal with μαστοῖσιν (‘with ever‑flowing breasts’).

lines.gr: ἀμφὶ δ' ἄρ' αὐχένι παιδὸς ἀερτάζουσα τιθήνη
lines.en: and then the nurse, hanging the stone about a child’s neck,
lines.note: ἀερτάζουσα (“dangling, suspending”) from ἀερτάζω; the scene is of a nurse hanging an apotropaic amulet (the stone) around a child’s neck (ἀμφὶ … αὐχένι παιδός).

lines.gr: λᾶαν ἐρητύσει κακομήτιος ὄσσε Μεγαίρης·
lines.en: will with the stone restrain the ill‑counseling eyes of Megaira;
lines.note: ἐρητύσει (“will restrain/curb”) here = “ward off.” The object is ὄσσε Μεγαίρης (“the eyes of Megaira,” dual ‘eyes’ = ‘gaze’). κακομήτιος (gen. agreeing with Μεγαίρης) = “ill‑counseling,” an epic epithet. Megaira is an Erinys; the line evokes averting the “evil eye.” The instrumental sense “with the stone” is understood from the context.

lines.gr: καὶ δέ σε καὶ βασιλῆες ἀμύμονες αἰδέσσονται
lines.en: and even blameless kings will stand in awe of you,
lines.note: αἰδέσσονται + acc. = “feel awe for, revere.” βασιλῆες ἀμύμονες is Homeric formula “blameless kings.” The “you” is the bearer of the stone.

lines.gr: ἐν χερὶ λᾶαν ἔχοντα καὶ ἄπλετα φῦλ' ἀνθρώπων·
lines.en: as you hold the stone in your hand—and the countless tribes of men;
lines.note: ἄπλετα (“boundless, countless”) modifies φῦλ’ ἀνθρώπων (“tribes/peoples of men”). ἔχοντα (acc. masc. sg.) agrees with σε, “you holding [it] in your hand.”

lines.gr: ἀθάνατοι δὲ μάλιστα θεοὶ καταθύμια σεῖο
lines.en: and most of all the immortal gods will bring to pass all things that accord with your heart,
lines.note: καταθύμια (neut. pl.) = “things in accord with one’s heart,” i.e., wishes/desires; σεῖο is epic genitive “of you.” τελευτήσουσιν = “will bring to pass, accomplish.”

lines.gr: πάντα τελευτήσουσιν ἐπ' ἀράων ἀΐοντες.
lines.en: heeding your prayers.
lines.note: ἐπ’ ἀρὰων ἀΐοντες = “heeding/hearing prayers”; ἀρά in epic can denote both prayer and imprecation, apt to the magical context. ἀΐοντες is the epic participle “hearing.”

lines.gr: - Χρὴ δὲ καὶ εὐπέταλον τετραυγέα λᾶαν ἔχοντας
lines.en: And one should also, holding the well‑petaled, four‑rayed stone,
lines.note: εὐπέταλον (“well‑petaled”) is a lapidary epithet likely describing a foliated/laminar structure; τετραυγέα (“four‑rayed/four‑gleaming,” from augē “beam”) modifies the same stone. λᾶαν is the epic acc. of λάας “stone.” The form τετραυγέα is textually awkward (elsewhere masc. acc. sg. of τετραυγής can be τετραυγῆ); sense is clear.

lines.gr: ἀρᾶσθαι παρὰ βωμὸν ἐναιρομένης ἑκατόμβης.
lines.en: pray beside the altar while a hecatomb is being slain.
lines.note: ἐναιρομένης ἑκατόμβης is a genitive absolute, “while a hecatomb is being slain.” ἀρᾶσθαι here = “to pray,” in a ritual context to enhance the stone’s efficacy.

lines.gr: - Εἰ καὶ δενδροφύτοιο φέροις τρύφος ἐν χερὶ πέτρης
lines.en: Even if you should bear in your hand a chip of a tree‑grown stone,
lines.note: “δενδροφύτοιο … πέτρης” = “of a tree‑grown stone”; lapidary idiom, often taken of substances like amber or jet; “τρύφος” is a rare word meaning “chip/fragment.”

lines.gr: μᾶλλόν κεν θάλποιτο θεῶν νόος αἰὲν ἐόντων.
lines.en: the mind of the ever‑existing gods would be all the more propitiated.
lines.note: “θάλποιτο” literally “be warmed,” here metaphorically “be soothed/propitiated”; “θεῶν … αἰὲν ἐόντων” = “the ever‑existing gods,” a Homeric epithet; “νόος” (mind/counsel) stands for divine will.

lines.gr: δένδρεα γὰρ μάλα πολλὰ κατόψεαι ὡς ἐνὶ κήπῳ
lines.en: For you shall behold very many trees, as in a flowery garden,
lines.note: ἀνθεμόεντι modifies κήπῳ: “as in a flowery garden.” In context (a didactic poem on stones), the “trees” likely describe dendritic patterns in minerals that resemble a garden of trees.

lines.gr: ἀνθεμόεντι κλάδοισιν ἐπασσυτέροις κομόωντα.
lines.en: luxuriant with close‑set branches.
lines.note: κομόωντα (from κομάω, “to let the hair grow long”) is a poetic term for luxuriant foliage; κλάδοισιν is instrumental (“with branches”); ἐπασσυτέροις (comparative of ἐπασσύς) means “thick-set, close-packed,” hence “close-set branches.”

lines.gr: τοὔνεκά οἱ καὶ φῶτες ἀχάτῃ δενδρήεντι
lines.en: For this reason, men too bestowed upon it—upon the tree‑like agate—
lines.note: The verb of the clause (they bestowed) comes in the next line; ἀχάτῃ δενδρήεντι is a dative of the object receiving the epithet. I render δενδρήεις as “tree‑like” (cf. dendritic agate).

lines.gr: θῆκαν ἐπωνυμίην, ὅτι οἱ τὸ μὲν ἔπλετ' ἀχάτου,
lines.en: a by‑name, because for it one part was of agate,
lines.note: θῆκαν ἐπωνυμίην = “they set/placed a by‑name (epithet).” ἔπλετ’ is epic for ἔπλετο (“was”); οἱ is a dative of reference (“for it,” i.e., the stone). The μὲν here is balanced by δέ in the following line.

lines.gr: ἄλλο δ' ἔχει λασίης ὕλης δέμας εἰσοράασθαι.
lines.en: while another part has, to be looked upon, the form of shaggy woodland.
lines.note: λασίης ὕλης (“shaggy woodland”) evokes dense, brushy growth; δέμας εἰσορᾶσθαι means “a form to be seen,” i.e., an appearance to the eye, describing the dendritic, branch‑like figures in the stone.

lines.gr: τὸν δὲ τεοῖσι βόεσσιν ἀνασχίζουσιν ἄρουραν
lines.en: and it, for your oxen who cleave the plough‑land,
lines.note: “ton de” (“and it”) resumes the stone just described; “anaskhizousin arouran” is an epic idiom, “to rend/cleave the field,” of ploughing oxen.

lines.gr: ἀμφὶ κέρα δοιὼ βαλέειν, ἢ καρτερὸν ἀμφὶς
lines.en: to fasten about both horns, or else around the stout
lines.note: “balein amphi” here means “to fasten/hang around,” not literally “to throw”; “doiō kera” is dual, “both horns.”

lines.gr: ὦμον ἀροτρεύοντος ἀτειρέος ἀγροιώτου·
lines.en: shoulder of the unwearied, ploughing ploughman;
lines.note: The construction continues: “amphis ōmon” = “around the shoulder.” “ateireos” = “unwearied, tireless”; “agroiōtos” = “countryman, ploughman.”

lines.gr: καί κεν ἀπ' οὐρανόθεν σταχυοπλόκαμος Δημήτηρ
lines.en: and then from heaven grain‑tressed Dēmētēr
lines.note: “stachyoplokamos” literally “with tresses plaited of ears (of grain),” rendered as “grain‑tressed.” “ap’ ouranothen” (“from heaven”) highlights divine descent with fertility, though Dēmētēr is often chthonic.

lines.gr: μεστὸν ἴοι φερέκαρπον ἐς αὔλακα κόλπον ἔχουσα.
lines.en: would come into the furrow, her bosom full of fruit.
lines.note: “kolpos” (“bosom/lap”) is a metaphor for abundance; “pherekárpon” = “fruit‑bearing/harvest‑bringing.” The line depicts Dēmētēr entering the furrow with overflowing bounty.

lines.gr: - Σκέπτεο, καὶ θηητὸν ἔχων ἐλάφοιο πέλαζε
lines.en: Examine, and, having a marvel of a deer, draw near with it,
lines.note: θηητόν = “marvel, wonder.” πέλαζε (imperative) governs the dative in the next line (“to the Immortals”), hence the sense “draw near/bring [it] to the Immortals.” Many take the passage to refer to a ‘stag-horn’ stone (cf. elaphites or stag-horn coral), offered or shown as a marvel.

lines.gr: ἀθανάτοισι κέρας· ποτὶ γὰρ νόος οὐρανιώνων
lines.en: a horn for the Immortals; for the mind of the heaven-dwellers
lines.note: οὐρανιώνων = “heaven-dwellers,” a periphrasis for the gods; νόος μειδιάει personifies their “mind” as smiling at the sight (completed in the next line).

lines.gr: μειδιάει φύσεως πολυδαιδάλου ἔργον ἰδόντων·
lines.en: smiles when they behold the work of much-wrought nature;
lines.note: πολυδαίδαλος = “much-wrought, richly-crafted,” a standard epic epithet for Nature’s cunning workmanship; ἰδόντων is a genitive absolute with the gods as understood subject.

lines.gr: ἤτοι μὲν κέρας ἐστί, ταναύποδος οἷα φύονται
lines.en: indeed it is a horn, such as grow from the head of the long-footed deer;
lines.note: ταναύποδος = “long-footed,” a conventional epic epithet of deer; οἷα φύονται = “such as are produced/grow,” stressing likeness to natural antlers.

lines.gr: ἐκ κεφαλῆς ἐλάφοιο· φύει γε μὲν οὔποτε κόρση
lines.en: the crown of the head, to be sure, never produces a stone,
lines.note: κόρση = “crown/top of the head” (rare); the line asserts that heads do not produce stone, underscoring the paradox of a lithic antler-like object.

lines.gr: πέτρην, ἀλλ' ἔμπης πέλεται στερεὴ τόγε πέτρη·
lines.en: yet nonetheless that thing proves to be a hard stone;
lines.note: ἔμπης = “nevertheless”; πέλεται (epic) = “is/becomes”; στερεὴ πέτρη = “hard/solid stone.”

lines.gr: οὐ δέ κεν ἂν γνοίης κέρας ἀτρεκές, ἢ λίθος ἐστί,
lines.en: nor could you know for certain whether it is horn or stone,
lines.note: ἀτρεκές = “exact, certain”; the point is that appearance alone cannot distinguish horn from stone.

lines.gr: πρίν κέ μιν ἀμφαφόων εὕρῃς νημερτέα λᾶαν.
lines.en: until, by handling it all around, you find it to be a true stone.
lines.note: ἀμφαφόων = “feeling/handling all around” (epic); νημερτέα λᾶαν = “a true/unerring stone” (λᾶας is epic for “stone”): tactile examination reveals its lithic nature.

lines.gr: αἰεί τοι θήσει λασίην ἐπὶ κράατι λάχνην,
lines.en: Always it will set shaggy down upon your head,
lines.note: λασίην λάχνην (“shaggy down”) denotes soft new hair; κράατι is the epic dative of “head.” The future θήσει conveys a promise of efficacy.

lines.gr: εἰ καὶ ψεδνοκάρηνος ἔοις· εἰ γάρ μιν ἐλαίῳ
lines.en: even if you are thin‑haired; for if you, with oil—
lines.note: ψεδνοκάρῃνος is “scant-/thin-haired, balding.” μιν (“it”) refers to the stone; the syntax breaks off because of the following lacuna after ἐλαίῳ (“with oil”).

lines.gr: [missing]
lines.en: [missing]
lines.note: Lacuna: the line is lost. Context and the participle τριβόμενον in 256 suggest something like “having ground it with oil” or “mixing it with oil.”

lines.gr: τριβόμενον τρίβειν κροτάφους πάντ' ἤματα σεῖο,
lines.en: once it has been ground, rub your temples with it every day,
lines.note: τριβόμενον (“once it has been rubbed/ground [with oil]”) picks up the lost instruction; τρίβειν here functions as an infinitive of instruction typical of didactic verse. κροτάφους = “temples”; πάντ’ ἤματα = “every day.”

lines.gr: αἱ δὲ νέαι περὶ βρέγμα τεὸν τρίχες ἀνθήσουσι.
lines.en: and new hairs will blossom around your brow.
lines.note: ἀνθήσουσι (“will blossom”) is a metaphor for sprouting hair; βρέγμα denotes the brow/crown region.

lines.gr: πρωτόγαμον δ' αἰζηὸς ἄγων ἐς δέμνια κούρην
lines.en: A stalwart man, leading his first‑wedded maiden to the marriage‑bed,
lines.note: αἰζηός = a man in his prime, “stalwart”; πρωτόγαμον κόρην = “first‑wedded maiden,” i.e., a maiden entering her first marriage; δέμνια = the (marriage) bed.

lines.gr: τερπωλῆς ἐρατῆς ἐπιμάρτυρα τόνδε φέροιτο
lines.en: should carry this stone as a witness of lovely delight;
lines.note: ἐπιμάρτυρα = “as a witness/guarantor,” a forensic term adapted to amuletic context; τερπωλῆς (rare) = “delight, enjoyment,” here of marital pleasures; τόνδε λᾶαν = “this stone,” referring to the stone described in the preceding section.

lines.gr: λᾶαν· ὃ δ' ἀρρήκτοισιν ὁμοφροσύνῃσιν ἅμ' ἄμφω
lines.en: and it will keep the two together in unbreakable concord,
lines.note: ἀρρήκτοισιν ὁμοφροσύνῃσιν = “unbreakable concord(s)”; plural is stylistic/hendiadys; ἅμ’ ἄμφω = formula “both together.”

lines.gr: ὕστατον ἐς γῆρας καὶ ἐς ἤματα πάντα καθέξει.
lines.en: unto latest old age and through all their days.
lines.note: καθέξει (fut.) = “will hold/maintain, keep fast”; ὕστατον ἐς γῆρας = “unto latest/utmost old age”; ἐς ἤματα πάντα = “through all [their] days.”

lines.gr: - Ποιμένι δ' ἀγραύλων ταύρων, Διὸς αἰγιόχοιο
lines.en: And to the herdsman of field‑roaming bulls, of Zeus Aigiochos—
lines.note: “Herdsman of bulls” and the following apposition identify Dionysos; “Zeus Aigiochos” preserves the epithet. The syntax runs into the next line (enjambment).

lines.gr: υἱέϊ κισσοχίτωνι, λίθον καταθύμιον εἶναι
lines.en: to the ivy‑robed son—I declare a stone to be dear to his heart,
lines.note: “Ivy‑robed” (kissochitōn) is a Dionysiac epithet. “Katathymion” = “dear to the heart.”

lines.gr: βάρβαρον ἀγγέλλω, Συριηγενέος κελαδεινοῦ
lines.en: a foreign one, I announce, very radiant,
