lines.note: “Barbaron” means “foreign” (non‑Greek). “Zamilampin” is a rare intensive, “very bright/gleaming.”

lines.gr: ὕδασιν Εὐφρήταο διαινόμενον ζαμίλαμπιν·
lines.en: bathed by the waters of the Syrian‑born, loud‑resounding Euphrates;
lines.note: “Syrian‑born Euphrates” reflects Greco‑Roman geographic usage; “keladeinos” = “loud‑resounding.” “Diai(n)omenon hydasin” = “bathed/soaked by the waters.”

lines.gr: ὅς τοι φυταλιῆς ἕνεκεν ῥέξαντι θυηλὰς
lines.en: which, when you have offered victims for the sake of planting,
lines.note: “Thyēlas” = sacrificial victims; “phyitaliēs” denotes cultivation/planting, here with viticultural nuance given the context.

lines.gr: κλήμασιν αὐτίκα σεῖο φερεσταφύλοισιν ἀλωὴν
lines.en: straightway, clothing your vineyard with grape‑laden vine‑shoots,
lines.note: “Klēmata” = vine‑shoots; “alōē” = orchard/vineyard; “pherestaphylos” = “cluster‑bearing, grape‑laden”; “seio” is an archaic genitive “of you, your.”

lines.gr: ἀμφιέσας πολλόν τοι ἀφύσσασθαι μέθυ δώσει.
lines.en: will grant you to draw much wine.
lines.note: “Aphysasthai” is to draw/ladle off (liquid), here wine (methy).

lines.gr: - Καὶ γλαφυρὴν κομίσας ἐαρόχροον αἴκεν ἴασπιν
lines.en: And if, having brought a well‑wrought, spring‑hued jasper,
lines.note: αἴ κεν with subjunctive (“if…should”) sets a conditional; γλαφυρήν = “well‑wrought/polished”; ἐαρόχροον = “spring‑colored,” i.e., green in lapidary context; κομίσας = “having brought/procured.”

lines.gr: ἱερά τις ῥέζῃ, μακάρων ἰαίνεται ἦτορ,
lines.en: someone should perform holy rites, the heart of the Blessed is gladdened,
lines.note: ἱερὰ ῥέζειν = perform sacrifices/holy rites; ἰαίνεται ἦτορ = “the heart is gladdened/warmed,” idiom for divine favor; μακάρων = “the Blessed (gods).”

lines.gr: καί οἱ καρφαλέας νεφέλαις κορέσουσιν ἀρούρας·
lines.en: and for him they will sate the parched fields with clouds;
lines.note: οἱ = “for him” (dative of advantage); καρφαλέας = “parched, withered”; κορέσουσιν … νεφέλαις = “will sate/fill … with clouds” (instrumental dative), i.e., grant rain; subject understood as “the Blessed” from the previous line.

lines.gr: ἥδε γὰρ αὐχμηρῇσιν ἄγει πολὺν ὄμβρον ἀρούραις.
lines.en: for this stone brings abundant rain to the drought‑stricken fields.
lines.note: ἥδε (“this”) points back to the jasper; ὄμβρος = heavy rain; αὐχμηρός = dry, drought‑stricken.

lines.gr: - Λύχνι, σὺ δ' ἐκ πεδίου ῥόθιόν τ' ἀπόεργε χάλαζαν
lines.en: Lychnis, keep off from our plain the roaring spate and the hail,
lines.note: Λύχνι is the vocative of the stone Lychnis (often a red gem); ῥόθιον (‘roaring surge/roar’) is here taken of a torrential spate or storm-din; ἡμετέρου most naturally modifies πεδίου: “from our plain.”

lines.gr: ἡμετέρου καὶ κῆρας, ὅσαι στιχόωνται ἐπ' ἀγρούς·
lines.en: and our banes, all that are marshalled against the fields;
lines.note: κῆρες (‘banes, dooms’) is plural and personified; στιχόωνται (‘are set in ranks/array themselves’) is martial, describing afflictions massing “against” fields (ἐπ’ ἀγρούς).

lines.gr: καί σε γὰρ ἀθανάτων φιλέει νόος, ἐκ δ' ἄρα βωμῶν
lines.en: for the mind of the Immortals loves you, and from the altars
lines.note: ‘Immortals’ renders ἀθανάτων; the line frames Lychnis as ritually favored.

lines.gr: ἠΰτε περ κρύσταλλος ἄνευ πυρὸς ἐκ φλόγα πέμπεις·
lines.en: you send forth a flame, like crystal, without fire;
lines.note: The simile alludes to rock-crystal’s reputed ability to ignite tinder by focusing sunlight—“sending forth flame without fire”; hence the paradoxical phrasing.

lines.gr: ἐν δέ σοι ἀντίπαλον κεῖται μένος· ὁππότε δὴ πῦρ
lines.en: and in you there lies a counterpoised might: whenever fire
lines.note: ἀντίπαλον μένος (“countervailing/antagonistic might”) signals a paradoxical property of the stone.

lines.gr: νηδὺν ἀμφιέσῃσιν ἐνιπλείοιο λέβητος,
lines.en: wraps the belly of a brimming cauldron,
lines.note: νηδύς (“belly”) is a vivid term for the cauldron’s underside/interior; ἐνιπλείοιο = “very full/brimming.”

lines.gr: ψυχρὸν ἐπειγομένοιο πυρὸς μένει ἔνδοθεν ὕδωρ·
lines.en: the water within, though the fire presses hard, remains cold;
lines.note: ἐπειγόμενου πυρός = “the hastening/pressing fire”; the point is the water’s remaining cold under heat—an anti-thermal marvel attributed to the stone.

lines.gr: εἰ δέ τις ἐν ψυχρῇσι λίπῃ κονίῃσι λέβητα,
lines.en: but if someone leave the cauldron in cold ashes,
lines.note: ψυχραῖσι κονίῃσι (“cold ashes”) is a set phrase; λίπῃ is aorist subjunctive (“should leave/leave behind”), marking a hypothetical condition.

lines.gr: παφλάζει κρατεροῖο κυκώμενον ἔνδοθι χαλκοῦ.
lines.en: it bubbles, seething, within the stout bronze.
lines.note: παφλάζει (“bubbles/splashes”) and κυκώμενον (“being churned/seethed”) describe vigorous boiling; κρατερός of bronze emphasizes the stout vessel.

lines.gr: - Ἐσθλοὶ δ' αὖτ' ἐπὶ τοῖσι καὶ ὑαλοειδέες εἶναι
lines.en: And in turn, among these, they are said to be excellent and glass-like,
lines.note: ἐπὶ τοῖσι = “among these [stones]”; αὖτ’ = “again, in turn.” ὑαλοειδέες literally “glass-like, vitreous,” describing appearance/lustre.

lines.gr: κλείονται θνητοῖσι θυηπολέουσι τόπαζοι.
lines.en: by mortal sacrificers—the topaz-stones.
lines.note: κλείονται takes the infinitive εἶναι (“are said to be”), with θνητοῖσι θυηπολέουσι as dative of agent (“by mortal sacrificers,” i.e., priests). τόπαζοι = “topazes”; in ancient usage the term often denotes a yellow‑green gem (commonly identified with peridot/chrysolite) rather than the modern topaz.

lines.gr: - Φημὶ δέ τοι τέρπειν καὶ ὀπάλλιον οὐρανίωνας
lines.en: I declare to you that the bright opal too delights the Celestials,
lines.note: ὀπάλλιον (often ὀπάλιον) = opal; οὐρανίωνας “the Celestials” refers to the gods or heavenly beings; ἀγλαόν “splendid, bright.” The infinitive τέρπειν depends on φημί (“I declare that … delights”).

lines.gr: ἀγλαόν, ἱμερτοῦ τέρενα χρόα παιδὸς ἔχοντα·
lines.en: splendid, possessing the tender complexion of a lovely child;
lines.note: ἱμερτοῦ “desirable, alluring”; χρῶ(α) “skin, complexion.” The adjective τέρενα (“tender, delicate”) is poetically used with χρῶα; rendering as “complexion” suits the gem’s play of color likened to youthful skin.

lines.gr: καί ἑ καὶ ὀφθαλμοῖσιν ἀοσσητῆρα τετύχθαι.
lines.en: and that it too has been fashioned as a helper for the eyes.
lines.note: ἀοσσητῆρα is Homeric for “helper, assistant” (from ἀοσσητής), not “invisible”; thus the opal is said to aid eyesight. τετύχθαι (“has been fashioned/constituted”) is formulaic for a property inherent in the stone.

lines.gr: - Καὶ πίτυος δακρύοισι λίθου μένος ὀψιανοῖο,
lines.en: And with the pine’s tears empower the might of the obsidian stone,
lines.note: “πίτυος δακρύοισι” (‘tears of the pine’) = pine resin; the clause is elliptical, with the governing verb understood from κελεύω in 289. “μένος λίθου ὀψιανοῖο” = ‘the might of the obsidian stone,’ expressing its efficacy/power.

lines.gr: καὶ σμύρνην μίσγειν εὐώδεα, καὶ φολίδεσσιν
lines.en: and mix in fragrant myrrh, and with silver-white scales
lines.note: Present infinitive μίσγειν (‘to mix’) depends on κελεύω. “φολίδες” are ‘scales’ or ‘flakes/lamellae’; here likely thin shining flakes (perhaps metal leaf or mica). “ἀργυφέαις” = ‘silver-white, silver-bright.’

lines.gr: ἀργυφέαις λεπιδωτὸν ἀποστίλβοντα κελεύω.
lines.en: I bid you make it scale-covered and gleaming.
lines.note: “λεπιδωτόν” = ‘scale-covered,’ “ἀποστίλβοντα” = ‘gleaming back, glinting.’ The participles describe the intended finished appearance; the understood verb is ‘to make/render’ under κελεύω. “ὀψιανός” is the standard term for obsidian (cf. Latin lapis obsianus).

lines.gr: αὐτίκα γάρ τοι ταῦτα πυρὸς καθύπερθε πάσοντι
lines.en: For straightway, when you sprinkle these things above the fire,
lines.note: πάσοντι is likely for πάσσοντι (dat. sg. pres. part.) from πάσσω “sprinkle, strew”; hence “sprinkle these things.” τοι is an ethical dative. καθύπερθε = “from above, over,” i.e., over the fire in a fumigation rite.

lines.gr: ἀθάνατοι δώσουσι θεοπροπίας ἀγαθῶν τε
lines.en: the Immortals will grant divine oracles of things to come, both of good
lines.note: θεοπροπίας is the plural “oracular responses.” ἀθάνατοι (“the Immortals”) is the conventional epithet for the gods.

lines.gr: ἐσσομένων, λυγρῶν τε· καὶ εἴσεαι ἅσσ' ἐθέλησθα.
lines.en: and grievous; and you will know whatever you have desired.
lines.note: εἴσεαι is the epic future of οἶδα (“you will know”). ἅσσ’ ἐθέλησθα is the Homeric 2nd sg. perfect (“whatever you have wished”), conveying “whatever you wish to learn.” ἀγαθῶν … λυγρῶν is a balanced pair (“good” vs. “grievous”) of things to come.

lines.gr: καὶ νεύρων ἀλεγεινὰ πάθη λεπιδωτὸς ἀμύνει.
lines.en: and the scaly stone wards off the grievous pains of the sinews.
lines.note: νεύρων can denote ‘nerves’ or ‘sinews/tendons’ in ancient medical usage; I render ‘sinews’ to reflect classical physiology. λεπιδωτός (‘scaly’) is likely an epithet describing the stone’s scale-like surface (possibly the stone Lepidotos); ἀμύνει (‘wards off’) expresses a protective, apotropaic effect typical of the Lithica.

lines.gr: - Δοιὼ δ' Ἠελίου χρυσότριχε λᾶε πέλονται,
lines.en: Two stones of Helios are to be found, O golden‑haired one,
lines.note: Dual forms: Δοιώ and λᾶε (“two stones”). χρυσότριχε is vocative, an apostrophe to Helios; πέλονται in epic = “are (to be found), exist.”

lines.gr: ἄμφω θεσπεσίω· θάμβος δέ τοι ἔσσετ' ἰδόντι.
lines.en: both wondrous; and awe shall be yours when you behold them.
lines.note: ἄμφω and θεσπεσίω are dual; θεσπέσιος = “divinely wondrous.” τοι ἰδόντι is an ethical dative (“for you when you see”), rendered idiomatically as “shall be yours when you behold them.”

lines.gr: ἀμφοτέροις ἀκτῖνες ἐτήτυμοι ἐμπεφύασιν
lines.en: In both, true rays are implanted within,
lines.note: “Rays” (aktines) here are the internal, straight, needle-like inclusions that produce star-like or chatoyant effects; etētymoi = “genuine, true.”

lines.gr: ὀρθαί, λαμπετόωσαι· ἰδεῖν γε μὲν οἷον ἔθειραι,
lines.en: upright, gleaming; to behold, like hairs,
lines.note: Lambetoōsai is a Homeric/poetic participle (“shining”); etheirai (“hairs”) describes fibrous inclusions within the stone.

lines.gr: εἶδος δέ σφι λίθων ἄλλων· τὸν μέν τε νοήσεις
lines.en: yet their appearance is that of other stones; you will discern the one
lines.note: Sphi is enclitic 3rd plural (“their”); the verse sets up resemblance to well-known gems.

lines.gr: κρύσταλλον λευκήν· εἰ δ' οὐκ ἔχεν ἔνδον ἐθείρας,
lines.en: as a white crystal; and if it did not have hairs within,
lines.note: The phrase krystallon leukēn shows a gender mismatch (perhaps poetical/feminine usage of krystallos or textual irregularity); sense = “white rock-crystal.” “Hairs within” again refers to inclusions; ken ēēn = potential optative (“would have been”).

lines.gr: κρύσταλλός κεν ἔην· ὃ δὲ χρυσολίθῳ δέμας ἄντην
lines.en: it would have been crystal; and the other, in form when viewed full-on, is like chrysolite to behold;
lines.note: Antēn (“full-on, face to face”) intensifies the visual comparison; eisideein is Homeric “to behold.” Chrysolithos (“chrysolite”) in ancient gemology typically refers to a yellow-green stone (often our peridot/topaz range).

lines.gr: εἴκελος εἰσιδέειν· εἰ δ' οὐκ ἔχεν οὐδ' ὅγ' ἐθείρας,
lines.en: and if it too did not have hairs,
lines.note: Hog’ = ὅγε (“that one indeed”), here “it too.”

lines.gr: χρυσόλιθός κεν ἔην· ἀτὰρ ἐσθλώ φημι τετύχθαι.
lines.en: it would have been chrysolite; yet I declare the pair to be well made.
lines.note: Esthlō is dual (“the two”); tetuchthai is perf. inf. of teuchō (“to be made/formed”): “I affirm the pair are of excellent make,” i.e., fine specimens despite the inclusions.

lines.gr: ἐν γάρ σφιν μέγα δή τι φερέσβιος ἔμβαλε πνεῦμα
lines.en: For into them indeed Hēlios cast a great life-bringing breath,
lines.note: “in them” (sphin) most naturally refers to the stones under discussion; “life‑bringing” renders feresbios, an epic epithet (cf. “life‑bearing earth”), here transferred to pneuma (“breath/spirit”). The aorist “cast” (embale) conveys a decisive endowment by Hēlios.

lines.gr: Ἠέλιος, ῥέζειν ἐρικυδέας αὐτίκα φῶτας
lines.en: so that mortals straightway might accomplish illustrious deeds,
lines.note: The infinitive rhezein depends on “cast,” expressing purpose/result; phōtas is the accusative subject (“mortals”). Erikydeas is a Homeric epithet meaning “very glorious/illustrious,” and autika means “at once/straightway.”

lines.gr: σεμνοτέρους τ' ἰδέειν· καί τοι σέβας ἔσσεται αὐτῶν.
lines.en: and be more august to behold; and you will hold them in reverence.
lines.note: The infinitive ideein continues the construction: “to behold them more august.” The pronouns (“them”) can refer either to the mortals endowed by the stones or, less likely, back to the stones themselves; the former suits the sequence from line 304. “And you will hold them in reverence” renders kai toi sebas essetai autōn, with toi as a dative of advantage (“for you”).

lines.gr: αἶψα γὰρ ἡρώων σφιν ἐπέρχεται εἶδος ἀγαυόν,
lines.en: For at once the august form of heroes comes upon them,
lines.note: αἶψα = “at once.” ἡρώων … εἶδος ἀγαυόν literally “the noble/august form of heroes”; εἶδος suggests an epiphanic “aspect.” σφιν (dat. pl.) with ἐπέρχεται “comes upon them,” implying an overshadowing or possession-like coming.

lines.gr: οἵ κε θεοῦ μέγα δῶρον ἐπισταμένως φορέωσι.
lines.en: those who knowingly wear the god’s great gift about them.
lines.note: οἵ κε + subjunctive (φορέωσι) = a generalizing relative: “those who (may).” φορέω commonly of wearing/bearing habitually (e.g., amulets). ἐπισταμένως = “knowingly, skillfully.” θεοῦ μέγα δῶρον is the god-given stone/amulet in the poem’s context.

lines.gr: - Τόλμα δ' ἀθανάτους καὶ ἐνηέϊ μειλίσσεσθαι
lines.en: Dare even to appease the deathless with kindly intent, by means of the Magnesian stone;
lines.note: τόλμα is a 2nd sg imperative (“dare!”), fitting the didactic register; μειλίσσεσθαι ‘appease, propitiate’ (often of divinities). ἐνήεϊ is a dative of manner (“with kindly intent”). μαγνήσσῃ is an instrumental dative, an epic/feminine variant for the Magnesian (magnet) stone (cf. Μαγνήτις).

lines.gr: μαγνήσσῃ· τὴν δ' ἔξοχ' ἐφίλατο θούριος Ἄρης,
lines.en: and her the battle-furious Ares loved exceedingly,
lines.note: θούριος ‘battle‑furious’ is a fixed epithet of Ares; the line offers a mythic aition for the magnet’s attraction to iron (Ares’ metal).

lines.gr: οὕνεκεν, ὁππότε κεν πελάσῃ πολιοῖο σιδήρου,
lines.en: since, whenever she draws near to the grey iron,
lines.note: ὁππότε κεν with subjunctive gives a general temporal clause (“whenever”); πολιοῖο ‘grey/hoary’ is a conventional epithet of iron.

lines.gr: ἠΰτε παρθενικὴ τερενόχροα χερσὶν ἑλοῦσα
lines.en: just as a maiden, soft‑skinned, taking [him] by the hands,
lines.note: τερενόχροα ‘soft‑skinned’ is Homeric; χερσὶν ἑλοῦσα = ‘taking [him] by the hands’ (aorist participle of αἱρέω).

lines.gr: ἠΐθεον στέρνῳ προσπτύσσεται ἱμερόεντι,
lines.en: embraces the unwed youth at her desirous bosom,
lines.note: ἠίθεος = ‘unwed youth’; προσπτύσσεται ‘embraces, clings to’; ἱμερόεντι ‘desirable’ modifies στέρνῳ ‘bosom’.

lines.gr: ὣς ἥγ' ἁρπάζουσα ποτὶ σφετερὸν δέμας αἰεὶ
lines.en: so she, snatching, ever draws it toward her own body,
lines.note: σφετερόν δέμας = ‘her own body’ (δέμας is epic for ‘body’); ἥγ’ = ἥ γε. The feminine pronoun personifies the stone (Μαγνήτις is fem.).

lines.gr: ἂψ πάλιν οὐκ ἐθέλει μεθέμεν πολεμιστὰ σίδηρον.
lines.en: and back again is unwilling to let go the warlike iron.
lines.note: μεθέμεν is an epic infinitive (‘to let go, release’); πολεμιστά ‘warlike’ (from πολεμιστής) personifies iron as a warrior; ἂψ πάλιν is pleonastic, intensifying the notion of ‘back again.’

lines.gr: ἤτοι μέν μίν φασι καὶ Ἠελίοιο πέλεσθαι
lines.en: Indeed, they say it is even the attendant of Helios’ maiden,
lines.note: Accusative-and-infinitive with φασὶ … μίν … πέλεσθαι; ἀμφίπολος = “attendant/handmaid.” “Helios’ maiden” is an epic expression; in context (see vv. 317–18) it points to Medea, a descendant of Helios (granddaughter), though the phrase can broadly denote a Helian maiden.

lines.gr: ἀμφίπολον κούρης, ὅτε κεν θέλγητρα παλύνῃ·
lines.en: whenever she scatters enchantments;
lines.note: θέλγητρα (“enchantments, charms”) and παλύνειν (“to strew, scatter”) are standard epic-magic diction; the subject is the maiden (Medea) performing spells.

lines.gr: καί μιν ὑπερθύμοιο τεκοκτόνος Αἰήταο
lines.en: and of overbold Aeëtes, the child‑slaying [daughter],
lines.note: τεκοκτόνος is the epic/variant form of τεκνοκτόνος (“child‑slaying”), an epithet of Medea. Its genitive here stands in hyperbaton with ὑπερθύμοιο … Αἰήταο (“of overbold Aeëtes”), effectively “the child‑slaying daughter of overbold Aeëtes.”

lines.gr: κύδηνεν κούρη πολυμήχανος. αὐτὰρ ἔγωγε
lines.en: the many‑devising maiden made it renowned. But I, for my part,
lines.note: κῦδος-verb κύδηνεν = “made glorious/renowned”; πολύμηχανος = “many‑devising, resourceful,” a conventional epithet of Medea as a skilled witch.

lines.gr: σῆς ἀλόχου κέλομαί σε δαήμεναι, εἰ ἕθεν ἁγνὸν
lines.en: bid you to learn concerning your wife, whether it
lines.note: κελόμαι + infinitive δαήμεναι (“I bid/urge you to learn/ascertain”); σῆς ἀλόχου is a possessive genitive understood with λέχος καὶ σῶμα in the next line (“your wife’s bed and body”).

lines.gr: ἀνδρὸς ἀπ' ἀλλοτρίοιο λέχος καὶ σῶμα φυλάσσει.
lines.en: keeps her bed and body pure from another man.
lines.note: ἕθεν (“from him/her”) is proleptic, clarified by ἀνδρὸς ἀπ’ ἀλλοτρίοιο (“from another/alien man”); λέχος (“bed”) is metonymic for sexual relations. φυλάσσει = “keeps/guards,” describing the stone’s apotropaic, chastity‑preserving power.

lines.gr: ἐς γάρ μιν κομίσας ὑπὸ δέμνια κάτθεο λάθρη
lines.en: For indeed, having brought it in, set it secretly beneath the bedding;
lines.note: μιν likely refers to the stone (the subject of the recipe); κάτθεο is 2nd sg aorist middle imperative “set, lay down (for yourself)”; δέμνια = “bedding/bedclothes”; λάθρη = “in secret.”

lines.gr: χείλεσιν ἀείδων θελξίμβροτον ἀτρέμας ᾠδήν·
lines.en: singing with your lips a mortal-bewitching song, softly;
lines.note: θελξίμβροτον (lit. “bewitching to mortals”) is a traditional magical epithet; ἀτρέμας = “without motion, gently/softly.”

lines.gr: ἣ δὲ κατακνώσσουσα καὶ ἡδέϊ περ μάλ' ἐν ὕπνῳ
lines.en: and she, settling to slumber and very sweetly indeed in sleep,
lines.note: κατακνώσσουσα is a rare epic form meaning “to settle down to sleep, slumber soundly”; ἡδέϊ περ μάλ’ intensifies “very sweetly indeed.”

lines.gr: ἀμφί σε χεῖρ' ὀρέγουσα ποτιπτύσσειν μενεαίνει·
lines.en: stretching her hands about you, longs to enfold you;
lines.note: ποτιπτύσσειν (from πτύσσω “to fold, wrap”) here means “to enfold/embrace”; μενεαίνει = “is eager/longs vehemently.”

lines.gr: εἰ δέ ἑ μαχλοσύνῃσιν ἐλαύνοι δῖ' Ἀφροδίτη,
lines.en: and if divine Aphrodite should drive her on with wantonness,
lines.note: μαχλοσύνῃσιν (dat. pl.) = “with wanton desires/lewdness”; δῖ’ Aphrodite preserves the epic epithet “divine/splendid.”

lines.gr: ὑψόθεν ἐς γαῖαν τετανύσσεται ἐκπροπεσοῦσα.
lines.en: from aloft to the earth she will be stretched out, having fallen headlong.
lines.note: τετανύσσεται is an epic (middle) future “will be stretched out”; ἐκπροπεσοῦσα = “having fallen headlong/out,” with ὑψόθεν (“from aloft”) likely evoking a couch or height; the image is hyperbolic of overwhelming passion.

lines.gr: καὶ δοιὼ μάγνησσαν ἀδελφειὼ φορεόντων
lines.en: And let two brothers wear the Magnesian stone,
lines.note: μάγνησσαν = the Magnesian stone (lodestone, magnetite); φορεόντων is a 3rd-pl. imperative “let them wear/carry,” used with the dual δοιώ ἀδελφειώ (“two brothers”) in epic style, implying an amuletic use.

lines.gr: θυμὸν ἀπειρεσίης φυγέειν ἔριδος ποθέοντε·
lines.en: longing to flee the temper of boundless strife;
lines.note: θυμὸν ἀπειρεσίης ἔριδος is “the temper/spirit of boundless strife”; ποθέοντε is dual (“the two desiring”). The construction means they wish to escape/banish contentious anger.

lines.gr: καὶ λαοὺς ἀγορήνδε συναγρομένους ὀπὶ καλῇ
lines.en: and the peoples gathered into the assembly, with a fair voice,
lines.note: ἀγορῆνδε uses the directional -δε “into/to the assembly (agora)”; ὀπὶ καλῇ is instrumental (“with a fair voice”). The line runs on to the verb in 330. συναγρομένους = “gathered together.”

lines.gr: θέλξεις, ἐν στήθεσσιν ἄγων μελιηδέα πειθώ.
lines.en: you will enchant, bringing honey-sweet Peitho into their breasts.
lines.note: μελιηδέα Πειθώ likely personifies Peitho (Persuasion); ἐν στήθεσσιν ἄγων = “bringing into the breasts,” i.e., instilling persuasion in the audience.

lines.gr: καί τοι πολλά κεν ἄλλα δυνησόμενος καταλέξαι
lines.en: And indeed I, being able, could recount many other things as well,
lines.note: καὶ τοι adds emphatic/explicative force (“indeed”); δυνησόμενος καταλέξαι = “being able to recount in full.”

lines.gr: θέσκελα τοῖο λίθοιο, τί τοι πλέον οὐρανιώνων
lines.en: wondrous marvels of this stone; but why should I speak further to you of the heavenly ones?
lines.note: θέσκελα = “divinely wondrous, numinous”; τοῖο λίθοιο = “of this stone” (picking up the specific stone under discussion); οὐρανιῶνων is substantival, “the heavenly ones” (gods/astral powers).

lines.gr: φθέγγωμαι; τῶν αἶψα καὶ ὑψόθι περ μάλ' ἐόντων
lines.en: It swiftly inclines and draws the heart of those who, though far aloft,
lines.note: Subject of ἐπιγνάμπτει/ἐφέλκεται is the stone (understood from λίθος); αἶψα “swiftly”; ὑψόθι περ μάλ᾽ ἐόντων = “though they are far on high.” The sense is that the stone wins/attracts the favor of the celestials.

lines.gr: ἦτορ ἐπιγνάμπτει καὶ ἐφέλκεται, ὄφρα κε σεῖο
lines.en: so that, for your sake,
lines.note: ὄφρα κε introduces a purpose clause (“so that”); σεῖο is genitive of σύ, here “for your sake/with regard to you.”

lines.gr: ὦκα μάλ', ὥστε τοκῆες, ἐέλδωρ ἐκτελέσωσιν.
lines.en: very quickly, like parents, they may bring your desire to fulfillment.
lines.note: ὥστε τοκῆες is a simile (“like parents”), stressing eager beneficence; ἐέλδωρ is Homeric for “desire, wish”; ἐκτελέσωσιν = “bring to fulfillment.”

lines.gr: ἀλλ' ἤτοι τάδε μὲν καὶ ἐπαυτίκα πειρηθῆναι
lines.en: But indeed these things can even be put to the test straightaway,
lines.note: ἐπαυτίκα = “immediately, on the spot”; πειρηθῆναι (aor. pass. inf.) has deponent sense “to make trial” and is used impersonal/infinitival: “can be put to the test.”

lines.gr: πάντα μάλ', ὅσσ' ἀγόρευσα, παρέσσεται, εἴ κ' ἐπὶ βωμὸν
lines.en: all, as many as I have proclaimed, will be at hand, if to the altar
lines.note: παρέσσεται (fut. of πάρειμι) = “will be present/available”; πάντα μάλ(α) = “altogether, indeed”; ὅσσ’ ἀγόρευσα = “as many as I have declared.” εἴ κ’ (for εἴ κεν) with aor. subj. ἔλθωμεν (in the next line) forms a future-vivid condition: “if we go.”

lines.gr: ἔλθωμεν. καὶ γάρ τοι ἐπισπόμενός μοι ὅγ' ἀνὴρ
lines.en: we should go. For indeed, you know, the man who follows after me
lines.note: καὶ γὰρ τοι = formulaic “for indeed, you know/assuredly”; ἐπισπόμενος (from ἐπίσπομαι) = “following after” (epic compound of ἕπομαι); ὅγ’ ἀνήρ = ὅ γε ἀνήρ, “that man (there).”

lines.gr: ὤμοισι κρατεροῖσι λίθων φέρει αἰόλον ὕλην.
lines.en: carries upon his mighty shoulders a variegated stock of stones.
lines.note: ὤμοισι κρατεροῖσι = Homeric dative “upon his mighty shoulders”; ὕλη, in this context, = “stock/material/mass” (not “wood”); αἰόλος = “variegated, iridescent,” apt for stones.

lines.gr: - Νῦν δ' ἐπεὶ ἀτραπιτοῖο πολὺ πλέον ἄμμι λέλειπται,
lines.en: Now, since far more of the bypath remains for us,
lines.note: ἀτραπιτοῖο (“of the bypath”) is a metaphor for the course of the discourse/instruction; ἄμμι = epic/Doric for ἡμῖν (“for us”); πολὺ πλέον = “far more,” and λέλειπται here means “remains.”

lines.gr: σεῖο δ' ἔτι κραδίην κλονέει μέγα δέργμα δράκοντος,
lines.en: and yet the great glare of the serpent still shakes your heart,
lines.note: σεῖο = poetic genitive “of you, your”; κλονέει = “throws into turmoil, shakes”; δέργμα (“gaze, glare”) suggests a baleful or petrifying look—apt for serpent lore.

lines.gr: μάνθανε καὶ δολιχῶν ὄφεων μὴ δειδέμεν ἰούς.
lines.en: learn too not to fear the poisons of long snakes.
lines.note: μάνθανε + μὴ δειδέμεν = “learn not to fear”; δολιχῶν (“long, long‑bodied”) is a conventional snake epithet; ἰούς here means “poisons/venoms” (not the Homeric “arrows”).

lines.gr: τρίψαι γὰρ λεπτὴν ὀφιήτιδα κέκλεο πέτρην,
lines.en: For you are bidden to grind the Ophiētis stone fine,
lines.note: ὀφιήτιδα πέτρην: the Ophiētis (“snakestone”), a lithic associated with snakes; λεπτὴν modifies the result of grinding (“fine”). κέκλεο is the epic middle imperative of κελομαι, functioning as a didactic injunction (“you are bidden”).

lines.gr: ἤν ποτέ τις κρατεροῖσι πεπαρμένος ἔλθῃ ὀδοῦσι,
lines.en: if ever someone should come, pierced by strong teeth,
lines.note: πεπαρμένος (from πείρω, “pierce”) with ὀδοῦσι (“teeth”) expresses “bitten”; in context the “strong teeth” implies snake’s fangs. ἤν ποτε τις ἔλθῃ has an implicit ‘to you’.

lines.gr: καί μιν ἐφ' ἕλκεϊ πάσσε· καὶ ἀτρεκὲς ἔσσετ' ὄνειαρ.
lines.en: and sprinkle it upon the wound; and it will be a sure remedy.
lines.note: πάσσε (2 sg. imper. of πάσσω) means “sprinkle, strew,” often of powders. ἀτρεκές = “sure, unfailing”; ὄνειαρ is Homeric for “boon, benefit,” here “remedy.”

lines.gr: σὺν δὲ καὶ ὀστρίτην οἴνῳ λίθον ἐντρίψαντας
lines.en: And in addition, after grinding the Ostrites stone in wine,
lines.note: ὀστρίτην: the “Ostrites” stone (gem-name; probably connected with ὄστρεον ‘shell/oyster’), identification uncertain. ἐντρίψαντας: aorist participle acc. pl.; the understood object of κέλομαι + infinitive; the stone is triturated into the wine to make a draught.

lines.gr: ἀκρήτῳ κέλομαι πίνειν ὀδυνήφατον εἰδώς.
lines.en: I bid one to drink it unmixed, knowing it to be pain‑assuaging.
lines.note: ἀκρήτῳ (οἴνῳ) = ‘unmixed’ (neat) wine. ὀδυνήφατον: ‘pain-assuaging/pain-quelling’ (lit. ‘making pains subside’).

lines.gr: - Καὶ σέο, δαιμονίη, μεμνήσομαι αὐτίκα, πέτρη,
lines.en: And of you too, daimonic one, I shall at once make mention, O stone,
lines.note: δαιμονίη (“daimonic”) marks numinous potency rather than moral “demonic.” μνήσομαι + gen. (“I shall remember of you”) is an epic formula; πέτρη is vocative (“O stone”).

lines.gr: αὐτοκασιγνήτη πολιῆς καὶ ὁμώνυμ' ἐχίδνης·
lines.en: own-sister of the hoary viper and namesake of the viper;
lines.note: αὐτοκασιγνήτη (“own-sister”) expresses kinship with the snake; πολιῆς (“hoary/gray”) is a stock epithet for serpents; ὁμώνυμος (“namesake”) suggests the stone bears the same name as the ἐχίδνα (viper). Ancient lapidaries know a stone called “echidna/serpent-stone,” used against snakebite.

lines.gr: ἥ ῥά ποτ' εἰναετῆ λώβην ἀμενηνὸν ἔθηκας
lines.en: who once made powerless the nine‑year affliction
lines.note: εἰναετῆ modifies λώβην (“injury, mutilation”): “the nine‑year affliction.” ἀμενηνόν is best taken predicatively with ἔθηκας: “you made [it] powerless/ineffective,” rather than attributively with λώβην.

lines.gr: ῥίμφα Φιλοκτήταο Μαχαονίης ὑπὸ τέχνης.
lines.en: of Philoctetes, swiftly, under the craft of Machaon.
lines.note: ῥίμφα (“swiftly”) underscores sudden cure after long suffering. Μᾰχαονίης ὑπὸ τέχνης = “under/by the craft of Machaon,” the healer son of Asklepios; the line alludes to Philoctetes’ famous snake‑wound and its eventual healing in some traditions by Machaon.

lines.gr: οὐ μέν πως κείνην Ποιάντιος ἔλπετο θυμῷ
lines.en: In no way did the Poïantian in his heart expect that
lines.note: “Poïantian” (Poiantios) = ‘son of Poias,’ i.e., Philoctetes. The demonstrative “that” anticipates the noun “disease” in the next verse.

lines.gr: νοῦσον ὑπεκφεύξεσθαι ἀταρτηρὴν ποθέων περ·
lines.en: he would escape the baneful disease, though he longed to.
lines.note: ποθέων περ is concessive: ‘though he longed [for it].’

lines.gr: ἀλλ' ὅγ' ἀλεξικάκοιο μαθὼν παρὰ πατρὸς ἀρωγήν,
lines.en: But he, having learned from his father an evil‑averting aid—
lines.note: ἀλεξικάκοιο ἀρωγήν = ‘aid/remedy that averts evil.’ In this Lithica context it refers to the protective/healing efficacy associated with a stone; ἀλεξικάκος can also be a divine epithet (e.g., Apollo), but here functions adjectivally of the remedy.

lines.gr: λᾶαν ὅτις κ' ἀκέοιτο βαλὼν ἔπι φάρμακα μηρῷ,
lines.en: a stone by which one might be healed by casting drugs upon the thigh—
lines.note: λᾶαν in apposition explains the ‘aid’: it is a stone. βαλών ‘casting’ here means ‘applying/placing’; μηρός ‘thigh’ may stand generically for the limb. The detail anticipates the restoration of Philoctetes’ mobility in v. 357.

lines.gr: σεῦεν ἐπὶ Τρώεσσιν Ἀλεξάνδροιο φονῆα·
lines.en: dispatched against the Trojans the slayer of Alexandros;
lines.note: Ἀλέξανδρος = Paris; ‘the slayer of Alexandros’ is Philoctetes. σεῦεν ‘sent/urged on/dispatched’ is poetically vivid; the subject (‘he’) is the same as above, with epic freedom of reference; the sense is that, once healed, Philoctetes was launched against the Trojans.

lines.gr: τόν ῥα μεθ' ὑσμίνην ἥκειν ποσὶν ἀρτεμέεσσι
lines.en: whom, after the battle, to have come with sound feet,
lines.note: ἀρτεμέεσσι (from ἀρτεμής) = ‘sound, uninjured.’ The infinitive ἥκειν depends on ἀπίστει in the next line.

lines.gr: Πριαμίδης Πάρις αὐτὸς ἀποθνήσκων περ ἀπίστει.
lines.en: Priamides Paris himself, though dying, did not believe.
lines.note: ἀπίστει ‘did not believe’ governs the complementary infinitive ἥκειν: Paris, even as he was dying from Philoctetes’ shot, could not believe that his former victim had come with sound feet.

lines.gr: ἔκτανε δ' ἠπεροπῆα Πάριν Ποιάντιος ἥρως,
lines.en: And the Poïantian hero slew Paris the deceiver,
lines.note: “Poïantian hero” = Philoctetes, son of Poias; ἠπεροπῆα is an epic epithet meaning “deceitful/overweening,” here applied to Paris.

lines.gr: κεκλομένου Δαναοῖς Ἑλένου Τροίηνδε κομίσσαι
lines.en: as Helenus was being summoned by the Danaans to bring to Troy
lines.note: Genitive absolute: keklomenou (κεκλομένου) with dative agent Δαναοῖς (“by the Danaans”); Helenus is the Trojan seer whom the Greeks, in some traditions, consult or compel.

lines.gr: λοιγὸν ἀδελφειοῖο μιαιφόνον ἐκ Λήμνοιο.
lines.en: from Lemnos the brother‑murdering bane of his brother.
lines.note: “Brother‑murdering bane” (λοιγὸν … μιαιφόνον) refers to Philoctetes—summoned from Lemnos—who becomes the slayer of Paris, Helenus’s brother; μιαιφόνος = blood‑guilty/murder‑stained. The phrase ἀδελφειοῖο (“of his brother”) depends on Helenus.

lines.gr: τῷ γὰρ Ἀπόλλων Φοῖβος ἔχειν λίθον αὐδήεντα
lines.en: For to him Phoibos Apollon granted to possess a speaking stone,
lines.note: αὐδήεις literally “voice-bearing, speaking,” a marked epithet for oracular or responsive stones in lapidary/magical contexts; divine name transliterated as Phoibos Apollon.

lines.gr: δῶκε, σιδηρίτην νημερτέα· τόν ῥα βροτοῖσιν
lines.en: an unerring siderite; which indeed to mortals
lines.note: σιδηρίτης (siderite) can denote an iron-stone, often identified with lodestone/magnetite; νημερτέα = “unerring, infallible,” a truth-epithet applied here to the stone’s reliable efficacy.

lines.gr: ἥνδανεν ἄλλοισιν καλέειν ἔμψυχον ὀρείτην,
lines.en: it pleased others to call the ensouled Oreites,
lines.note: ἔμψυχος (“ensouled”) is technical in magical lapidaries for stones that seem animate (e.g., magnets); Ὀρείτης (Oreites) is a stone-name, probably a variety of magnet/ironstone; the phrase means “others preferred to call it ….”

lines.gr: γυρόν, ὑποτρηχύν, στιβαρόν, μελανόχροα, πυκνόν·
lines.en: rounded, somewhat rough, sturdy, dark-hued, compact;
lines.note: ὑποτρηχύς = “somewhat rough/rugged,” a rarer descriptive; μελανόχροος = “dark-skinned/dark-hued”; the line lists tactile/visual qualities of the stone.

lines.gr: ἀμφὶ δέ μιν κύκλῳ περί τ' ἀμφί τε πάντοθεν ἶνες
lines.en: and around it in a ring, around and on every side, fibers
lines.note: ἶνες = “fibers/veins,” i.e., natural striations/veining in the stone; κύκλῳ, περί, ἀμφί, πάντοθεν intensify the idea of encirclement on every side.

lines.gr: ἐμφερέες ῥυτίδεσσιν ἐπιγράβδην τανύονται.
lines.en: stretch, like wrinkles, drawn across as if incised.
lines.note: ἐπιγράβδην (often printed ἐπιγράφδην) is a rare adverb, “as if inscribed/engraved”; ῥυτίδες (“wrinkles”) metaphorically describes the stone’s fine striations.

lines.gr: ἤματα μὲν τρί' ἐφ' ἑπτὰ βίην Ἑλένοιο πέπυσμαι
lines.en: I have learned that for three days out of seven one should avoid the might of Helios,
lines.note: βίην Ἑλένοιο is likely a corrupt form for βίην Ἠελίοιο (“the might of Helios”); cf. Homeric Ἠελίοιο. Hence “Helios.” ἤματα τρὶ’ ἐφ’ ἑπτὰ = “three days out of seven,” a standard purificatory span. The infinitives in the following lines depend on πέπυσμαι (“I have learned [that one must] …”).

lines.gr: θηλυτέρης τε λέχος φεύγειν καὶ κοινὰ λοετρά,
lines.en: and shun a woman’s bed and the public baths,
lines.note: κοινὰ λοετρά = “public/shared baths,” shunned for ritual purity; φεύγειν (“flee, avoid”) governs both this and the previous object.

lines.gr: καὶ μίμνειν ἀμίαντον ἐδωδῆς ἐμψύχοιο·
lines.en: and remain undefiled from the food of ensouled creatures;
lines.note: ἐμψύχου ἐδωδῆς = “food of living/ensouled beings,” i.e., meat; ἀμίαντος stresses ritual cleanliness.

lines.gr: ἀενάῳ δ' ἐνὶ πέτρον ἐχέφρονα πίδακι λούων
lines.en: and, washing the mindful stone in an ever‑flowing spring,
lines.note: ἐχέφρονα (“sensible, mindful”) personifies the stone, characteristic of the Lithica’s animating outlook; ἀενάῳ πιδάκι = “ever‑flowing spring,” i.e., running lustral water.

lines.gr: φάρεσιν ἐν μαλακοῖσιν ἅτε βρέφος ἀλδήσασκε,
lines.en: to cherish it with soft cloths as though it were an infant,
lines.note: ἀλδῆσασκε is iterative (“keep nourishing/cherishing”); the simile “like a baby” underscores tender, continuous care; φάρεσιν = “cloths, wrappings.”

lines.gr: καὶ θεὸν ὣς λιπαρῇσιν ἀρεσσάμενος θυσίῃσι
lines.en: and, having propitiated it like a god with glistening sacrifices,
lines.note: λιπαρός (“shining, oily, rich”) suits unctuous offerings; “like a god” marks the stone’s numinous treatment; ἀρέσσω = “to propitiate, win favor.”

lines.gr: λᾶαν ὑπερμενέεσσιν ἀοιδαῖς ἔμπνοον ἔρδεν.
lines.en: to make the stone ensouled with very mighty songs.
lines.note: ἔμπνοον (“breathing, inspirited”) rendered “ensouled”; ὑπερμενέεσσιν ἀοιδαῖς = “with very mighty songs,” i.e., potent hymns/incantations animating the stone.

lines.gr: ἐν καθαρῷ δὲ φάος μεγάρῳ λύχνοισιν ἀνάπτων,
lines.en: And in a pure hall, kindling the light with lamps,
lines.note: μέγαρον is “hall/inner chamber”; ἐν καθαρῷ marks ritual purity. φάος is epic for “light”; λύχνοισιν (“with lamps”) is instrumental, describing preparation of a purified space.

lines.gr: χερσὶν ἑαῖς ἀτίταλλε, θεουδέα πέτρον ἀείρων,
lines.en: with your own hands tend it, lifting the god-revered stone,
lines.note: ἀτίταλλε is an imperative “nurse, dandle, tend,” suggesting careful cradling. θεουδέα (lit. “god-fearing/filled with awe for the gods”) is transferred to the stone; I render “god‑revered” (others take “god‑fearing” or “awful with divinity”). πέτρον is the neuter “stone.” ἀείρων = “lifting/raising.”

lines.gr: μητέρι νήπιον υἱὸν ἐοικὼς ἀγκὰς ἐχούσῃ.
lines.en: like a mother holding her infant son in her arms.
lines.note: ἀγκὰς (“in her arms”) is an adverbial form (from ἀγκών, “arm/elbow”). ἐοικώς is the perfect participle “being like,” introducing the maternal simile that underscores reverent handling.

lines.gr: καὶ σὺ δ', ἐπὴν ἐθέλῃς ὄπα δαιμονίην ἐπακοῦσαι,
lines.en: And you too, whenever you wish to hearken to a daimonic voice,
lines.note: “ὄπα δαιμονίην” = “voice of a daimon”; ἐπακοῦσαι often implies hearing in response (oracular/auditory epiphany).

lines.gr: ὧδ' ἔρδειν, ἵνα θαῦμα μετὰ φρεσὶ σῇσι δαείης·
lines.en: do thus, so that you may learn a marvel within your mind;
lines.note: ἔρδειν is the didactic “do thus”; δαείης = “come to know, learn.”

lines.gr: ὁππότε γάρ μιν πάγχυ κάμῃς ἐνὶ χείρεσι πάλλων,
lines.en: for whenever you wear it out completely, shaking it in your hands,
lines.note: μιν refers to the stone under discussion; πάλλων = “shaking/brandishing.” The transitive sense of κάμνω (“wear out, tire”) suits the context.

lines.gr: ἐξαπίνης ὄρσει νεογιλοῦ παιδὸς ἀϋτὴν
lines.en: all at once it will rouse the cry of a newborn child
lines.note: νεογιλοῦ (rare) = “newborn”; ὄρσει = “will set up/rouse (a sound).”

lines.gr: μαίης ἐν κόλπῳ κεκληγότος ἀμφὶ γάλακτι.
lines.en: who has cried out in a nurse’s bosom for milk.
lines.note: μαῖα can mean “midwife” or “nurse”; here likely “nurse.” ἀμφὶ γάλακτι = “for milk.” The participle κεκληγότος modifies παιδός (“child”).

lines.gr: χρὴ δέ σε τετληῶτι νόῳ ἐπακουέμεν αἰεί,
lines.en: You must always keep listening with a steadfast mind,
lines.note: tetlēōti noōi: “with a dauntless/steadfast mind.” The participle epakouemen with chrē expresses continued obligation (“keep listening”).

lines.gr: μήπως ἠπεδανοῖο λυθεὶς ὑπὸ δείματος ἔξω
lines.en: lest, loosened by fear like a weakling,
lines.note: ēpedanoio (genitive of quality) = “like a feeble/weakling”; lutheis hypo deimatos = “slackened/unglued by fear.”

lines.gr: ἐκ χειρῶν οὖδάσδε βαλὼν χόλον αἰνὸν ὀρίνῃς
lines.en: casting it from your hands to the ground, you rouse
lines.note: oudasde: the -de particle gives “to the ground.” Cholon ainon is a traditional epic formula for “dread wrath.” The “it” is the divinatory stone handled in the rite.

lines.gr: ἀθανάτων. τόλμα δὲ θεοπροπίην ἐρεείνειν·
lines.en: the dread wrath of the Immortals. But dare to press for the oracle;
lines.note: theopropiēn ereinein: Homeric/epic idiom “to inquire/press for the oracle/prophecy.”

lines.gr: πάντα γὰρ ἐξερέει νημερτέα. καί μιν ἔπειτα
lines.en: for it will declare everything unerringly. And then it,
lines.note: exerei nēmertea = “will declare unerringly.” Subject is the stone (or its indwelling daimōn). Min = “it,” picking up the same referent.

lines.gr: πλησίον ὀφθαλμῶν, ὅτε κεν λήγῃσι, πελάσσας
lines.en: when it falls silent, bringing it close beside your eyes,
lines.note: lēgēsi = “it ceases (speaking/sounding).” Pelassas = “bringing [it] near.” Plēsion ophthalmōn = “close to [your] eyes.”

lines.gr: δέρκεο· θεσπεσίως γὰρ ἀποψύχοντα νοήσεις.
lines.en: gaze; for you will discern it divinely as it cools.
lines.note: apopsychonta literally “growing cold/expiring”; in context likely the heated stone cooling as its voice dies away. Thespesiōs = “divinely, wondrously.”

lines.gr: τῷδε μὲν Ἀτρείδῃσιν ἁλώσιμον ἔφρασε πάτρην
lines.en: By this [stone] he declared to the Atreidai that his fatherland was liable to capture,
lines.note: τῷδε is deictic and likely instrumental (“by this [stone]”), referring to the stone discussed in the surrounding verses. Ἀτρεΐδῃσιν = the sons of Atreus (Agamemnon and Menelaos). ἁλώσιμον = “liable to capture, doomed to be taken.” πάτρην is best taken as “his own fatherland,” i.e., Troy; the subject is supplied by the next line.

lines.gr: Λαομεδοντιάδης, φοιβήτορι λᾶϊ πιθήσας.
lines.en: the Laomedontiad, having obeyed the oracular stone.
lines.note: Λαομεδοντιάδης (“the Laomedontiad”) = a descendant of Laomedon; in this context likely Helenos, who revealed to the Atreidai how Troy might be taken. φοιβήτορι λᾶϊ = “the oracular (Phoibian) stone”; πιθήσας takes the dative after πείθομαι (“obey, heed”). The line underscores the stone’s prophetic function.

lines.gr: σοὶ δέ τι καὶ σθένος ἄλλο σιδηρίταο πιφαύσκω·
lines.en: And I also make known to you another potency of the siderite (magnet-stone).
lines.note: σιδηρίταο: gen. of σιδηρῖτης, the ‘iron-stone,’ i.e., the lodestone/magnet; not the modern mineral siderite. πιφαύσκω is a poetic verb meaning ‘declare, make known.’

lines.gr: ἑρπετὰ γὰρ δὴ πάμπαν ὑποτρομέοντι ἔοικας.
lines.en: for you indeed appear as one before whom creeping things altogether cower.
lines.note: ἑρπετὰ = ‘creeping things,’ esp. snakes. ὑποτρομέοντι (‘cowering before’) is dat. with ἔοικας ‘you seem/are like,’ yielding an elliptical sense: ‘you seem like (one) before whom reptiles cower.’ The syntax is compressed and has been thought difficult; the meaning is that the bearer of the stone causes reptiles to cower. πάμπαν intensifies (‘utterly, altogether’).

lines.gr: σεῖο δ' ἔχεν πολὺ μεῖζον ἀκοίμητόν τε νόοιο
lines.en: But he had a far greater and unsleeping dread in his mind,
lines.note: The MSS read seio nooo (“of you, of mind”), which is awkward in context; many take it as corrupt for heoio (“of himself, of his own”), which I follow in sense (“in his mind”). The object deima (“dread”) is enjambed to the next line; akoimeton = “unsleeping” is a formulaic epithet of ceaseless states.

lines.gr: δεῖμα Φιλοκτήτης μεμνημένος αἰὲν ἐχίδνης.
lines.en: Philoctetes, ever remembering the viper.
lines.note: deima is the object of echen from the previous line; Philoktetes is the subject, with memnemenos (“remembering, mindful”) referring to his perpetual recollection of the echidna (viper) that bit him.

lines.gr: τοὔνεκα Πριαμίδαο σαόφρονος οὔποτε νόσφιν
lines.en: For this cause he would never wish to depart from the prudent son of Priam,
lines.note: “Priamid, prudent” likely refers to Hector; νόσφιν (“apart from”) governs the genitive. The subject (“he”) is not specified here and is probably the man in the preceding context (the bearer/consultant) who clings to the Priamid for counsel; τοὔνεκα (“for this cause”) resumes prior material.

lines.gr: ἤθελεν ἔρχεσθαι, γουνούμενος, ὄφρα τιν' εἴπῃ
lines.en: supplicating him, that he might utter some succor,
lines.note: γουνούμενος is the conventional ‘clasping-the-knees’ supplication; the object is understood (the Priamid). θαλπωρή is ‘warmth’ metaphorically ‘relief/comfort,’ here ‘succor’ or remedy.

lines.gr: θαλπωρήν, εἴ πέρ ποτ' ἐπὶ χθόνα μητέρα θηρῶν
lines.en: if ever he should go upon the earth, the mother of beasts,
lines.note: χθόνα μητέρα θηρῶν is an elevated formula for “Earth, mother of beasts,” fitting epic-didactic register and evoking wilderness travel.

lines.gr: ἔρχηται, πῶς κεν πολιὸν γένος ἐκπροφύγῃσι.
lines.en: how he might wholly escape the hoary race.
lines.note: πολιὸν γένος, literally “the hoary/grey race,” is ambiguous; in this context it most plausibly denotes the grey breed of wild beasts (esp. wolves). ἐκπροφύγῃσι (with ἐκ-) intensifies: ‘escape completely/wholly.’

lines.gr: τῷ δ' ὅγε Λητοΐδην ἐπέων ἐπιμάρτυρα Φοῖβον
lines.en: And to him, Phoibos, the Leto‑born, as witness to his words—
lines.note: Λητοΐδην (“Leto‑born”) is an epithet of Phoibos (Apollo). ἐπέων ἐπιμάρτυρα = “as witness to his words,” a forensic/solemn formula; Φοῖβον and Λητοΐδην (acc.) depend on the participle in the next line, hence the enjambment.

lines.gr: κικλήσκων ἀγόρευε, τὰ δὴ νῦν σοι καταλέξω.
lines.en: —invoking him, he declared: “These things indeed I shall now recount to you.”
lines.note: κικλήσκων (present participle of κικλέω “call upon/invoke”) governs the deity as object; ἀγόρευε = “declared/spoke (formally),” and καταλέξω = “I will recount (in due order),” a didactic marker; δὴ adds emphasis to νῦν (“indeed now”).

lines.gr: - Εὖτέ με παῖδ' ἐδίδασκεν Ἀκειρεκόμης ἀγορεύειν
lines.en: When Akeirekomes was teaching me, a child, to proclaim prophecies,
lines.note: Akeirekomes: likely the variant Akersekomes, the epithet “Unshorn‑haired” of Apollo; here the god is cast as teacher of mantic speech. ἀγορεύειν “to speak publicly, proclaim”; μαντοσύνας (pl.) “prophecies, oracular lore.”

lines.gr: μαντοσύνας, μέγαν ὅρκον ἐκέκλετο πρῶτον ὀμόσσαι,
lines.en: he first bade me swear a mighty oath,
lines.note: ἐκέκλετο (middle of καλέω) means “he bade, called upon” in elevated diction; πρῶτον underscores that the oath precedes instruction.

lines.gr: ψευδέα μήποτε μῦθον ἐνισπεῖν ἀνθρώποισι.
lines.en: never to utter a false word to men.
lines.note: ἐνισπεῖν is a Homeric poetic infinitive “to utter, tell”; ψευδέα μῦθον is the formulaic “false word,” with ἀνθρώποισι (dat.) “to men/humankind.”

lines.gr: τοὔνεκεν ἀτρεκέως μάλα τοι ἐρέω τὰ ἕκαστα.
lines.en: Therefore I will relate to you, with full exactness, each particular.
lines.note: τοὔνεκεν = τοῦ ἕνεκα (“for this reason”); ἀτρεκέως (“exactly, without deviation”) with μάλα for emphasis; τοι is 2nd-person dative (“to you,” perhaps ethical); τὰ ἕκαστα = “the particulars, details.” A formulaic didactic transition.

lines.gr: φράζεο νῦν, ἥρως ἑκατηβόλε, μῦθον ἐμεῖο.
lines.en: Attend now, far-darting hero, to my word.
lines.note: φράζεο is a middle imperative meaning “take note/mark/heed.” ἥρως is a conventional honorific form of address in didactic epic. ἑκατηβόλε is a variant of the common epic epithet ἑκηβόλος (“far‑darting,” esp. of Apollo), here transferred to the addressee; some editors print ἑκηβόλε. μῦθος in this context is an authoritative instruction or teaching, hence “word.”

lines.gr: - Αὐτὴ γαῖα μέλαινα πολυκλαύτοισι βροτοῖσι
lines.en: Black Gaia herself, for much-wept mortals,
lines.note: πολυκλαύτοισι (“much-wept”) is an epic compound in the dative, ‘for’ or ‘to’ mortals who are the object of many laments; μέλαινα (“black”) is a conventional epithet of Gaia with chthonic and soil connotations.

lines.gr: τίκτει καὶ κακότητα καὶ ἄλγεος ἄλκαρ ἑκάστου·
lines.en: bears both wickedness and the remedy for each pain;
lines.note: ἄλκαρ (‘ward, cure, remedy’) governs the genitive ἄλγεος (“of pain”): hence “the remedy for each pain.” κακότητα can mean moral ‘wickedness’ or general ‘harm/misery.’

lines.gr: γαῖα μὲν ἑρπετὰ τίκτε, τέκεν δ' ἐπὶ τοῖσιν ἀρωγήν·
lines.en: Gaia brings forth creeping things, and against them she bore a help;
lines.note: ἑρπετά (“crawling things”) typically includes serpents and vermin. ἐπὶ τοῖσιν here has adversative force, ‘against them’; ἀρωγή = ‘aid, help,’ i.e., protective remedies.

lines.gr: ἐκ γαίης δὲ λίθων πάντων γένος, ἐν δ' ἄρα τοῖσι
lines.en: and from Gaia is the stock of all stones, and within them indeed
lines.note: γένος (“stock, kind”) is used in epic for classes of beings; rendering as “stock” preserves the didactic-register generality.

lines.gr: κάρτος ἀπειρέσιον καὶ ποικίλον· ὅσσα δύνανται
lines.en: there is strength without limit and manifold; as many powers as
lines.note: ἀπείρεσιον is Homeric ‘boundless, without end’; ποικίλον (‘manifold, variegated’) highlights the diversity of powers attributed to stones.

lines.gr: ῥίζαι, τόσσα λίθοι. μέγα μὲν σθένος ἔπλετο ῥίζης,
lines.en: roots possess, so many do the stones; great indeed was the might of root,
lines.note: The gnomic comparison ὅσσα… τόσσα (‘as many… so many’) equates the efficacies of roots and stones. The singular ῥίζης (‘of root’) is generic; I render the first clause with plural ‘roots’ for idiomatic clarity.

lines.gr: ἀλλὰ λίθου πολὺ μεῖζον, ἐπεὶ μένος ἄφθιτον αἰεὶ
lines.en: yet that of stone is far greater, since an unfailing force forever
lines.note: μένος ἄφθιτον (‘imperishable force’) is a marked epic formula; the contrast elevates stone over root in enduring potency.

lines.gr: γεινομένῳ μήτηρ καὶ ἀγήραον ἐγγυάλιξεν.
lines.en: the Mother bestowed on the newborn, and one that is ageless.
lines.note: ἐγγυαλίξεν (‘put into the hand, bestowed’) takes the dative γεινομένῳ (‘to the one being born’), i.e., to the stone; μήτηρ (‘Mother’) is Gaia. ἀγήραον (‘ageless’) apposes ἄφθιτον for emphatic permanence.

lines.gr: ἣ δὲ καταθνήσκει τε μινυνθάδιον θαλέθουσα,
lines.en: but she perishes, though blooming for only a very brief while,
lines.note: “she” reflects the Greek feminine and refers to the plant/herb (βοτάνη). μινυνθάδιον = “for a very short while”; θαλέθουσα = “blooming, flourishing.”

lines.gr: καὶ τόσον αὐτῆς κάρτος, ἐφ' ὁππόσον ἔμπνοός ἐστιν·
lines.en: and her might lasts only so long as she draws breath;
lines.note: κάρτος = “might, potency.” ἔμπνοος = “having breath, alive.” The sense is temporal: the plant’s power endures only while it lives.

lines.gr: εἰ δέ κ' ἀποπνεύσῃ, τίς ἔτ' ἐλπωρὴ παρὰ νεκρῆς;
lines.en: but if she breathes out her life, what hope is there any longer from a corpse?
lines.note: ἀποπνεύσῃ = “expire, breathe out [life].” ἐλπωρή = “hope, expectation.” παρὰ νεκρῆς = “from a dead thing/corpse”; a rhetorical question underscoring the plant’s loss of efficacy when dead.

lines.gr: ἐν μὲν δὴ βοτάναις ἄγυριν λυγρῶν τε καὶ ἐσθλῶν
lines.en: indeed, in plants there is an assemblage of baneful and of good things,
lines.note: ἄγυρις = “gathering, assemblage, assortment.” βοτάναις = “herbs/plants.” λυγρός vs. ἐσθλός mark harmful vs. beneficial properties.

lines.gr: δήεις, ἐν δὲ λίθοις ἄτην οὐ ῥεῖά κεν εὕροις.
lines.en: you will learn; whereas in stones you would not easily find ruin.
lines.note: δήεις = epic “you will learn/come to know” (2 sg fut of δάω/δαήσομαι). ἄτη = “ruin, delusion, harmful mischief.” οὐ ῥεῖά κεν εὕροις = potential construction, “you would not easily find.”

lines.gr: ἤτοι ὅσαι βοτάναι, τόσσοι λίθοι. Ἀλλὰ σύ γ' ἥρως,
lines.en: Indeed, as many as the herbs, so many are the stones; but you, hero,
lines.note: ἤτοι is emphatic (“indeed”); ὅσαι…τόσσοι is a correlative formula. βοτάναι = “herbs” (botanical, with didactic/lapidary resonance).

lines.gr: λᾶϊ σιδηρίτῃ πεφυλαγμένος ἑρπετὰ πάντα
lines.en: protected with the Siderite stone from all creeping things,
lines.note: λᾶϊ σιδηρίτῃ: dative of instrument, “with the Siderite stone.” Sideritēs is variously identified in lapidaries (often lodestone/magnetite or an iron-ore) and is credited with apotropaic power against reptiles. πεφυλαγμένος = “protected.” ἑρπετά = “creeping things,” esp. reptiles/snakes.

lines.gr: θαρσαλέως, εἰ καί τοι ὁμιλαδὸν ἀντιόωσιν,
lines.en: be bold, even if they come against you in a throng,
lines.note: ὁμιλαδόν = “in a body, en masse.” ἀντιόωσιν with dative τοι = “come against you.” θαρσαλέως = “boldly.”

lines.gr: ἔρχεσθαι διὰ μέσσα κελαινῆς οὐκ ἀλεγίζων
lines.en: go through the very midst of black mischief, not heeding
lines.note: διὰ μέσσα is epic for “through the midst.” κελαινῆς λώβης = “black/dark harm, outrage,” here of snake-inflicted injury. ἔρχεσθαι is an imperatival infinitive in didactic style.

lines.gr: λώβης. οὐ γὰρ ἔτι σφι θέμις μεμνῆσθαι ὀδόντων,
lines.en: harm; for it is no longer permitted them to be mindful of their teeth,
lines.note: σφι = enclitic 3rd-pl. dative “for them.” θέμις with infinitive = “it is permitted/allowed.” μεμνῆσθαι ὀδόντων literally “to remember their teeth,” idiomatic for “to resort to/use their teeth,” i.e., to bite; the stone renders them unable to bite.

lines.gr: οὐδ' εἴ κεν στείχοντος ἐνιχρίμπτοιντο πόδεσσιν.
lines.en: not even if, as you walk, they should brush against your feet.
lines.note: ἐνιχρίμπτοιντο (potential optative with κεν) = “might brush/graze against.” στείχοντος (genitive absolute) = “as you go.” πόδεσσιν dative = “at/with your feet.”

lines.gr: οὐδὲ γὰρ οὐδὲ μένειν περ ἔτι προφανέντα δύνανται,
lines.en: For they are not even able any longer to stand their ground once they have come into view,

lines.gr: ἀλλὰ μετά σφισι θάμβος, ἐλαυνομένοισι δ' ὁμοῖα
lines.en: but amazement is upon them, and, like creatures being driven,
lines.note: ἐλαυνομένοιςι (“being driven”) evokes herding or hunted animals under compulsion.

lines.gr: ἔσσυνται. τὰ δὲ καίπερ ἐναντίον ἀΐξαντα
lines.en: they rush together; and those, although they had darted in the opposite direction,
lines.note: ἔσσυνται (“they rush together”) is vivid of crowding animals; the neuter plural subject (sc. θήρεα, “beasts”) governs singular verbs elsewhere.

lines.gr: ἂψ ὀπίσω παλίνορσα μεθερπύζειν μενεαίνει·
lines.en: straight back again are eager to turn and follow after;
lines.note: μεθερπύζειν (“to creep/follow after”) is a rare compound of ἕρπω; παλίνορσα is an adverb “back again,” Homeric in color.

lines.gr: καί σφισιν ἐξαπίνης ῥόθος ἵσταται· οὐδέ τι πρόσσω
lines.en: and all at once for them the din is checked; nor do they advance at all,
lines.note: ῥόθος is a “roar/din,” here plausibly the growl/barking of the beasts; the sudden cessation (ἵσταται) underscores the charm’s effect.

lines.gr: νίσσεται, ἀλλ' ὀρέγοντα πέλας περιμήκεα δειρὴν
lines.en: but, reaching out their very long necks close at hand,
lines.note: The neuter plural subject takes a singular verb in Greek (νίσσεται), but English plural sense is clearer. ὀρέγοντα … δειρήν is the idiom “stretch out the neck”; πέλας implies “toward the charmer/bearer [of the stone].”

lines.gr: γλώσσῃσιν μεμάασι περισσαίνειν, σκύλακες ὥς.
lines.en: with their tongues they are eager to fawn around, like whelps.
lines.note: περισσαίνειν is a dog-specific verb, “to fawn (wagging the tail),” and the simile σκύλακες ὥς (“like whelps/puppies”) confirms the canine imagery; γλώσσῃσιν suggests licking.

lines.gr: πολλάκι καὶ κατέδαρθε δαφοινῶν ἄγχι δρακόντων,
lines.en: Often too he fell asleep close by the blood-dark serpents,
lines.note: κατέδαρθε is aorist 3sg of καταδαρθάνω (“fell asleep”); δαφοινός means “blood-dark/bloody,” here of serpents (δράκοντες = large snakes).

lines.gr: ἀμφὶ κυνηγεσίῃσι μένων ἐν τάρφεσιν Ἴδης,
lines.en: staying about the hunt in the thickets of Ida,
lines.note: κυνηγεσίῃσι is an epic dative plural “in/at hunting pursuits”; τάρφεα are “thickets.” Ἴδη is Mount Ida (likely the Troad).

lines.gr: θηρητὴρ Εὔφορβος ἀρωγῇ τῇδε πεποιθώς.
lines.en: the hunter Euphorbos, relying on this aid.
lines.note: θηρητὴρ Εὔφορβος stands in apposition as the subject of the preceding verbs. ἀρωγή (“aid, help”) with τῇδε (“this”) points deictically to the stone/charm just described; πεποιθώς = “trusting/relying.” The name need not be the Homeric Trojan Euphorbos.

lines.gr: δῶκα γὰρ ἀντομένῳ λίθον ἱερόν, οὐδέ ποτ' αὐτῷ
lines.en: For I gave to the one who met me a sacred stone, and never against him
lines.note: ἀντομένῳ is dative “to the one who encountered (me).” The ‘sacred stone’ (λίθον ἱερόν) alludes to a talismanic gem typical of the Lithica’s magical context.

lines.gr: ἐκ μάλα περ πολλῶν ἐλθεῖν κατεναντίον ἔτλη
lines.en: did any from among the very many dare to come and stand face-to-face.
lines.note: The subject of ἔτλη (“dared”) is understood; I supply “did any” for sense. ἐκ μάλα περ πολλῶν = “though they were very many.” κατεναντίον ἐλθεῖν is a battle-phrase “to come and stand opposite (in opposition).”

lines.gr: [missing]
lines.en: [line missing]
lines.note: Textual lacuna: the line is missing in our source.

lines.gr: τέρπετο δ' Εὐφόρβῳ περικαλλέϊ φέρτατος ἀνδρῶν
lines.en: And the best of men, the spearman Melanippus, took delight in very beautiful Euphorbus,
lines.note: τέρπετο with dative = “took delight in.” Euphorbus is the Homeric youth famed for beauty; φέρτατος ἀνδρῶν αἰχμητής is a formulaic “best of men, a spearman.”

lines.gr: αἰχμητὴς Μελάνιππος, ἀνεψιὸς ἐσθλὸς ἐμεῖο,
lines.en: my noble cousin,
lines.note: ἀνεψιὸς ἐσθλὸς ἐμεῖο = “my noble cousin,” the narrator’s identity is not explicit here; the apposition most naturally modifies Melanippus.

lines.gr: εἶδος ἀμώμητον καὶ ἐπ' εἴδεϊ κάρτος ἄρειον
lines.en: longing for a faultless form and, besides the looks, a might more excellent,
lines.note: ἐπ’ εἴδεϊ = “besides/in addition to the looks.” κάρτος ἄρειον = “a might more excellent/superior.”

lines.gr: αἰζηοῦ ποθέων δουρικλυτοῦ, εὐπλοκάμοιο.
lines.en: of a stalwart youth, spear-famed and fair-tressed.
lines.note: αἰζηός denotes a man in his prime; δουρικλυτός = “spear-famed”; εὐπλόκαμος = “fair-tressed,” a Homeric epithet especially apt for Euphorbus. The genitives depend on ποθέων (“longing for”).

lines.gr: τοὔνεκα καὶ μετὰ θῆρας ἀλωμένου οὔποτε νόσφιν
lines.en: Therefore, even while roaming in the hunt, never apart
lines.note: μετὰ θῆρας ἀλωμένου is syntactically awkward (genitive participle); many take it as an adverbial genitive (“while ranging after the prey”), and some emend to ἀλώμενος (nominative).

lines.gr: ἔσθενεν Εὐφόρβοιο μένειν Ἱκετάονος υἱός,
lines.en: had the son of Hiketaon the strength to remain from Euphorbos,
lines.note: ἔσθενεν (from σθένω) = “had the strength.” νόσφιν + genitive with μένειν gives “remain apart from.” The subject is “the son of Hiketaon”; Euphorbos is the genitive of separation. (The identification of this Euphorbos vis-à-vis other traditions is uncertain.)

lines.gr: ἀλλ' αἰεὶ λασίοισιν ἐν οὔρεσιν ἀντιθέοιο
lines.en: but always in the shaggy mountains,

lines.gr: καγχαλόων κούροιο μετ' ἴχνια σύν τε κύνεσσιν
lines.en: laughing aloud, he followed the tracks of the godlike youth with the hounds
lines.note: κούροιο (“of the youth”) most naturally depends on ἴχνια: “the youth’s tracks,” here understood of Euphorbos; καγχαλόων = “laughing/exulting aloud.”

lines.gr: ἕσπετο σύν θ' ἑτάροις, ἔθελέν τέ οἱ οἶος ἕπεσθαι.
lines.en: and with his companions, and he wished that he alone should attend him.
lines.note: οἶος = “alone, by himself”; οἱ is a dative of reference/advantage (“for him”), i.e., he wished that he alone should follow/attend him.

lines.gr: ἦ μέν κέν μιν πολλὰ πατὴρ μενέαινεν ἐρύκειν,
lines.en: Indeed, his father would in many ways be eager to hold him back,
lines.note: μενέαινεν ἐρύκειν is a Homeric-sounding periphrasis (“was eager to restrain”); μιν is the enclitic object pronoun (“him”).

lines.gr: ἀσχαλόων ἑὸν υἷα φίλον θήρεσσι μάχεσθαι,
lines.en: vexed that his dear son should fight with wild beasts,
lines.note: ἀσχαλόων = “vexed, distressed.” θήρεσσι μάχεσθαι literally “to fight with wild beasts,” suited to a hunter’s rage in epic diction.

lines.gr: καὶ Πριάμοιο βίη μιν ἐρήτυεν· οὐδ' ὅγε θυμῷ
lines.en: and the might of Priam would restrain him; yet not even then in his heart
lines.note: Πριάμοιο βίη (“the might/authority of Priam”) is an epic idiom for royal constraint; ἐρήτυεν = “held back, reined in.”

lines.gr: πείθετ' ἐπεὶ οὐ ἐθέλεσκέ ποτ' Εὐφόρβοιο λιπέσθαι·
lines.en: was he persuaded, since he would never consent to leave Euphórbos;
lines.note: Εὐφόρβοιο is most naturally the personal name Euphórbos (the Trojan, son of Panthoos). The subject who “would not leave Euphórbos” is thus likely a close companion or brother; the poem may allude loosely to Trojan figures without strict Homeric consistency.

lines.gr: ῥεῖά γε μὴν ἀέκοντα μέλας ἠρύκακεν ὕδρος,
lines.en: yet easily, though against his will, a black adder checked him,
lines.note: ὕδρος here is best taken as “adder/viper” (often ‘water-snake’ in older usage), with μέλας emphasizing its ominous color; ἠρύκακεν “checked/held back,” echoing ἐρύκειν above.

lines.gr: νέρθεν ὑπὸ κνήμην ὀλεσίμβροτον ἰὸν ἐλάσσας·
lines.en: having driven a man-destroying venom from beneath his shin;
lines.note: ὀλεσίμβροτον ἰόν = “man-destroying/demise-bringing venom.” Νέρθεν ὑπὸ κνήμην pinpoints a typical snakebite site on the lower leg.

lines.gr: τὸν μὲν ἔπειτ' ὀλοὴ νόσος ἔλλαβεν, οὕνεκ' ἔμελλεν
lines.en: then a deadly sickness seized him, because he was about to
lines.note: ὀλοὴ νόσος ἔλλαβεν is epic for lethal envenomation taking hold; οὕνεκ’ = “because/since.”

lines.gr: αὖθι λελείψεσθαι, τό ῥά μιν καὶ μᾶλλον ἔτειρεν.
lines.en: be left there on the spot; and that wore him down all the more.
lines.note: αὖθι λελείψεσθαι (middle) is an epic idiom for “to be left there” = to die on the spot; τὸ ῥά refers deictically to that impending fate, “and that (fact) wore him down even more.”

lines.gr: οἰκτείρων δ' ὀρέγοντα χέρας ποτὶ γούνατ' ἐμεῖο,
lines.en: And pitying him as he stretched his hands toward my knees,
lines.note: The phrase “stretching his hands toward my knees” reflects the epic gesture of supplication (grasping the knees).

lines.gr: αὐτοῦ τοῦδε λίθοιο διατρίψαντα κέλευσα
lines.en: then and there I bade him, after grinding this very stone,
lines.note: αὐτοῦ is taken adverbially (“then and there”); some take it intensively with τοῦδε (“of this very stone itself”). διατρίψαντα = “having ground down, triturated.”

lines.gr: λεπταλέην ἄχνην ἐπιπασσέμεν ἕλκεϊ λυγρῷ·
lines.en: to sprinkle the fine powder upon the baleful wound;
lines.note: ἄχνη (“bloom, scurf”) here = fine powder of the stone; ἐπιπασσέμεν is the epic infinitive “to sprinkle upon.”

lines.gr: καί ῥα μάλ' αὐτίκα φῶτα κραταιὴ κάλλιπε νοῦσος.
lines.en: and straightway the mighty sickness left the man.
lines.note: κραταιὴ νοῦσος personifies the disease as a powerful agent; κάλλιπε = “left, abandoned,” and φῶτα is the epic word for “man.”

lines.gr: τοῖον γαῖα βροτοῖσιν ἀρηγόνα τίκτεν ὀρείτην,
lines.en: Such a helper for mortals did Gaia bear—the mountain‑stone Oreitēs,
lines.note: ὀρείτην (Oreitēs) is the stone’s name, literally “mountain(-stone)”; treated here as a proper mineral name in -ites. ἀρηγόνα (“helper, aid-bringer”) stands in apposition, yielding “such a helper … the Oreitēs.” “Gaia” is retained as a theonym rather than “Earth.”

lines.gr: ὅς τε καὶ οὐταμένοις ἄκος ἡρώεσσι κομίζει,
lines.en: who also brings a remedy to heroes when they are wounded,
lines.note: ἡρώεσσι is the epic dative plural “to heroes,” which in didactic epic can denote noble men generally, not necessarily mythic figures. οὐταμένοις = “wounded.” ἄκος = “remedy, cure.”

lines.gr: καὶ στείρῃσι γυναιξὶ τεκεῖν φίλα τέκνα δίδωσι.
lines.en: and to barren women grants to bear their dear children.
lines.note: στείρῃσι γυναιξί = “to barren women” (dat. pl.). τεκεῖν is an epexegetic infinitive after δίδωσι, “grants (them) to bear.” φίλα τέκνα = “dear/beloved children.”

lines.gr: ποικίλα γὰρ θνητοῖσι λίθους ἔρδειν ἀγορεύω.
lines.en: for I proclaim to mortals to accomplish manifold things by means of stones.
lines.note: The construction ἀγορεύω + infinitive is didactic (“I proclaim/ prescribe … to do …”). ἔρδειν normally means “do, perform” (often of sacrifices) and here aptly “effect” in a magical/technical context. The double accusative ποικίλα … λίθους is syntactically knotty: ποικίλα may be taken either as an internal object (“manifold [deeds]”) with λίθους as an instrumental-like accusative (“with stones”), or as an adjective modifying λίθους (“variegated stones”); in either case the sense is that mortals are instructed in performing diverse operations involving stones.

lines.gr: ὡς καὶ ἑῆς ποτὲ μητρὸς Ἀβαρβαρέης ἐπακούσας,
lines.en: as once too, when he had hearkened to his own mother Abarbareê,
lines.note: Abarbareê (Ἀβαρβαρέη) is the Naiad known from Il. 6.21–24; here she appears as a healer. ἐπακούσας = “having listened/hearkened to.” The subject is Euphorbus (named in 466).

lines.gr: ἀνδρῶν εὖ μάλα νοῦσον ἐπισταμένης ἀκέσασθαι,
lines.en: who full well knew how to heal the sickness of men,
lines.note: ἐπισταμένης ἀκέσασθαι = “knowing how to cure”; νόσον ἀνδρῶν is a generic “disease of men.”

lines.gr: Βουκολίδης Εὔφορβος ἀγαυοῦ φάσκεν ὀφίτου
lines.en: Boukolides Euphorbus declared that the remedies of the illustrious ophites-stone
lines.note: Boukolides = “son of Boukolion,” an epic patronymic; attributing this to Euphorbus is non-Homeric and may reflect Orphic/late mythographic reshaping. ἀγαυός = “illustrious, proud.” ὀφίτης is a lapidary term for the “ophites/serpentine” stone; φάρμακα here are the stone’s “remedies/virtues.” φάσκεν = “he used to say/declared” (iterative in tone).

lines.gr: φάρμακα μὴ μούνων ὄφεων κατένωπα δύνασθαι,
lines.en: have power not only when face-to-face against serpents,
lines.note: κατένωπα (adv.) = “face-to-face, in direct encounter”; thus “effective against serpents when confronted by them.” The line articulates the anti-snake efficacy of the ophites beyond mere snakebite lore.

lines.gr: ἀλλὰ καὶ ὀφθαλμοῖσι φέρειν φάος, ἠδὲ βαρεῖαν
lines.en: but also to bring light to the eyes, and to draw the grievous
lines.note: φάος φέρειν = idiomatically “to bring light,” i.e., restore sight. The list moves from anti-venom to ophthalmic and cephalalgic uses.

lines.gr: ἐκ κεφαλῆς ἕλκειν ὀδύνην· ἤδη δέ τιν' ἀνδρῶν
lines.en: pain out from the head; and once indeed,
lines.note: ἕλκειν ὀδύνην = “draw out pain,” a common medical/magical extraction metaphor.

lines.gr: οὔασι δηθύνοντα καθήρας ὤπασεν αἶψα
lines.en: having purified a man whose ears suffered a lingering trouble, he straightway bestowed
lines.note: οὔασι = “in the ears” (dative). δηθύνων/δηθύνοντα = “lingering, chronic.” καθῆρας = “having purified/cleansed,” suggesting a ritual application of the stone’s power. ὤπασεν = “he bestowed/granted,” with Euphorbus as subject.

lines.gr: καὶ δὴ καὶ λεπτῆς ἐριήκοον ἔμμεν ἀϋτῆς.
lines.en: that he should be keen-hearing even for a delicate cry.
lines.note: ἐριήκοον = “keen-hearing” (epic/poetic). λεπτῆς ἀϋτῆς = “of a thin/faint cry/voice,” i.e., even very soft sound.

lines.gr: ἤδη καί τινα φῶτα χόλῳ χρυσέης Ἀφροδίτης
lines.en: Even once a certain man, under the wrath of golden Aphrodite,
lines.note: χόλῳ χρυσέης Ἀφροδίτης: “in/under the wrath of golden Aphrodite.” The dative χόλῳ with a subjective genitive expresses the cause of the man’s condition; χρυσέης is the conventional epithet of Aphrodite. ἤδη καί introduces an exemplum (“even once”).

lines.gr: ἔργα πρὸς ἱμερόεντα γάμων ἀμενηνὸν ἐόντα
lines.en: being powerless for the desire‑kindling works of marriage,
lines.note: ἔργα γάμων is a euphemism for sexual intercourse; ἱμερόεντα (“desire‑kindling, lovely”) preserves epic diction. ἀμενηνός here conveys impotence (“powerless”). πρὸς + acc. indicates reference/fitness (“for, with respect to”).

lines.gr: μεμνῆσθαι φιλότητος ἀκεσσάμενος προΐαλλεν.
lines.en: it, having healed him, sent him forth to remember love.
lines.note: ἀκεσσάμενος is the aorist middle participle of ἀκέομαι (“to heal, cure”); the subject is the stone described in the context, which “heals” and then acts. προΐαλλεν is the imperfect of προΐημι/προΐαλλω (“sent forth”), taking τινα φῶτα as its object and the infinitive μεμνῆσθαι as a purpose/result construction; φιλότης in epic denotes sexual love. The sense is that the stone cured the man’s impotence and made him mindful of love again.

lines.gr: ἐν πυρὶ δ' εἴ κε βάλῃς μιν, ὀδωδὴν ἑρπετὰ τοῖο
lines.en: But if you should cast it into the fire, the reptiles will flee its odor,
lines.note: ‘ἑρπετά’ (neuter plural) is the subject; epic concord gives the singular verb ‘φεύξεται’. ‘ὀδωδή’ denotes ‘smell, reek’ (here unpleasant). ‘τοῖο’ is a pronominal genitive, ‘of it/this (stone)’.

lines.gr: φεύξεται, οὐδ' ἔτι πω μενέει σχεδόν, οὐδ' ἐνὶ χειῇ.
lines.en: nor will they any longer remain nearby, nor even in their lair.
lines.note: ‘χειῇ’ is a rare/uncertain word; most take it to mean ‘lair/den’ (of a snake). The sense is that, driven by the odor, the reptiles will not stay near—not even in their hole.

lines.gr: - Φεύγει καὶ κνίσσῃσι γαγάτην ὀρνυμένῃσι
lines.en: He even flees when the fumes are roused from gagate,
lines.note: γαγάτην = gagate (jet). The syntax is compressed: κνίσσῃσι … ὀρνυμένῃσι is instrumental (“with/at the fumes when they are raised”), and the understood subject (likely the serpent from the context of lapidary lore) is said to flee before the smoke of burning gagate. The accusative γαγάτην is awkward; some editors prefer a dative (γαγάτῃσι) or express the source with a preposition (“from gagate”).

lines.gr: τείροντα θνητοὺς ἐχεπευκέϊ πάντας ἀϋτμῇ.
lines.en: the one that wears down all mortals with a piercing exhalation.
lines.note: ἐχεπευκέϊ (Homeric ‘keen, piercing’) modifies ἀϋτμῇ (‘breath, vapour, exhalation’). The participle τείροντα (‘wearing down, afflicting’) characterizes the same subject as in the previous line (the harmful creature/force), here described as vexing all mortals by a sharp, noxious breath.

lines.gr: χροιὴν δ' αἰθαλόεις, πλατύς, οὐ μέγας ἔπλετ' ἰδέσθαι,
lines.en: Soot-dark in hue, broad, not large to behold,
lines.note: αἰθαλόεις = “soot-dark, smoky-black”; ἔπλετ’ (for ἔπλετο) ἰδέσθαι is the epic idiom “was to be seen/appeared.” πλατύς may suggest a flat, broad shape. The description likely suits a combustible black stone (often taken as gagates/jet).

lines.gr: καρφαλέῃ δ' ἴκελον πεύκῃ φλόγα δῖαν ὀρίνει.
lines.en: and, like dry pine, it stirs a bright flame.
lines.note: καρφαλέῃ πεύκῃ = “dry pine,” a standard ancient comparison for ready combustibility; ὀρίνει (“stirs up, kindles”) here of flame; δῖαν (“bright, radiant”) is the epic epithet of the flame.

lines.gr: ἀλλ' ὀλοὸν ποτὶ ῥῖνας ἄγει μένος· οὐδέ τι φῶτες
lines.en: but it brings a baneful might to the nostrils;
lines.note: ὀλοός = “baneful, deadly”; μένος = “might, force.” In context the subject is the stone just described, whose acrid fumes or power are directed at the nostrils (likely referring to the diagnostic use of its odor/fumes).

lines.gr: λήσονθ', ὧν κ' ἐθέλοις ἱερὴν ἀπὸ νοῦσον ἐλέγξαι.
lines.en: nor will mortals in any way forget the means by which you would wish to expose the sacred disease.
lines.note: λήσονθ' = λήσονται (epic future middle “will forget”), negated and intensified by οὐδέ τι (“not at all”). ὧν is a partitive genitive (“the means by which”). ἀπὸ ... ἐλέγξαι is epic tmesis for ἀπελέγξαι (“expose, unmask; drive off”); ἱερὴ νόσος = “the sacred disease,” i.e., epilepsy.

lines.gr: γνάμπτει γάρ σφεας αἶψα χαμαὶ προπρηνέας ἕλκων·
lines.en: for it straightway bows them down to the ground, dragging them prone;
lines.note: Line 483: γνάμπτει (“bows, bends”) with ἕλκων (“dragging”) takes σφέας (“them”) as object; προπρηνέας = “face-down, prone,” fitting the forcible toppling effected by the stone described in this section.

lines.gr: οἳ δ' ἄρ' ἀπὸ σφετέρου πεπαλαγμένοι ἀφλοισμοῖο
lines.en: and they, freed from their own clamor,
lines.note: Line 484: The phrase πεπαλαγμένοι ἀφλοισμοῖο is difficult. Many take πεπαλαγμένοι (perf. mid.-pass.) as “rid/cleansed (from),” and ἀφλοισμός as “din/uproar” (perhaps related to φλοῖσβος, “roar”), hence “freed from their own clamor.” Some editors have proposed emendations (e.g., ἀπηλλαγμένοι ἀλαλαγμοῖο, “released from their war-cry”). The translation reflects the transmitted text while conveying the likely sense.

lines.gr: στρωφῶντ' ἔνθα καὶ ἔνθα κυλινδόμενοι κατὰ γαῖαν.
lines.en: wheel to and fro, rolling along the earth.
lines.note: Line 485: στρωφῶντες … κυλινδόμενοι (“whirling … rolling”) pile up motion-verbs to depict the violent collapse and thrashing on the ground.

lines.gr: τοῖσι δὲ χωομένη φρένα τέρπεται, ὁππότ' ἴδῃσι
lines.en: And, angered at them, she delights her mind, whenever she beholds
lines.note: τοῖσι is a dative of reference (“at/against them”), with χωομένη (“being wroth”) governing it; φρένα τέρπεται is the idiom “delights her mind/heart.” ὁππότε (“whenever”) introduces the temporal clause, with enjambed object to the next line.

lines.gr: πήματα πάσχοντας κεραὴ πόδας ὠκέα Μήνη.
lines.en: them suffering woes, the horned, swift‑footed Mēnē.
lines.note: Μήνη is the personified Moon; κεραὴ (“horned”) refers to the crescent’s ‘horns,’ and πόδας ὠκέα (“swift‑footed”) is a Homeric-style epithet transferred to the Moon’s rapid course. Syntax is epic: the object πῆματα πάσχοντας (“suffering woes”) precedes the delayed subject.

lines.gr: θηλυτέρη δ' εἴ κεν πολυφάρμακον ἀμφιβεβῶσα
lines.en: And if a woman, having girded herself with the polupharmakon stone,
lines.note: θηλυτέρη is a comparative used substantively (“the female, the woman”); some witness a dative (θηλυτέρῃ). ἀμφιβεβῶσα suggests wearing the stone as an amulet; πολυφάρμακον (“rich in remedies/spells”) is a technical epithet of powerful stones (here likely Gagates/jet).

lines.gr: καπνὸν ὑπὸ σπλάγχνοισιν ἀναΐσσοντα δέχηται,
lines.en: should receive the smoke darting up beneath her entrails,
lines.note: “Beneath the entrails” denotes fumigation applied from below (a standard gynecological practice); ἀναΐσσοντα = “leaping up, darting upward.”

lines.gr: ἀθρόος ἔνδοθεν ὦκα μέλας καταλείβεται ἰχώρ,
lines.en: then, all at once from within, the black ichor is swiftly drained down,
lines.note: ἰχώρ, elsewhere the “fluid of the gods,” here denotes a pathological discharge; καταλείβεται “is made to drip/flow down” emphasizes evacuation.

lines.gr: ὅς τε γυναικοφόνος νεάτῃ μίμνων ἐνὶ γαστρὶ
lines.en: which, lingering in the deepest part of the womb, is called woman‑slaying;
lines.note: γυναικοφόνος (“woman‑slaying”) marks the discharge as deadly if retained; νεάτῃ … γαστρὶ = “the lowest/deepest part of the womb.”

lines.gr: κέκληται. τότε δ' αὖτις ὑπὸ πνοιῇσι λίθοιο
lines.en: then again, under the breaths of the stone,
lines.note: πνοιῇσι λίθοιο (“the stone’s breaths”) = its fumes or exhalations during heating/fumigation.

lines.gr: δερκομένη γάνυταί τις ἑῆς θολὸν ἐκβλύζοντα
lines.en: as she looks on, she rejoices to see her own womb belching out its turbid matter,
lines.note: δερκομένη (“seeing”) + ἐκβλύζοντα (“belching/gushing out”) depict visible evacuation; νηδύς here = “womb.”

lines.gr: νηδύος· ἐκ γὰρ νοῦσον ἀπειρεσίην ἀλεείνει.
lines.en: for thereby she wards off an endless sickness.
lines.note: ἀλείνει = “wards off, averts”; ἀπειρεσίην (“boundless, endless”) is hyperbolic in didactic style.

lines.gr: ἄλλα τε πόλλ' ἐπὶ τοῖσι γαγάτην θέσκελα ῥέζειν
lines.en: And besides these, gagates performs many other wondrous deeds;
lines.note: gagates = jet (a bituminous lignite); θέσκελα ῥέζειν is an epic formula “to do wondrous things”; ἐπὶ τοῖσι = “in addition to these.”

lines.gr: οἶδα· σὲ δὲ κνίσσῃσιν ἐλαύνων ἑρπετὰ τέρψει.
lines.en: I know; and with its fumes, driving off reptiles, it will delight you.
lines.note: κνίσσησιν is an epic/dialectal dative plural of κνίση (“savor, smoke, fumes”), here the fumes produced when gagates is burned; ἐλαύνων (“driving off”) expresses the stone’s apotropaic power; ἑρπετά = “creeping things,” especially snakes/reptiles.

lines.gr: - Σκορπίε, σεῖο δὲ λᾶαν ὁμώνυμον ἔμμεναι ἥρως
lines.en: Scorpio, that there was a stone of the same name as you,
lines.note: ὁμώνυμον “of the same name” points to a gem called after Scorpio (a scorpion-stone) believed to counter scorpion harm; λᾶαν is the epic form of ‘stone’; σεῖο is the epic genitive ‘of you.’

lines.gr: ἀγλαὸς Ὠρίων οὐκ ἔκλυεν· ἦ γὰρ ὀΐω,
lines.en: the glorious hero Orion did not heed; for, I ween,
lines.note: οὐκ ἔκλυεν can mean “did not hear of” or “did not heed”; ἀγλαὸς is the epic epithet “glorious”; ἦ γὰρ ὀΐω is a formulaic “for, I suppose/I ween.”

lines.gr: πικρῇσιν τότε γυῖα πεπαρμένος ἀμφ' ὀδύνῃσι
lines.en: his limbs then being pierced through with bitter pains,
lines.note: πεπαρμένος (perf. part. of πείρω) = “pierced/shot through,” well-suited to a scorpion’s sting; ἀμφ’ ὀδύνῃσι = “amid/with pains all about.”

lines.gr: μᾶλλον σφωϊτέρων κεν ἔχειν ἐθέλεσκέ μιν ἄστρων.
lines.en: he would have preferred to possess it rather than the stars of them both.
lines.note: σφωϊτέρων ἄστρων is a genitive dual, “of the stars of the two [of them],” i.e., Orion and Scorpio as constellations. The sense: wounded by the scorpion, Orion would have chosen the protective stone over the stellar glory of both constellations. ἐθέλεσκε is iterative (“would be wont to wish”); μιν refers to the stone.

lines.gr: - Οὐδ' ὅγε κορσήεντα λίθον κλύεν, οὕνεκα μιχθεὶς
lines.en: Nor did one hear of the ‘Korsēen’ stone, since, when mixed
lines.note: κορσήεντα: obscure; often taken as a proper name (‘Korsēen’). Some suspect corruption (cf. possible relation to “parching/burning”), and κλύεν here is epic “heard of/was reputed as.” The subject is impersonal/general.

lines.gr: δριμέϊ σὺν σκορόδοιο καρήατι, τοξευτῆρα
lines.en: together with the pungent head of garlic, the archer
lines.note: καρήατι is the epic dative of “head,” i.e., the garlic bulb; δριμέϊ “pungent/biting.” τοξευτῆρα is in hyperbaton with σκορπίον in the next line.

lines.gr: πευκεδανῶν ὤκιστα βελέμνων σκορπίον εἴργει.
lines.en: of sure‑aimed missiles, it most swiftly keeps the scorpion at bay.
lines.note: τοξευτῆρα … πευκεδανῶν βελέμνων = “archer of sure‑aimed darts,” a metaphor for the scorpion’s sting; εἴργει “keeps off/wards off,” ὤκιστα “most swiftly.”

lines.gr: τὸν μὲν ἐγὼ κόρσῃ μάλ' ἐοικότα φημὶ βροτείῃ
lines.en: This one, I declare, very much resembling a mortal belly,
lines.note: korsē (κόρσῃ): a rare/poetic word for “belly, stomach” (≈ gastrí, γαστρί). The participle eoikota (ἐοικότα) modifies tón (τὸν), describing the stone’s shape.

lines.gr: παύειν ὀξυτάτῳ τετριμμένον ἄμμιγα Βάκχῳ
lines.en: when ground and mixed together with the sharpest Bakkhos, checks
lines.note: “Bakkhos” stands metonymically for wine; oxytátōi (ὀξυτάτῳ) suggests very sharp/sour wine, effectively vinegar. tetrimménon (τετριμμένον) = “ground”; ámmiga (ἄμμιγα) is an epic/dialectal form meaning “together with.”

lines.gr: ἀμφίπολον θανάτοιο κελαινῆς ἀσπίδος ἰόν.
lines.en: the poison of the black asp, handmaid of Thanatos.
lines.note: aspís (ἀσπίς) here means “asp (snake),” not “shield.” amphípolon thanatoio (ἀμφίπολον θανάτοιο) = “handmaid/attendant of Thanatos,” modifying ión (ἰόν, “poison”), personifying the venom as Death’s servant.

lines.gr: μέτρῳ δ' ὅς κεν ἴσῳ μίξῃ ῥοδόεντος ἐλαίου
lines.en: And whoever in equal measure mixes it with rose-scented oil,
lines.note: The object (“it”) is the stone under discussion in the context; ῥοδόεντος ἐλαίου = rose-scented (rose-infused) oil; ἴσῳ μέτρῳ indicates equal parts.

lines.gr: κόψας ἐκ πυρὸς ὀπτόν, ἐν αὐχενίαις ὀδύνῃσιν
lines.en: having first baked it in the fire and pounded it, for pains of the neck,
lines.note: ἐκ πυρὸς ὀπτόν = “calcined, baked by fire”; κόψας = “having pounded/ground (to powder)”; αὐχενίαις may denote the neck/throat region.

lines.gr: ἄλκαρ ἄγει· μέλιτος δὲ μετὰ γλυκεροῖο κερασθεὶς
lines.en: brings a cure; and, when blended with sweet honey
lines.note: ἄλκαρ (“defence, remedy”) is a poetic medical term; the verb here completes the construction begun in the previous line.

lines.gr: ὕδατος ἀτηρὴν ὀλέκει κατὰ γαστέρος ἰλύν,
lines.en: and with water, it destroys the baneful slime in the stomach,
lines.note: κερασθείς ὕδατος (by enjambment) = “mixed with water”; ἀτηρὴν ἰλύν = harmful “slime/sediment” in the stomach (gastric mucus).

lines.gr: ἥτε καταΐγδην ὑπὸ νέρτερα νηδύος ἀνδρῶν
lines.en: which, sinking straight down beneath the lower parts of men’s belly,
lines.note: καταΐγδην is a rare adverb meaning “straight down, headlong”; νέρτερα νηδύος = “the lower parts of the belly/gut.”

lines.gr: δυομένη φέρει ὄγκον ἀεικέα βουβώνεσσιν.
lines.en: brings an unsightly swelling upon the groins.
lines.note: ὄγκος = “mass, swelling, tumor”; βουβῶνες = “groins” (hence medical “buboes,” i.e., inguinal swellings).

lines.gr: - Ἴσθι δ' ἀμαλδύνειν σκορπήϊα κέντρα δύνασθαι
lines.en: Know, too, that it has the power to soften scorpion-stings,
lines.note: “It” refers to the stone under discussion in the surrounding context; ἀμαλδύνειν = “to soften, mitigate, blunt.”

lines.gr: καὶ Περσηϊάδαο μένος μέγα κουραλίοιο,
lines.en: and the great might of the Perseid coral,
lines.note: Περσηϊάδαο is “of the Perseid,” i.e., of Perseus; coral (κουράλιος here, a variant of κοράλλιον) is traditionally linked to Perseus (the Gorgon’s head turning seaweed to coral). Some editors emend κουραλ‑ to κοραλλ‑; the sense is “coral.”

lines.gr: ἠδὲ παλαμναίην ἀνεμώλιον ἀσπίδα θεῖναι.
lines.en: and to set in place an avenging wind‑shield.
lines.note: παλαμναίην (often ‘avenging,’ of Erinyes, or ‘expiatory/apotropaic’) and ἀνεμώλιον (‘wind‑borne/windy,’ elsewhere ‘vain’) form a difficult phrase; here likely ‘apotropaic shield against airy/blasting influences.’ θεῖναι = ‘to set up/establish (as protection).”

lines.gr: τοῦδε δέ μοι πάντων περιώσιον, ὅσσα φύονται
lines.en: But of this, to me, the most surpassing thing of all that come to be,
lines.note: τοῦδε (“of this”) points to the stone under discussion; περιώσιον = “preeminent/most exceptional.” The clause is syntactically completed by the following lines (enjambment). ὅσσα φύονται = “all that come to be/are produced.”

lines.gr: Φοῖβος ἀκειρεκόμης φύσιν ἔμμεναι ἐξ ἑτέροιο
lines.en: —Phoibos of the unshorn hair—its nature to be from another,
