lines.note: ἀκειρεκόμης is the traditional epithet “of the unshorn hair.” ἔμμεναι is Homeric for “to be.” ἐξ ἑτέροιο = “from another [thing],” implying derivation from a different substance/stone.

lines.gr: μυθεῖτ' εἰς ἕτερον στρωφωμένου εἶδος· ὅ τίς τοι
lines.en: declares, as it is turned into another form; whoever, I assure you,
lines.note: μυθεῖτ’ = “he declares/says,” resuming the main verb across the enjambment. εἰς ἕτερον … εἶδος = “into another form/shape.” στρωφομένου (from a verb meaning “to turn/whirl”) describes the change of appearance; the genitive is adnominal with εἶδος (“the form of one being turned”) or may be taken loosely as “as it is being turned.” ὅ τίς τοι = “whoever, I assure you,” with to-i giving a tone of assurance.

lines.gr: ψεῦδός κεν φαίη· τὸ δ' ἐτήτυμον οἶδα τετύχθαι.
lines.en: would call that a falsehood; but I know the truth has been wrought.
lines.note: ψεῦδός κεν φαίη is a potential optative (“would say it is false”). ἐτήτυμον = “true, genuine.” τετύχθαι (perf. inf. of τεύχω) = “has been wrought/has come to pass,” asserting the speaker’s certain knowledge against anticipated skepticism.

lines.gr: χλωρὴ γὰρ βοτάνη πρῶτον φύει· οὐδ' ἐνὶ γαίῃ,
lines.en: For first a green plant springs up; not in the earth,
lines.note: “Green plant” likely describes the initial, plantlike stage of coral in the Lithica’s account of its genesis; φύει = “springs up, puts forth.”

lines.gr: ἥν γε φυτῶν ἴσμεν στερεὴν τροφόν, ἀλλ' ἐνὶ πόντῳ
lines.en: which indeed we know as the firm nurse of plants, but in the unharvested sea,
lines.note: ἥν … ἴσμεν στερεὴν τροφόν: accusative + predicate accusative after ἴσμεν (“we know [it as] the firm/steadfast nurse”). “Nurse” is a conventional epic metaphor for the earth as nourisher of plants.

lines.gr: ἀτρυγέτῳ, ἵνα φύκι', ἵνα βρύα γίνετ' ἐλαφρά.
lines.en: where seaweed, where light mosses come into being.
lines.note: ἀτρυγέτῳ (Homeric epithet) = “unharvested” of the sea; φύκι' is an elided plural of φῦκα (“seaweed”); βρύα = “mosses” (here, marine growths). ἐλαφρά = “light/delicate,” primarily qualifying βρύα, though it may color both items.

lines.gr: αὐτὰρ ἐπεί κ' ἔλθῃσι μαραινομένη ποτὶ γῆρας,
lines.en: But when she, withering, comes upon old age,
lines.note: ἐπεί κ’ + aorist subjunctive (ἔλθῃσι) expresses a future eventual condition (“whenever/when she comes”); μαραινομένη = “wasting/withering away”; the feminine subject continues from the previous context; ποτὶ γῆρας = “toward/upon old age.”

lines.gr: ἤτοι μέν οἱ φύλλα περιφθινύθουσιν ὑφ' ἅλμης·
lines.en: then indeed her leaves wither away utterly under the brine;
lines.note: οἱ is a dative of possession (“her leaves”); περιφθινύθουσι is an intensive compound (“waste away utterly”); ἅλμη = “brine,” i.e., the salt sea, functioning as agent (“under/by the brine”).

lines.gr: αὐτὴ δ' ἐν βένθεσσιν ὑπὸ φλοίσβοιο θαλάσσης
lines.en: but she herself, in the depths beneath the sea’s surf,
lines.note: βένθεσσιν (poetic dat. pl.) = “in the depths”; φλοίσβος denotes the wash/roar of surf; ὑπό = “beneath.”

lines.gr: νήχεται, ὄφρα ἑ κύματ' ἀποπτύσῃ αἰγιαλόνδε.
lines.en: swims until the waves spit her out upon the shore.
lines.note: νήχεται can denote “swim” or “float” (of objects) in epic diction; ὄφρα + subjunctive = “until/so that”; ἀποπτύσῃ = “spit/disgorge”; αἰγιαλόνδε is a directional adverb “to(ward) the shore.”

lines.gr: ἔνθα δ' ἄρ' ἐξαπίνης μιν ἀναπλησθεῖσαν ὑπ' αἴθρης
lines.en: Thereupon, all at once, her, filled full by the clear aether,
lines.note: μιν is the enclitic object pronoun (“her/it”); the gender depends on the antecedent in the larger context. ἀναπλησθεῖσαν is an aorist passive participle (“having been filled up, replenished”); αἴθρη is the cloudless, bright “aether/clear sky,” which here suggests reanimation or empowerment by the upper air.

lines.gr: βάζουσ', οἵ περ ἴδοντο, κρατυνομένην ὁράασθαι.
lines.en: they say—those who indeed saw—was to be seen being strengthened.
lines.note: βάζουσ’ is the epic/poetic verb “they say.” οἵ περ ἴδοντο adds emphatic authentication (“those who indeed saw”). ὁράασθαι is the Homeric middle infinitive “to be seen.” κρανομένην is difficult: many editors emend to κρατυνομένην (“being strengthened, made firm”); if κρανομένην is retained from κραίνω, it would mean “being brought to fulfillment.” The translation adopts the sense “being strengthened.”

lines.gr: δηρὸν δ' οὐ μετέπειτα πάγῳ περιπαχνωθεῖσα
lines.en: But not long thereafter, having been thickly congealed by frost,
lines.note: δηρὸν οὐ μετέπειτα = “not long thereafter” (Homeric idiom). πάγος here means frost/ice. περιπαχνωθεῖσα (aor. pass. ptc.) = “having been thoroughly congealed/encrusted.”

lines.gr: πετροῦται, καὶ χερσὶν ἐν ὀκριόεντα τεῇσιν
lines.en: it is turned to stone; and in your own hands, jagged,
lines.note: πετροῦται is middle/passive “is turned to stone, is petrified.” The phrase χερσὶν ἐν τεῇσιν = “in your own hands.” ὀκριόεντα (“jagged, craggy”) modifies λίθον by hyperbaton; the sense is enjambed into the next line.

lines.gr: ἀμφαφάεις λίθον, ὃς πρὶν ἔχων ὑγρὸν δέμας ἦεν.
lines.en: you will handle the stone, which before had a moist form.
lines.note: ἀμφαφάεις is 2nd sg., likely future (“you will handle, feel all around”) from ἀμφαφάω. δέμας = “body, form.” ὑγρός = “wet, moist” (hence “formerly liquid” by implication). The line marks the contrast between prior fluidity and subsequent petrifaction.

lines.gr: σχῆμα μὲν οὖν βοτάνης ἔτι οἱ μένει, οἷον ἔην περ,
lines.en: Its shape, at any rate, of a plant still remains to it, just as once it was,
lines.note: “Form of a plant” (schêma botanês) signals that the outward appearance persists despite a change of substance—part of a description of a plant-like lithos.

lines.gr: οἵ τε κλάδοι, ὅσα τέ σφιν ἀκρόδρυα προσπεφύασιν,
lines.en: the branches too, and all the tree‑nuts that have grown fast upon them,
lines.note: Akródrya are “tree‑nuts” (hard-shelled fruits); here likely used metaphorically for knob-like growths on the branches. The perfect prosppephýasin (“have grown onto”) with the dative sfin (“on them,” i.e., the branches) emphasizes adhesion.

lines.gr: ἥ τέ οἱ ἐβλάστησε καὶ ἐτράφη εἰν ἁλὶ ῥίζα·
lines.en: and the root that sprouted for it and was nourished in the sea,
lines.note: “In the sea” (en hali) points to a marine origin; ancient descriptions of coral emphasize a plant-like growth in seawater before hardening.

lines.gr: φλοιός θ' ὅσπερ ἔην· φλοιὸς δέ γε λάϊνός ἐστι.
lines.en: and the bark just as it had been; yet the bark, for its part, is of stone.
lines.note: Lainos (“stony, of stone”) marks the substance as stone though the outline remains. The juxtaposition “the bark as it was … yet the bark is stone” underscores petrification while preserving form.

lines.gr: τερπωλὴ δ' ἡδεῖα θεωμένου ἐς φρένα σεῖο
lines.en: And a sweet delight, at the sight of you, into my heart
lines.note: θεωμένου … σεῖο is a genitive of the thing seen, “at the sight of you”; σεῖο is epic for σοῦ. The verb βήσετ’ is enjambed to the next line.

lines.gr: βήσετ'· ἐγὼ δ' οὐκ οἶδα, τί μοι θέλγητρον ἰδόντι
lines.en: will go; but I do not know what enchantment, when I look,
lines.note: θέλγητρον (“enchantment, charm”) suits the magical register; ἰδόντι is a dative of circumstance with μοι, “for me as I look.”

lines.gr: αἰὲν ἐπὶ πραπίδας καταλείβεται· οὐδὲ δύνανται
lines.en: ever is distilled upon my wits; nor are my eyes able
lines.note: πραπίδες (“wits, midriff”) is epic for the seat of thought; καταλείβεται (“is distilled/trickles down”) evokes a charm seeping into the mind.

lines.gr: ὄσσε κορεσθῆναι θηευμένου, ἀλλά με θάμβος
lines.en: to be sated with gazing, but amazement
lines.note: ὄσσε is the epic dual “eyes.” θηευμένου is from θηεύομαι (“to gaze in wonder”), not merely “to look” (θεάομαι).

lines.gr: σεύεται ἐν στέρνοισιν ὀϊόμενον τέρας εἶναι·
lines.en: races in my breast, as I suppose it to be a prodigy;
lines.note: σεύεται (“rushes/darts”) takes θάμβος (“amazement”) as subject; ὀϊόμενον is acc. sg. agreeing with με, “as I suppose it to be a portent.”

lines.gr: καί οἱ πιστεύων περ ἔολπά μιν εἶναι ἄπιστον.
lines.en: and even while trusting in it, I have deemed it incredible.
lines.note: καί οἱ = “and in it/and to it” (dative); μιν = “it.” ἔολπα (perf. of ἐλπίζω) here means “I deem/hold”; ἄπιστον is “incredible, beyond belief,” capturing the paradox of πιστεύων vs. ἄπιστον.

lines.gr: ἀλλ' οὐ Γοργείην μὲν ἐτώσιος ἀνθρώποισι
lines.en: But among mortals the report of the Gorgonian dread head is no mere rumor,
lines.note: οὐ … φάτις ἔμμεναι with ἐτώσιος (“true, genuine”) yields the idiom “no mere rumor,” i.e., the tradition is affirmed as real rather than idle talk; ἀνθρώποισι = “among men/mortals.”

lines.gr: σμερδαλέην κεφαλὴν φάτις ἔμμεναι· οὐδ' ἄρα Περσεὺς
lines.en: that there is a dread head—so runs the tale; nor indeed did Perseus
lines.note: φάτις ἔμμεναι literally “to be a report/rumor”; σμερδαλέην (“dread, fearsome”) is a conventional epic epithet.

lines.gr: ὠκυπέτης πέλεται ψευδὲς τέρας ἡγήσασθαι.
lines.en: the swift‑flying, deem it a lying portent.
lines.note: ὠκυπέτης (“swift‑flying”) is the epic epithet of Perseus; ψευδὲς τέρας = “lying/false portent.” πέλεται + infinitive is a poetic construction meaning “is/comes to be (so as) to …,” here rendered idiomatically as “deem.”

lines.gr: Γοργόνα γὰρ Περσῆϊ δρακοντοέθειραν ἀκούεις
lines.en: For you hear that the Gorgon, serpent-maned, by Perseus—
lines.note: δρακοντοέθειραν = “serpent-maned” (from δράκων ‘serpent’ + ἔθειρα ‘mane/locks’), not ‘dragon-slaying’; Περσῆϊ is a poetic dative of agent with the passive; ἀκούεις marks direct didactic address.

lines.gr: Ἄτλαντος νεάτοισιν ὑπὸ κρημνοῖσι δαμῆναι,
lines.en: —was subdued beneath the uttermost crags of Atlas,
lines.note: νεάτοισιν = ‘lowest/uttermost,’ placing the scene at the world’s western limit; Ἄτλαντος … κρημνοῖσι = ‘the crags of Atlas’; δαμῆναι ‘to be subdued/slain.’

lines.gr: παρθένον ἀργαλέην, ἐρεβώπιδα, κῆρα μέλαιναν
lines.en: a grievous maiden, Erebus-eyed, a black doom
lines.note: ἀργαλέην ‘grievous, hard to bear’; ἐρεβώπιδα ‘Erebus-eyed, gloom-eyed’ (from Ἔρεβος ‘Erebus’); κῆρα μέλαιναν ‘black doom/baneful Ker.’

lines.gr: ἀνθρώπων, οἷσίν κεν ἐπ' ἀνδροφόνω βάλεν ὄσσε·
lines.en: of mortals, on whomsoever she would cast her man-slaying eyes;
lines.note: οἷσίν κεν … βάλεν ὄσσε = ‘on whomsoever she would cast her eyes’; ὄσσε is dual (‘both eyes’); ἀνδροφόνω modifies ὄσσε (‘man-slaying eyes’), pointing to the lethal gaze.

lines.gr: οἵ μιν δεῖμα πέλωρον ἀάσχετον ἀθρήσαντες
lines.en: who, beholding her—the monstrous, unendurable dread—
lines.note: δεῖμα πέλωρον ἀάσχετον = ‘monstrous, unendurable dread,’ in apposition to μιν ‘her’; ἀθρῆσαντες ‘having gazed (fixedly) upon,’ echoing the peril of her look.

lines.gr: αἴσῃ λαϊνέῃ τεθνηότες ἑστήκασι.
lines.en: stand dead with a stony fate.
lines.note: τεθνηότες ἑστήκασι ‘they stand dead’ expresses petrifaction; αἴσῃ λαϊνέῃ ‘with a stony fate’ personifies their transformation into stone, apt for the Lithica.

lines.gr: τὴν δ' οὔτ' εὐρύστερνος ἐναντίον Ἀτρυτώνη
lines.en: But her not even broad-breasted Atrytone consented to look upon face to face,
lines.note: Atrytone = Athena; eurysternos “broad-breasted” is an epic epithet (more usual of other goddesses), and enantion derkhesthai “to look straight at” is pointed in the context of the Gorgon’s deadly gaze.

lines.gr: δέρκεσθαι μενέαινεν, ἀδείμαντός περ ἐοῦσα,
lines.en: fearless though she was,
lines.note: Adeimantos “fearless”: emphasizes that even Athena, though fearless, avoids a direct gaze.

lines.gr: οὔτε κασιγνήτῳ κέλετο, κρατερόφρονι φωτί,
lines.en: nor did she bid her brother, the stout-minded man,
lines.note: Kasinētoi “to her brother” likely refers to Hermes (Athena’s half-brother as children of Zeus); “kraterephron phōs” = “stout-minded man.”

lines.gr: χρυσογόνῳ Περσῆϊ φονευομένην περ ἰδέσθαι,
lines.en: to look upon her even as she was being slain by gold-born Perseus;
lines.note: Chrysogonos “gold-born” alludes to Perseus’ begetting from Zeus’ golden shower upon Danae; Persēi is an epic dative of Perseus. The object of idesthai (“to see”) is the same “her” (the Gorgon), “even while being slain” (phoneuomenēn).

lines.gr: ἀλλὰ δόλῳ θήρειον ἀφήρπασεν αὐχένα κούρης
lines.en: but by guile he snatched the maiden’s beast-like neck,
lines.note: Thēreion auchena “beast-like neck” marks the Gorgon’s monstrous nature; kourē “maiden” is conventional epic diction applied paradoxically to the Gorgon.

lines.gr: ἦκα μάλ' ἐξόπιθεν γαμψώνυχον οὐ προϊδούσης
lines.en: very softly from behind, she not foreseeing the hook-taloned blade,
lines.note: Ēka “softly, gently”; gampsōnychon “hook-taloned” is best taken as a transferred epithet of the sickle-blade; ou proidousēs “without her having foreseen it.”

lines.gr: ἀμφιβαλὼν ἅρπην Κυλληνίδα λευκανΐῃσι.
lines.en: casting about with his white hands the Cyllenian harpe.
lines.note: Kyllēnida harpēn “the Cyllenian harpe” = the sickle-sword of Hermes (Cyllenian), here wielded by Perseus; leukanīēsi “with white hands” is a conventional epic formula.

lines.gr: τῆς δ' ἄρα καὶ φθιμένης περ ὀλέθριος ἔσκεν ὀπωπή,
lines.en: And even of her, though dead, the gaze was deadly,
lines.note: ὀπωπή (“gaze/vision”) suits the Gorgon’s lethal look; ἔσκεν (epic imperfect of “to be”) conveys enduring effect—‘even dead, her gaze remained deadly.’

lines.gr: καὶ στυγεροῦ Κρονίδαο μολεῖν ὑπὸ δῶμα κελαινὸν
lines.en: and to go beneath the murky house of the hateful Kronid
lines.note: Kronid (“son of Kronos”) here most plausibly denotes Hades, not Zeus; δῶμα κελαινόν (“murky/dark house”) is a conventional periphrasis for the Underworld, and στυγερός (“hateful”) is a standard epithet of Hades.

lines.gr: πολλοῖς αἴσιμον ἔπλετ' ἐναιρομένοις ὑπὸ νεκρῆς.
lines.en: proved fated for many, as they were being slain by the dead woman.
lines.note: ἐναιρομένοις (“being slain,” dat. pl.) takes a genitive of agent ὑπὸ νεκρῆς (“by the dead [woman]”), i.e., the decapitated Gorgon/Medusa; αἴσιμον (“fated, allotted by Aisa”) underlines the doom brought by her posthumous gaze.

lines.gr: ἀλλὰ τότ' αἰγιαλόνδε φόνῳ πεπαλαγμένος ἥρως
lines.en: But then to the beach came the hero, spattered with bloodshed,
lines.note: αἰγιαλόνδε is the epic directional adverb “to the seashore”; the unnamed ἥρως is Perseus.

lines.gr: ἐλθών, εἰσόκε λύθρον ἀποπλύνειε θαλάσσῃ,
lines.en: having come, he kept at it until he washed the gore away in the sea,
lines.note: εἰσόκε = “until”; ἀποπλύνειε is iterative imperfect, “kept washing off”; λύθρον denotes blood-gore/defilement, suggesting a lustral washing in the sea.

lines.gr: θερμὴν ἐξ ὁμάδου κεφαλὴν ἔτι καὶ τρομέουσαν
lines.en: the head still warm from the fray and even trembling,
lines.note: ἐξ ὁμάδου = “from the (battle-)din/fray,” i.e., freshly from combat; θερμήν … ἔτι καὶ τρομέουσαν underscores the immediacy of the decapitation.

lines.gr: Γοργείην κατέθηκεν ἐπὶ χλοεραῖς βοτάνῃσιν.
lines.en: the Gorgonian he set upon the green-growing plants.
lines.note: Γοργείην = “Gorgonian” (of the Gorgon, sc. Medousa); χλοεραῖς βοτάνῃσιν likely refers to green seaweeds on the shore, hinting at the coral-formation motif (cf. Ovid, Met. 4.740–752), fitting the Lithica’s mineralogical concerns.

lines.gr: ὄφρα δ' ὅγ' ἐν δίνῃσιν ἀναψύχεσκε θαλάσσης,
lines.en: While he kept catching his breath in the eddies of the sea,
lines.note: ἀναψύχεσκε is an iterative imperfect (“kept catching his breath”); ὄφρα here balances τόφρα in line 567 (“while … meanwhile”).

lines.gr: στείχων ἔκ τ' ὀλοοῖο πόνου, δολιχοῦ τε κελεύθου,
lines.en: stepping forth from baneful toil and the long way,
lines.note: στείχων is circumstantial (“as he went/stepped”); ὀλοοῖο (“baneful, deadly”) is epic; κελεύθος is the poetic ‘path/way’.

lines.gr: τόφρα δὲ πορφυρέοιο διαινόμενοι κορέσαντο
lines.en: meanwhile, feasting on the dark‑purple blood, they were sated—
lines.note: πορφυρέοιο αἵματος = “dark‑purple blood,” a standard epic color for clotted or fresh blood. διαινόμενοι (“feasting”) is striking with a non‑animal subject and anticipates θάμνοι in the next line; the diction is metaphorical.

lines.gr: αἵματος, οἵ ῥα κέχυντο χαμαὶ ὑπὸ κράατι θάμνοι.
lines.en: the bushes that had been spattered on the ground beneath the head.
lines.note: κέχυντο is perf. mid./pass. of χέω (“be poured/spilled; be drenched”): here best “were spattered/drenched (with blood).” θάμνοι is the delayed subject (hyperbaton), modified by the relative clause; ὑπὸ κράατι suggests a head lying above (likely severed) in the larger narrative context.

lines.gr: ἀμφὶ δ' ἄρα σφίσιν αἶψα θοαὶ πόντοιο θύγατρες
lines.en: And straightway around them the swift daughters of the Sea,
lines.note: “Daughters of the Sea” is appositional to the “breezes” (αὖραι) named in the next verse; ἀμφὶ σφίσιν (“around them”) likely anticipates the bushes (θαμνοῖς) of v. 570.

lines.gr: λύθρον ἐπεσσύμεναι θάμνοις περιπήγνυον αὖραι·
lines.en: the breezes, rushing upon the gore, were congealing it about the bushes;
lines.note: λύθρον (“gore, blood”) evokes the Gorgon-blood/coral aetiology; θάμνοι (“bushes”) here denotes branching sea‑plants/‘sea‑shrubs’ on which the gore hardens; περιπήγνυον = “were fixing/congealing around.”

lines.gr: πήγνυτο δ', ὥστε σε πάγχυ λίθον στερεὴν ὀΐσασθαι·
lines.en: and it was hardening, so that you would wholly take it for a solid stone;
lines.note: ὥστε σε … ὀΐσασθαι uses the generic second person (“you would think”); πάγχυ = “wholly, utterly”; στερεὴ λίθος = “solid stone.”

lines.gr: οὐδ' ἔτ' ἔην ὀΐσασθαι, ἐπεὶ στερεὴ λίθος ἦεν.
lines.en: nor any longer was it possible to suppose otherwise, since it was solid stone.
lines.note: οὐδ’ ἔτ’ ἔην ὀΐσασθαι is impersonal (“it was no longer possible to suppose [otherwise]”); ἦεν is Ionic for ἦν, marking the completion of petrification.

lines.gr: ἐκ δ' ὄλεσεν βοτάνης ὑγρὸν δέμας· ἀλλὰ καὶ ἔμπης
lines.en: and it stripped away from the plant its moist body; yet even so,
lines.note: ἐκ…ὄλεσεν conveys removal (“stripped away”). The subject is supplied from context (the drying/stonifying agent). ὑγρὸν δέμας, literally “moist body,” poetically denotes the plant’s sap or wet substance.

lines.gr: ὀλλυμένης πάμπαν βοτάνης οὐκ ὤλεσεν εἶδος.
lines.en: though the plant was perishing altogether, it did not destroy the form.
lines.note: Genitive absolute (ὀλλυμένης…βοτάνης). εἶδος (“form, shape”) is contrasted with δέμας, indicating that while the plant’s moist substance perished, its outward form remained—apt for a description of petrifaction.

lines.gr: τὴν μὲν ἄρα χροιὴν ἐξ αἵματος ἔσχεν ἐρυθρήν,
lines.en: Then indeed it took on a red hue from the blood,
lines.note: The subject (“it”) is the marine plant/weed that becomes coral; the redness is attributed to blood (sc. from the Gorgon).

lines.gr: ἀμφασίη δ' ἥρωα λάβε θρασύν, ὡς ἐνόησεν
lines.en: and bewilderment seized the bold hero, when he perceived
lines.note: amphasis here = bewilderment/astonishment; the “bold hero” is Perseus.

lines.gr: ἐξαπίνης μέγα θαῦμα· τὸ καὶ πέλας αἶψα κιοῦσα
lines.en: all of a sudden a great marvel; at which, coming close nearby straightaway,
lines.note: kiousa (“coming”) is a fem. participle anticipating the subject in the next line; πέλας = ‘nearby.’

lines.gr: διογενὴς πολύμητις ἐθαύμασεν Ὀβριμοπάτρη
lines.en: Diogenes, Polymetis, Obrimopatre marveled,
lines.note: A string of epithets for Athēna: Diogenes (‘Zeus-born’), Polymetis (‘of many counsels’), and Obrimopatre (‘daughter of a mighty father’).

lines.gr: θῆκε δ' ἀδελφειοῦ κλέος ἄφθιτον ὥς κε πέλοιτο,
lines.en: and she established her brother’s fame as imperishable, so that it might be,
lines.note: adelphiou (‘of her brother’) refers to Perseus; kleos aphthiton (‘undying fame’) is a traditional epic formula.

lines.gr: αἰεὶ κουράλιον προτέρην φύσιν ἀλλάσσεσθαι.
lines.en: that the coral should always change its former nature.
lines.note: kouralion = ‘coral’ (cf. variant korallion). The line states the instituted property: coral perpetually changes its former state (soft plant in the sea) upon exposure, hardening and reddening, thus memorializing Perseus’ deed.

lines.gr: ἐν δὲ βίην οἱ δῶκεν ἀπειρεσίην Ἀγελείη
lines.en: And Ageleie set within it boundless might,
lines.note: Ageleie (Ἀγελείη) is a cult-epithet, most commonly of Athena (also attested of Artemis); given the martial context, Athena is likely meant. The phrase “set within it boundless might” renders the Homeric idiom ἐν δὲ βίην οἱ δῶκεν (“put might in him/it”); “it” refers to the stone described in the surrounding context.

lines.gr: φῦλα φυλασσέμεναι κρυερὴν ἐς δῆριν ἰόντα,
lines.en: to guard the hosts as they go into chill strife,
lines.note: φῦλα is rendered “hosts” to suit the martial setting. κρυερὴ δῆρις (“chill strife”) is a Homeric epithet for battle. The infinitive φυλάσσεμεναι (for φυλάσσεσθαι) functions purposefully: “to guard.”

lines.gr: ἢ δολιχὴν ἕρπων ἐς ἀταρπιτὸν εἴ μιν ἔχει τις,
lines.en: or, going a long way on a trackless path, if someone has it,
lines.note: ἕρπων literally “crawling,” but in epic often “going (on foot),” hence “going a long way.” ἀταρπιτός is a poetic term for a “trackless path/way.” εἴ μιν ἔχει τις = “if someone has it,” with μιν referring to the stone.

lines.gr: ἢ περόων ἅλα δῖαν ἐϋσσέλμῳ ἐνὶ νηΐ.
lines.en: or crossing the bright sea in a well-benched ship.
lines.note: ἅλα δῖαν is the epic “bright/divine sea”; “bright” is chosen here. ἐϋσσέλμῳ (“well-benched”) is a standard ship-epithet. περόων is the present participle of περάω/περόω, “crossing.”

lines.gr: καὶ γὰρ Ἐνυαλίοιο θοὸν δόρυ μαινομένοιο,
lines.en: For even the swift spear of raving Enyalios,
lines.note: Enyalios is a war‑epithet (often of Ares). The line is elliptic; the sense “to escape” is supplied by the following infinitives (586–587).

lines.gr: καὶ λόχον ἀνδροφόνων φεύγειν ἄπο ληϊστήρων,
lines.en: and to escape the ambush of man‑slaying raiders,
lines.note: Lochos = “ambush.” Lēistērōn can mean pirates/brigands/raiders; “raiders” suits the martial context. Pheugein apo = “escape from.”

lines.gr: καὶ πολιὸν Νηρῆα κυκώμενον ἐξυπαλύξαι
lines.en: and to slip away from hoary Nereus when he is churned,
lines.note: “Hoary Nereus” personifies the grey sea; kykōmenos = “being churned/stirred,” i.e., storm‑tossed waters. Exypalyxai = “slip away/evade,” with a nuance of dodging danger.

lines.gr: ἐσθλὴ κουραλίοιο βίη θνητοῖσιν ὀπάσσει.
lines.en: the noble might of coral vouchsafes to mortals.
lines.note: Kouralioio = “of coral” (variant form of korallion); the phrase “noble might” (esthlē biē) is the subject of opassei (“bestows, vouchsafes”). The infinitives in 586–587 depend on this verb.

lines.gr: γλαυκὴν δ' ἐγρεκύδοιμον ἀταρβέα Τριτογένειαν
lines.en: and the grey‑eyed, battle‑rousing, fearless Tritogeneia
lines.note: ἐγρεκύδοιμον literally “rousing the kydoimos (din of battle),” an epithet more commonly of Ares but apt for Athena’s warlike aspect; ἀταρβέα = “undaunted, fearless.” “Tritogeneia” is the traditional epithet of Athena (etymology debated).

lines.gr: σφωϊτέρων καμάτων ἐπαμύντορα κικλήσκουσι.
lines.en: they invoke as a warder‑off of their own toils.
lines.note: ἐπαμύντορα takes a genitive of the thing warded off (καμάτων, “toils”). σφωϊτέρων is a dual possessive (“of the two of them/you two”); many take it as idiomatic “their own,” and some emend to σφετέρων. I translate generically as “their own.”

lines.gr: φάρμακα δ' ὅσσα πέλονται ἀτάσθαλα καὶ κατάδεσμα,
lines.en: and all the drugs that are wicked, and the binding‑spell,
lines.note: φάρμακα can mean drugs/charms/poisons; κατάδεσμα is a technical term for a binding‑curse (defixio), here singular but generic/collective.

lines.gr: ἀραί τ' ἀγνάμπτοισιν Ἐριννύσι πάγχυ μέλουσαι,
lines.en: and imprecations wholly the concern of the unbending Erinyes,
lines.note: ἀγνάμπτοισιν (“unbending/unyielding”) is a rare epithet; μέλουσαι with the dative expresses “belong to/are in the charge of.” Erinyes is kept in transliteration.

lines.gr: εἴτε μύσος κεύθων οἰκοφθόρον οὐκ ἐνόησεν
lines.en: whether a man has not perceived a house‑ruining defilement lying hidden,
lines.note: μύσος denotes ritual pollution; οἰκοφθόρον “house‑destroying.” Note the enjambment: the subject ἀνήρ follows in the next line.

lines.gr: ἀνήρ, εἴθ' ὅσα λύματ' ἐπί σφισιν ἠδ' ἐπαοιδὰς
lines.en: or whatever pollutions upon themselves and incantations
lines.note: λύματα are defilements/filth (ritual impurities); ἐπὶ σφισιν can mean “upon/against themselves (among themselves).” ἐπαοιδαί are incantations/spells.

lines.gr: σχέτλιοι ἀλλήλοισι μεγαίροντες τελέουσι,
lines.en: the wretches, begrudging one another, perform,
lines.note: σχέτλιοι conveys “wretched” or “pitiless”; μεγαίροντες = “begrudging, envying,” marking hostile intent behind such rites.

lines.gr: πάντων ἀντίλυτρον δήεις κρατερώτατον εἶναι.
lines.en: know it to be the mightiest counter‑charm against them all.
lines.note: ἀντίλυτρον literally “counter‑ransom,” here metaphorically “counter‑charm.” δήεις functions as a didactic imperative (“you must know”). The understood referent is the stone treated in the preceding context.

lines.gr: κόψας δὲ σπείρειν ξανθῇ Δημήτερι μίσγων·
lines.en: and having pounded it, sow it, mixing it with fair‑haired Demeter;
lines.note: “kópsas” = ‘having pounded/ground (the stone).’ “mixing with fair‑haired Demeter” uses Demeter metonymically for grain/seed; i.e., mix the powder with the seed to be sown (alternatively, ‘for Demeter’ as a cultic nuance).

lines.gr: καί τοι λοιγὸν ἅπαντα τεῆς ἀπάτερθεν ἀρούρης,
lines.en: and all bane far away from your field,
lines.note: “loigós” = baneful ruin/blight; “apáterthen” = ‘far away from.’ The verb governing the line comes in 599.

lines.gr: αὐχμούς τ' ἐξελάσει σταχύων γλάγος ἐκπίνοντας,
lines.en: it will drive out the droughts that drain the milk of the ears,
lines.note: “glágos” is the sweet/milky juice of the grain at the ‘milk’ stage; “ekpínontas” = ‘drinking dry,’ describing the action of the droughts on the ears (stachýōn).

lines.gr: ἀτηρήν τε χάλαζαν ἀπειρεσίοισι βελέμνοις
lines.en: and the baleful hail with its countless missiles,
lines.note: “atērḗn” = ‘baleful, destructive’; “apeiresioîsi belémnois” = ‘with countless missiles,’ a metaphor for hailstones as darts.

lines.gr: ἀγρῷ τραῦμα φέρουσαν ἀμήχανον ἐξακέσασθαι.
lines.en: bringing upon the field a wound impossible to heal.
lines.note: “amḗchanon exakesasthai” = ‘impossible to heal’; “traûma” (wound) metaphorically of crop-damage inflicted by hail.

lines.gr: βρωτήρων τ' ἐπὶ τοῖσι γένος πάντων ἀλαπάξει
lines.en: and upon them it will lay waste the whole tribe of gnawers,
lines.note: βρωτῆρες (“gnawers”) denotes crop-devouring pests; ἀλαπάξει (“will lay waste”) is strong, ‘plunder, utterly destroy’; ἐπὶ τοῖσι (“upon them”) sc. the crops previously mentioned.

lines.gr: εὐλάς τε κάμπας τε καὶ αἰθερίην ἐρυσίβην,
lines.en: grubs and caterpillars and the aetherial mildew,
lines.note: εὐλάς (“grubs/worms”) and κάμπες (“caterpillars”) are agricultural pests; ἐρυσίβη is ‘mildew/rust’, here called “aetherial” (αἰθερίη) for its sky-borne origin.

lines.gr: ἥ τε κατ' οὐρανόθεν πταμένη ποτὶ καρπὸν ἐρυθρὴ
lines.en: which, flying down from heaven toward the fruit, red,
lines.note: ἐρυθρή (“red”) points to the rust-like color of ἐρυσίβη; πταμένη (“flying”) and κατ’ οὐρανόθεν together mean ‘flying down from heaven.’

lines.gr: ἀμφὶ περὶ σταχύεσσι περισμύχουσα κάθηται.
lines.en: settles, shriveling all around the ears of grain.
lines.note: περισμύχουσα suggests scorching/shriveling; hence “shriveling all around.” ἀμφὶ περὶ is an emphatic encirclement; σταχύεσσι = ‘ears of grain.’

lines.gr: ἔκ τε μυῶν ἀγέλας ἔκ τ' ἀκρίδος ἄπλετον ἔθνος
lines.en: the droves of mice and the boundless nation of locusts
lines.note: ἀγέλας (“herds”) applied to mice is vivid and somewhat ironic; ἀκρίς is collective (“locust-swarm”). ἄπλετον ἔθνος = “boundless/immeasurable nation.” The preposition ἐκ anticipates the verb in the next line and suits the sense “drive off/out.”

lines.gr: ῥαίσει, καὶ Κρονίδαο παραΐσσουσι κεραυνοὶ
lines.en: it will drive away, and the thunderbolts of the Son of Kronos dart past,
lines.note: ῥαίσει is future of ῥαίω (“dash, shatter;” here with ἐκ = “drive away”). Κρονίδαο = “of the Son of Kronos” (Zeus). παραΐσσουσι (“dart past, bypass”) is a vivid present alongside a future, a common epic technique; the idea is that the place/thing in question (sc. the stone described in context) even causes Zeus’ thunderbolts to pass it by.

lines.gr: παιδὸς ἑοῦ κλέος ἔρξαι ἐτώσιον ἁζομένοιο.
lines.en: shrinking from bringing about empty renown for his own child.
lines.note: κλέος ἔρξαι is a poetic collocation (“to work/bring about glory”); ἐτώσιον = “vain, empty.” ἁζομένου (“being in awe, shrinking from”) is best taken with an implicit subject = Zeus (the Son of Kronos), hence “shrinking from bringing about empty renown for his own child.” The identity of “his child” is not specified here; the line suggests a scruple on Zeus’s part not to grant idle fame to one of his offspring.

lines.gr: κεῖνο πολὺ πρώτιστον ἀνερχόμενος περάτηθεν
lines.en: That one, by far the foremost, as he came up from beyond,
lines.note: περάτηθεν = “from across, from beyond (the sea/border).” The participle ἀνερχόμενος is masculine and most naturally refers to Argeiphontes (Hermes) anticipated in the next line; “that one” (κεῖνο) is the stone (sc. the subject under discussion).

lines.gr: κουράλιον θνητοῖσι φέρων πόρεν Ἀργειφόντης·
lines.en: Argeiphontes, bringing coral to mortals, bestowed it;
lines.note: κουράλιον is a variant of κοράλλιον “coral.” Argeiphontes is the epithet of Hermes. The sense is that Hermes brought/gave coral to humankind.

lines.gr: τύνη δ' ἀκρήτοιο μετ' οἴνου πινέμεν αἰεὶ
lines.en: But you, remember always to drink it with unmixed wine
lines.note: The object of “drink” is understood (sc. the coral, typically in powdered form) to be taken in undiluted wine (ἀκρήτοιο οἴνου), a common pharmacopeic instruction.

lines.gr: μέμνεο πευκεδανῆς ἕνεκ' ἀσπίδος, ὥσπερ ἔειπον.
lines.en: on account of the resin-scented asp, as I have said.
lines.note: ἀσπίς here is best taken as “asp (cobra),” not “shield”; πευκεδανής means “resinous, pitch-scented.” The line prescribes coral taken with unmixed wine as an antidote or protection against the asp’s bite, alluding back to an earlier mention (“as I have said”).

lines.gr: - Καὶ πολυειδέα πῖνε μετ' ἀκρήτου Βρομίοιο
lines.en: And drink the variegated one along with the unmixed wine of Bromios,
lines.note: Bromios is Dionysus; “unmixed” denotes undiluted wine. In lapidary practice πίνειν + stone implies ingesting the powdered gem with wine; πολυειδέα anticipates the identification in the next line.

lines.gr: μορφὴν παντοίην ἐπιειμένον ἐσθλὸν ἀχάτην.
lines.en: the noble agate, arrayed in every kind of form.
lines.note: ἐπιειμένον (“clad in”) metaphorically describes the stone’s banded/variegated appearance; μορφὴν παντοίην = “of every form.” ἐσθλός conveys noble/efficacious; ἀχάτης = agate.

lines.gr: πολλὰ μὲν οὖν ῥέα γ' ἐστὶν ἀχάτου χρώματ' ἰδέσθαι·
lines.en: Indeed, it is easy to behold many hues of the agate;
lines.note: ἀχάτης (agate/Achates) is characteristically multicolored; ῥέα γ’ = “indeed easily.”

lines.gr: ἐν γάρ οἱ δήεις ὁρόων ὑάλωπιν ἴασπιν
lines.en: for in it you will discern, as you look, hyaline jasper,
lines.note: δήεις = “you will discern/learn,” 2 sg fut of δαήσω; ὑάλωπις = “hyaline, glass‑like”; ἴασπις = jasper.

lines.gr: σάρδιά θ' αἱματόεντα καὶ αἰγλήεντα μάραγδον·
lines.en: and blood-colored sards and a gleaming emerald;
lines.note: σάρδια = sards (carnelian); αἱματόεντα = “blood‑colored”; μάραγδος = emerald (smaragd).

lines.gr: ἐν δ' ὅ γε μιλτοπάρῃος· ἀτὰρ καὶ χαλκὸν ἐν αὐτῷ
lines.en: and within it it is red‑ochre‑cheeked; and even bronze in it
lines.note: μιλτοπάρῃος, lit. “with red‑ochre cheeks” (μῖλτος = red ochre), describing reddish banding; ὅ γε refers to the agate.

lines.gr: δήεις καὶ χροιὴν ἐαροτρεφέος μήλοιο·
lines.en: you will discern, and the hue of a spring‑nurtured apple;
lines.note: χαλκόν here = “(the hue of) bronze”; χροιή = “color/complexion”; ἐαροτρεφέος μήλοιο = “spring‑nurtured apple,” i.e., apple‑green.

lines.gr: ἀλλ' οἶος πάντων προφερέστατος, εἴ κέ μιν εὕρῃς
lines.en: but one alone is most preeminent of all, if you should find it
lines.note: οἶος … προφερέστατος = “the single most outstanding one.”

lines.gr: εἶδος ἔχοντα δαφοινὸν ἀμαιμακέτοιο λέοντος·
lines.en: having the tawny aspect of an unconquerable lion;
lines.note: δαφοινός = “tawny”; ἀμαιμακέτος = epic “unconquerable, vast,” here of the lion’s might/majesty.

lines.gr: τῷ καί μιν προτέροισι λεοντοδέρην ὀνομῆναι
lines.en: to which, moreover, to call it ‘Lion‑neck’ in earlier times
lines.note: λεοντοδέρην = “Lion‑neck,” apparently a gem‑name; τῷ dative = “to this (stone)”; προτέροισι = “the former (race).” Some have discussed δέρη (“neck”) vs. a possible δερ‑ reading (“hide”), but δέρη is the transmitted text.

lines.gr: ἥνδανεν ἡμιθέοισι κατάστικτον σπιλάδεσσι
lines.en: was pleasing to the demigods, being dappled with little specks
lines.note: ἥνδανεν … ἡμιθέοισι = “pleased the demigods,” the mythic earlier race; κατάστικτον σπιλάδεσσι = “dappled with specks.”

lines.gr: πυρσῇσιν, λευκαῖς τε, μελαινομέναις, χλοεραῖς τε·
lines.en: fiery, and white, and blackened, and green;
lines.note: πυρσαῖσιν = “fiery (red)”; μελαινομέναις = “blackened/darkened”; χλοεραῖς = “greenish, grassy.”

lines.gr: τὸν δ', εἰ σκορπείην ὀλοφυρόμενός τις ἀκωκὴν
lines.en: and as for this one—if someone, lamenting a scorpion’s sting,
lines.note: σκορπείην ἀκωκήν = “scorpion’s sting”; ὀλοφυρόμενος = “lamenting,” of a suppliant in pain.

lines.gr: ἔλθοι, ἀερτάζειν περὶ ἕλκεϊ κέκλεο λυγρῷ,
lines.en: should come, bid him to swing it about the grievous wound,
lines.note: ἀερτάζειν is rare, “to suspend/swing,” likely of moving the stone over the wound as an amuletic act; κέκλεο = 2 sg aor. mid. impv. of κέλομαι, “bid.”

lines.gr: ἤ μιν ἐπιπλάσσειν· ἀπὸ γὰρ μινύθουσιν ἀνῖαι.
lines.en: or to apply it to him; for the pains diminish away from him.
lines.note: ἐπιπλάσσειν = “to plaster/apply (as a poultice)”; μινύθουσιν ἀνῖαι = “the pains diminish/abate.”

lines.gr: ἱμερτόν τε γυναιξὶ δυνήσεαι ἀνέρα θεῖναι,
lines.en: and you will be able to make a man desirable to women,
lines.note: ἱμερτόν = ‘desirable, lovely,’ often with erotic force; θεῖναι is the aorist infinitive of τίθημι ‘to make’; γυναιξί … ἄνερα = ‘a man (to/for) women,’ dative of reference/advantage.

lines.gr: καὶ θέλξεις μύθοισι βροτούς, καὶ πάντα κομίζων
lines.en: and you will bewitch mortals with words, and, bringing back all things,
lines.note: θέλξεις (from θέλγω) = ‘enchant, bewitch’; μύθοισι is instrumental dative ‘with/by words’; κομίζων is a circumstantial participle (‘bringing back’), enjambed with the finite verb in the next line; βροτούς = ‘mortals.’

lines.gr: ὅσσα κεν αἰτήσειας, ἀφίξεαι οἴκαδε χαίρων.
lines.en: whatever you may ask for, you will come home rejoicing.
lines.note: ὅσσα κεν αἰτήσειας: indefinite relative with κε(ν) + future optative (‘whatever you may/shall ask [for]’), an epic construction; ἀφίξεαι is epic future middle ‘you will arrive’; οἴκαδε ‘home(ward)’; χαίρων modifies the subject (‘rejoicing’).

lines.gr: καὶ νούσῳ κάμνοντα σαωθῆναι θέμις ἐστίν,
lines.en: and it is right that even one suffering with disease be healed,
lines.note: themis estin conveys normative sanction (“it is right/licit”); saōthēnai (“be saved”) in context = “be healed.”

lines.gr: ὅς μιν ἐνὶ σφετέρῃσι λαβὼν χεὶρεσσι κατάσχῃ·
lines.en: who, taking it in his own hands, holds it fast;
lines.note: min (“it”) most naturally refers to the stone under discussion; en(i) sphéterēisin cheiresin (“in his own hands”) stresses personal contact; kataschēi (“hold fast”) suits talismanic handling.

lines.gr: εἰ δὲ Ζεύς τοι τόν γε βιωσέμεν ἀρνήσηται,
lines.en: but if Zeus should refuse that man to live on,
lines.note: toi is an ethical dative, adding mild emphasis; biōsemen is a future infinitive “to live on”; ton ge refers to the sick man.

lines.gr: ἀλλὰ νόει σὺ τεῇσιν ἐνὶ φρεσὶν, οὕνεκεν αὐτῷ
lines.en: then understand in your own mind that it is because for him
lines.note: noei is imperative “understand/consider”; phresin (“mind, wits”). The clause continues to the next line.

lines.gr: ῥῆξε λίνον Κλωθώ· τὸ δέ κ' ἔρχεται ὕστατον ἦμαρ.
lines.en: Klotho has snapped his thread; and the last day will come.
lines.note: Klotho is one of the Moirai; linon (“thread”) = the life-thread; “his” is supplied from autōi. Hystaton ēmar (“last day”) is a standard idiom for death; ke (k’) marks potential/future, rendered here as “will come.”

lines.gr: - Εἰ δὲ πυριφλεγέθων ἑτερήμερος ἄνδρα θαμίζων,
lines.en: If an alternate‑day, fire‑blazing fever keeps visiting a man,
lines.note: ἑτερήμερος = “every other day,” i.e., an alternate‑day (tertian‑type) fever; πυριφλεγέθων “fire‑blazing.” θαμίζων = “frequenting, coming often,” used of recurring fits.

lines.gr: ἢ κρυερὸς μάρπτων πυρετὸς παραδηθύνῃσιν,
lines.en: or a chilly fever, seizing him, prolongs its course,
lines.note: παραδηθύνῃσιν (rare): lit. “make to linger, prolong.” μάρπτων (“seizing”) is standard for a disease’s onset; sense: the fever draws out its course.

lines.gr: ἠὲ τεταρταίης πῆμα βραδὺ μήποτε λήγειν
lines.en: or the slow bane of a quartan never consents to cease,
lines.note: τεταρταίης = quartan (fever), personified as feminine; πῆμα “bane.” μήποτε λήγειν βουλομένης conveys volition (“never willing to cease”).

lines.gr: βουλομένης, ἀλλ' αἰὲν ὅπη πελάσῃσι μενούσης,
lines.en: but always remains wherever she draws near,
lines.note: ὅπῃ πελάσῃσι = “wherever she draws near.” The fem. participles (βουλομένης, μενούσης) agree with τεταρταίης, not a genitive absolute but descriptive of the quartan’s behavior.

lines.gr: τόνδε σύ γ' ἰᾶσθαι δι' ἀμύμονος ἀντιαχάτου·
lines.en: do you heal this man by means of the peerless Anti‑achates;
lines.note: ἀντιαχάτου: the stone name is uncertain; usually taken as Anti‑achates, a variety/set against agate (ἀχάτης). δι’ + gen. = instrumental. ἰᾶσθαι is a jussive infinitive in didactic style (“do you heal”).

lines.gr: οὗτος γὰρ πυρετῶν πολὺ φέρτερος. αἶψα δὲ σῆμα
lines.en: for this stone is by far the better remedy against fevers.
lines.note: πυρετῶν gen. of reference/against: “as regards fevers,” hence “remedy against fevers.” φέρτερος = “better, superior.”

lines.gr: ἐξερέω, τό περ ὦκα βίην δείκνυσι λίθοιο.
lines.en: And I will straightway declare a token, which swiftly shows the stone’s might.
lines.note: σῆμα = diagnostic token/sign used in ancient gemology to recognize a stone; βίη = the stone’s “might/efficacy.”

lines.gr: ἐν γάρ μιν κεράεσσι βαλὼν μέσον ἑψομένοισι
lines.en: For, upon casting it into the midst of horns that are boiling,
lines.note: κεράεσσι is the epic dative plural of κέρας “horn,” here likely ‘horn-vessels’; the phrase “boiling horns” is striking, and some have taken it to mean boiling horns (e.g., for glue-making) or have proposed κεράμοισι (“earthenware pots”) as an emendation. μιν (“it”) refers to the stone under discussion.

lines.gr: τυτθὸν ἀνασχέσθαι· τὰ δὲ τήκεται ἔνδοθι πάντα.
lines.en: it will only just endure a little, while everything within melts away.
lines.note: τυτθὸν ἀνασχέσθαι = “to endure only a little (while),” with μιν as the understood subject. τὰ δὲ … πάντα is neuter plural with singular verb (common in Greek); it may refer either to the horns themselves (neut. pl.) or, more generally, to “the contents” within them. ἔνδοθι = “within.”

lines.gr: οὐ μέν τοι καὶ τόνδε πρὸς ἑρπετά φημι δύνασθαι,
lines.en: No indeed, I do not claim that even this stone has power against the creeping things,
lines.note: “τόνδε” refers to the previously discussed stone; “πρὸς ἑρπετά” = “against creeping things,” i.e., reptiles/serpents and similar venomous creatures.

lines.gr: ἀλλ' ἕτερον δώσω χατέοντί τοι ἰητῆρα
lines.en: but I will give you, since you are in need, another healer,
lines.note: “χατέοντι” is a dative of need (“to one in want/need”), a less common form; “ἰητήρ” (“healer”) metaphorically designates a remedial stone.

lines.gr: οὐρανόθεν γεγαῶτα· σὺ δ' ἐν φρεσὶ βάλλεο μῦθον.
lines.en: heaven-born; and do you set this word in your mind.
lines.note: “οὐρανόθεν γεγαῶτα” (“heaven-born”) likely hints at a celestial/meteoritic stone; “ἐν φρεσὶ βάλλεο μῦθον” is a didactic formula, ‘set/put this word in your mind.’

lines.gr: εὖτε γὰρ αἰγλῆεν σφέτερον δέμας εὐρύστερνος
lines.en: For when broad-chested Ouranos, his very body gleaming,
lines.note: εὐρύστερνος (broad‑chested) and αἰγλῆεν (radiant) are epic epithets of Οὐρανός; σφέτερον δέμας (“his own body”) underscores the bodily wounding.

lines.gr: Οὐρανὸς ὠμηστῆρος ὑπαὶ παλάμῃσι Κρόνοιο
lines.en: under the hands of Kronos the raw‑flesh‑eater,
lines.note: ὠμηστῆρος (“raw‑flesh‑eating”) marks Kronos’ savagery; cf. his cannibalistic reputation in myth.

lines.gr: δῃωθεὶς εἵλιξεν ἀπειρεσίην ἐπὶ γαῖαν
lines.en: mutilated, rolled down upon the boundless earth,
lines.note: δῃωθείς here conveys “mutilated, ravaged,” referring to the castration of Ouranos; εἵλιξεν = “rolled (down).”

lines.gr: αἰθέρος ἐκ δίης πεσέειν οὖδάσδε μενοινῶν,
lines.en: intent to fall from the bright Aither to the ground,
lines.note: Αἰθήρ (Aither) is the bright upper air; οὖδας = “ground, earth’s surface.”

lines.gr: ὄφρα κε πάντ' ἀΐδηλα πολύτροχον ἀμφιπετάσσας
lines.en: so that, overspreading the all‑unseen, much‑wheeled expanse,
lines.note: πάντ’ ἀΐδηλα πολύτροχον: “all‑unseen, much‑wheeled” likely describes the revolving heavenly expanse or cosmic wheelwork; ἀμφιπετάσσας = “overspreading.”

lines.gr: νῶτον ἑὸν τεύξαι, μηδ' Οὐρανοῦ ἀστερόεντος
lines.en: he might fashion his own back as a covering, nor should Kronos
lines.note: νῶτον ἑὸν τεύξαι = “to make his back [a vault/covering]”: an image of the firmament formed by Ouranos’ body.

lines.gr: θυμὸν ἀνιήσας Κρόνος οὐρανὸν εἰσέτι ναίοι·
lines.en: after vexing the spirit of starry Ouranos, still dwell in heaven;
lines.note: μηδ’ … Κρόνος … ναίοι: “nor should Kronos still dwell [there]”; note the play between the deity Οὐρανός and οὐρανόν “heaven.” θυμὸν ἀνιήσας = “after vexing/distressing the spirit.”

lines.gr: δή ῥα τότ' ἀμβροσίοιο κατειβόμεναι φορέοντο
lines.en: then indeed the drops, trickling of ambrosial blood, were borne down
lines.note: ἀμβροσίοιο αἵματος = “ambrosial (divine) blood”; φορέοντο (mid‑pass.) “were borne along/down,” of drops trickling.

lines.gr: αἵματος ὠτειλῆθεν ἐπὶ τραφερὴν ῥαθάμιγγες,
lines.en: from the wound onto the firm, dry land,
lines.note: ὠτειλῆθεν = “from the wound”; τραφερήν = “dry/firm” of land.

lines.gr: τὰς οὐ μόρσιμον ἦεν ἀπ' ἀθανάτοιο κιούσας
lines.en: and it was not fated for them, having departed from the immortal
lines.note: μόρσιμον = “fated”; κιόω/κίω “to go, depart”: here “having departed from the immortal (body).”

lines.gr: σώματος ὄλλυσθαι· μενέμεν δ' ἐριβώλακι Μοῖραι
lines.en: body, to perish; the Moirai bade them remain in the rich‑clodded
lines.note: ἐριβώλαξ = “rich‑clodded, fertile”; the Moirai (Fates) decree the drops’ abiding in earth.

lines.gr: ἐν γαίῃ προγόνοιο θεῶν σόον αἷμα κέλοντο.
lines.en: earth—the safe blood of the forefather of the gods.
lines.note: προγόνοιο θεῶν = “forefather of the gods,” i.e., Ouranos; σόον αἷμα “blood kept safe,” an etiological cue (in the Lithica’s context) for sacred substances arising from divine blood in earth.

lines.gr: μεῖνε μὲν οὖν, αὖον δὲ πυρίγληνοι θέσαν ἵπποι
lines.en: Wait then; the fire‑eyed horses of Helios have laid it out dry.
lines.note: μεῖνε is a 2nd‑sing. imperative “wait/stay”; αὖον is predicative “dry, parched.” πυρίγληνοι (from γλήνη “eyeball”) = “fire‑eyed”; ἵπποι Ἠελíου is a periphrasis for the Sun’s heat. θέσαν takes an implied object (“it”) from the context.

lines.gr: Ἠελίου· καί κέν τις ἐπιψαύων ἐρίσειε
lines.en: And a man, by merely touching it, would claim he holds a stone,
lines.note: κέ(ν) + optative expresses potentiality (“would”). ἐπιψαύων = “touching lightly.” ἐρίσειε here “would contend/claim.” λᾶαν is the Doric/Homeric acc. of λᾶας “stone.”

lines.gr: λᾶαν ἔχειν ἐνὶ χερσίν, ἔχει γε μὲν αἷμα πεπηγός.
lines.en: in his hands; yet he does in fact hold congealed blood.
lines.note: αἷμα πεπηγός = “congealed blood,” identifying the supposed “stone” as solidified blood (a bit of mineral lore). The subject remains τις from the previous line; γε μέν adds emphasis (“indeed/actually”).

lines.gr: ἐν γάρ οἱ χρὼς αὐτὸς ἐτήτυμον αἵματός ἐστιν,
lines.en: for in it the very hue is the true hue of blood,
lines.note: χρώς can mean “skin/surface” or “color”; here it denotes the stone’s visible hue. ἐτήτυμον αἵματος = “veritable/true [hue] of blood.” The enclitic οἱ is a dative of reference, “in it.”

lines.gr: ἐν δὲ καὶ ὕδατι ῥεῖα δαμασθεὶς ἀτρεκὲς αἷμα
lines.en: and even in water, when easily subdued, it becomes exact blood;
lines.note: ῥεῖα δαμασθείς literally “having been easily tamed/subdued”; in lapidary context this suggests being worked/ground or steeped so that in water it yields a blood-like coloration. ἀτρεκές = “exact, unfailing.” The description suits haematite/bloodstone.

lines.gr: γίνεται· αἱματόεις δὲ καὶ οὔνομα λᾶας ἔτ' ἀνδρῶν
lines.en: and even in name it is “bloody”: the stone has been so called by men of former times,
lines.note: αἱματόεις … οὔνομα “bloody even in name” alludes to the ancient appellation αἱματῖτης (haematite). ἔτ’ ἀνδρῶν ἐκ προτέρων = “already/by men of earlier times.”

lines.gr: ἐκ προτέρων κέκληται· ἀκήρατα δ' οὕνεκ' ἔοικε
lines.en: and since it seems to possess undefiled remedies,
lines.note: ἀκήρατα φάρμακα = “undefiled/pure remedies,” with φάρμακα covering both medicinal and magical “drugs/charms,” fitting the poem’s didactic-magical register.

lines.gr: φάρμακ' ἔχειν, νημερτὲς ἀπόρροιάν μιν ἀοιδοὶ
lines.en: the singers proclaim it an unerring efflux,
lines.note: νημερτές “unerring, infallible.” The phrase νημερτὲς ἀπόρροια treats νημερτές as qualifying ἀπόρροια (“efflux, emanation”). μιν is the accusative pronoun (“it,” i.e., the stone) governed by κλείουσιν in the next line.

lines.gr: οὐρανίην κλείουσιν ἐς ἀνθρώπους ἀφικέσθαι.
lines.en: heavenly, to have come to humankind.
lines.note: οὐρανίην … ἀφικέσθαι “a heavenly [efflux] to have come to men,” depending on κλείουσιν (“the singers proclaim”). “Heavenly efflux” reflects Orphic-cosmological language for sacred substances reaching mortals.

lines.gr: οὐ γὰρ ὅ γ' οὔτε νέην ἐθέλει θνητοῖσιν ὀϊζὺν
lines.en: For it does not allow a new affliction to come upon mortals’ eyes,
lines.note: ὀϊζύν (“woe, distress”) here = an ocular complaint; ὄσσε is the poetic dual “eyes.”

lines.gr: ἔρχεσθαι ποτὶ ὄσσε, παλαιοτέρην δ' ἀπερύκει
lines.en: but it keeps an older one away,

lines.gr: πινόμενος λευκοῖο μετὰ γλάγεος· κεράσας δὲ
lines.en: when it is drunk together with white milk; and,
lines.note: γλάγεος is an archaic/epic word for “milk” (cf. γάλα); hence “with white milk.”

lines.gr: ἰχῶρι σφετέρῳ γλυκερὸν μέλι, τὸν δὲ δαμάσσας
lines.en: mixing sweet honey with its own ichor, and having subdued it,
lines.note: ἰχῶρ (“ichor”) is used in pharmacological contexts for a liquid/sap; “its own ichor” likely means the stone’s exudate/solution; the mixed honey forms a collyrium. The object of δαμάσσας (“having subdued”) is supplied by the next (missing) line, probably the pain/ailment.

lines.gr: [missing]
lines.en: [lacuna]
lines.note: Line missing (lacuna); the preceding τὸν (“it/him”) lacks an explicit antecedent because of this gap.

lines.gr: ἐκ βλεφάρων ἀπὸ πᾶσαν ἄγει νόσον· ἀσχαλάᾳ γὰρ
lines.en: it carries off every disease from the eyelids;
lines.note: ἄγει ἀπό (“carry/lead away”) is an idiom for removing disease; the context is an eye‑salve.

lines.gr: εἴργεσθαι θνητοὺς ὁράαν ἐρατεινὰ πρόσωπα
lines.en: for it is vexed that mortals are hindered from seeing lovely faces
lines.note: ἀσχαλᾷ (“is vexed, is distressed”); the subject may be the stone personified or an implied divinity.

lines.gr: πρεσβυτάτου μακάρων ἀστροβλεφάρου βασιλῆος.
lines.en: of the eldest of the Blessed, the star‑eyed king.
lines.note: “the eldest of the Blessed, the star‑eyed king” most naturally evokes Ouranos (the starry Sky); some take it differently (e.g., Kronos), but the phrase likely depends on πρόσωπα (“faces/aspects”) as a genitive (“the faces of the star‑eyed king”).

lines.gr: καὶ γλήνῃσι τεῇσιν, ὁμιλήσας κυλίκεσσιν
lines.en: and for your own pupils, once it has consorted with cups,
lines.note: γλήνῃσι (dat. pl. of γλήνη) = “pupils/eyeballs.” τεῇσιν = “your (own).” ὁμιλήσας with the dative (“having consorted with”) is used of the stone, i.e., “after being steeped/mingled in cups”; κυλίκεσσιν are sympotic cups (kylikes). The subject (“the stone”) is supplied from context, so the line is syntactically elliptical.

lines.gr: [missing]
lines.en: [line missing]
lines.note: Lacuna: the verse is missing in our text; any procedure that may have connected the eye-use with the drinking is not preserved.

lines.gr: ἀνέρος αἰδοίων ἄκος ἔσσεται, ὅς κε πίῃσι.
lines.en: it will be a remedy for a man’s privy parts, for whoever shall drink.
lines.note: ἀνέρος αἰδοίων = “a man’s privy parts/genitals.” ὅς κε πίῃσι is an indefinite relative with κε + subjunctive, “whoever shall drink (it),” sc. the liquid in which the stone has been steeped.

lines.gr: καί μιν ἐγὼν Αἴαντι δαΐφρονι πόλλ' ἐπέτελλον
lines.en: And as for it, I myself laid many injunctions upon battle‑minded Aias,
lines.note: μιν (“it”) is the accusative of the thing enjoined; ἐπέτελλον governs accusative (thing) + dative (person). The referent is the stone just described. δαΐφρων is the stock epithet “battle‑minded.”

lines.gr: ἔντεσι δῆριν θεῖναι ἀμύμονος ἀμφ' Ἀχιλῆος
lines.en: to set the fray in arms about blameless Achilleus,
lines.note: δῆριν θεῖναι is a Homeric idiom, “to set the strife,” i.e., to engage in battle. ἔντεσι = “in arms/armor.” ἀμύμονος (“blameless”) is a fixed epithet of Achilleus.

lines.gr: ἐσσυμένῳ, νίκης ἐπαρηγόνα χειρὶ κομίζειν.
lines.en: as he rushed, to bear in his hand a helper of victory.
lines.note: ἐσσυμένος = “rushing, impetuous.” νίκης ἐπαρήγονα (“a helper of victory”) likely denotes the stone as a talisman; χειρὶ κομίζειν = “to carry in/by the hand,” i.e., on one’s person.

lines.gr: καί κεν Ὀδυσσῆος ταλασίφρονος ἀντίον αὐτῷ
lines.en: And even against steadfast‑minded Odysseus himself
lines.note: ταλασίφρονος = “steadfast/enduring in mind.” ἀντίον with genitive = “against; face‑to‑face with.” The dative αὐτῷ is the recipient of the κῦδος given in the next line.

lines.gr: κῦδος Ἀθηναίη περ ἑλέπτολις ἐγγυάλιξεν·
lines.en: Athênê the city‑seizer would have put glory into his hands;
lines.note: ἑλέπτολις is a Homeric epithet of Athênê (“city‑seizer”). ἐγγυάλιξεν = “put into (his) hands.” κεν + aorist gives potential sense (“would have”). κῦδος here ≈ victory/renown.

lines.gr: ἀλλ' οὔ οἱ μοῖρ' ἔσκε παραιφαμένοιο πιθέσθαι·
lines.en: but it was not his lot to heed the one who advised him;
lines.note: παραιφαμένου (“advising, counseling”) carries the nuance of gentle or side‑advice. Formulaic οὐ οἱ μοῖρ’ ἔσκε … πιθέσθαι = “it was not his fate to obey.”

lines.gr: τοὔνεκα θεσπέσιόν μιν ἀνὴρ ἀθέριζεν ὄνειαρ,
lines.en: therefore a man slighted the divinely wondrous boon,
lines.note: ἀθερίζεν = “made light of, slighted.” θεσπέσιον ὄνειαρ = “divinely wondrous boon,” likely the efficacy of the magical stone referred to below; μιν (“him/it”) is resumptive.

lines.gr: λάζετο δ' οὐλοὸν ἆορ. ἀτὰρ σύ γε τοῖο μὲν αἶσαν
lines.en: and he seized the baneful sword. But you—the lot of such a one—
lines.note: οὐλοὸν ἆορ = “baneful sword,” a traditional epic collocation. λάζετο = “grasped, seized.” The didactic address begins with ἀτὰρ σὺ γε …

lines.gr: ἅζεο, πρὸς δὲ μέλαιναν ὀλισθηροῖο γενέθλην
lines.en: shrink from it, and go to the black brood of the slippery serpent,
lines.note: ἅζεο = “shrink from, beware (of).” πρὸς with accusative marks approach/direction. μέλαιναν γενέθλην ὀλισθηροῖο ἑρπετοῦ = “the black brood of the slippery reptile,” i.e., serpents.

lines.gr: ἑρπετοῦ αἱματόεντα δαεὶς λίθον, αἰὲν ἑταίρους
lines.en: having learned the reptile’s blood‑stained stone, always bid the companions
lines.note: δαεὶς = “having learned/been instructed (about).” αἱματόεντα λίθον ἑρπετοῦ alludes to the drakonitis (serpent‑stone), said to be obtained from a living serpent and to ‘bleed’—hence “blood‑stained.”

lines.gr: πινέμεναι νύμφαις ἐνὶ νηϊάδεσσι κέλευε.
lines.en: to drink among the Naiad nymphs.
lines.note: ἑταίρους (“companions”) is likely the stone’s companion‑stones; πινέμεναι (“to drink”) is a conventional idiom in Lithica for soaking stones. Νύμφαι Νηϊάδες = Naiad nymphs, i.e., fresh‑water springs where the soaking is done.

lines.gr: καὶ μὲν ἐγὼ λαιψηρὸν ἐμὸν θεράποντα Δόλωνα
lines.en: And I, my nimble attendant Dolon,
lines.note: λαιψηρὸν = “nimble, light, swift”; θεράπων = “attendant/henchman.” Dolon recalls the swift spy of Il. 10.

lines.gr: αὐτοκασιγνήτῳ μεμαὼς φίλον Ἕκτορι θεῖναι
lines.en: being eager to make him dear to my own brother Hektor,
lines.note: αὐτοκασιγνήτῳ (“to my own full brother”) is dat. with Ἕκτορι; the first-person speaker is thus a brother of Hektor (likely Alexandros/Paris).

lines.gr: πρόφρων ὤπασα λᾶαν Ὀλύμπιον αἰτήσαντι·
lines.en: readily bestowed the Olympian stone when he asked;
lines.note: λᾶας Ὀλύμπιος (“the Olympian stone”) is a lithic name in the poem; here a charm-stone whose gift secures favor. πρόφρων ὤπασα = “I gladly bestowed.”

lines.gr: αὐτὰρ ὅ γ' ἐξαπίνης Τρώων προπάροιθεν ἁπάντων
lines.en: but he straightway, before all the Trojans,
lines.note: ἐξαπίνης = “suddenly, straightway.” Τρώων προπάροιθεν ἁπάντων = “before all the Trojans,” i.e., publicly, in full view.

lines.gr: Ἕκτορι Πριαμίδῃ κεχαρισμένος ἔπλεθ' ἑταῖρος.
lines.en: became a favored companion to Hektor, son of Priamos.
lines.note: κεχαρισμένος ἑταῖρος = “a companion in favor [with him],” the perfect indicating established favor; Priamides = “son of Priamos.”

lines.gr: τοῖο δ' ἕκητί μ' ἐκεῖνος ἀμοιβήδην ἀρέσασθαι
lines.en: By that one’s leave he set himself to gratify me in requital,
lines.note: ἕκητι + gen. = “by the agency/leave of.” The referent of τοῖο (“of that one”) depends on the larger context. ἀρέσασθαι ἀμοιβήδην = “to do a favor in return, requite.”

lines.gr: ἱέμενος λιπαραῖον ἐπίκλησιν παρὰ πατρὸς
lines.en: and, eager, with an earnest appeal to his father, he bestowed
lines.note: λιπαραῖον ἐπίκλησιν is taken as “earnest/pressing entreaty” (cf. λιπαραί λιταί); thus “with an earnest appeal.” παρὰ πατρὸς refers most plausibly to Memnon’s father (Tithonus), fitting the Assyrian setting and ἀφνειοῖος (“wealthy”).

lines.gr: ὤπασεν ἀφνειοῖο λαβὼν λίθον, ὅν ποτ' ἄρ' αὐτὸς
lines.en: a stone, taken from his wealthy father, which once he himself—
lines.note: ὤπασεν = “bestowed/granted” (epic). ἀφνειοῖο agrees with πατρὸς (“wealthy father”). The object (λίθον) is picked up by ὅν in the next lines.

lines.gr: ἐλθὼν Ἰλιόθεν κρατερὸν μετὰ Μέμνονα κῆρυξ
lines.en: the herald, having come from Ilion with mighty Memnon—
lines.note: μετά with acc. can mean “with” or “after”; “with” is adopted here. κρατερός as epic epithet of Memnon. κῆρυξ = “herald” (Memnon’s herald).

lines.gr: σήματ' ἐμεῖο πορόντος ἀνευρὼν Ἀσσυρίηθεν
lines.en: found from Assyria, guided by the signs I supplied, and
lines.note: σήματ’ ἐμεῖο πορόντος is a genitive absolute, “as I supplied the signs,” i.e., “guided by the indications I provided.” Ἀσσυρίηθεν is the epic ablatival “from Assyria.”

lines.gr: χρυσοῦ τιμήεντος ἀρείονα δεῦρο κόμισσε
lines.en: brought here, better than precious gold,
lines.note: τιμήεντος = “honored/precious.” ἀρείονα = “better, superior.” δεῦρο = “hither,” rendered “here.”

lines.gr: μυρία κεῖθι μάγοισι πορὼν πολυΐδμοσι δῶρα.
lines.en: after giving myriad gifts there to the resourceful magoi.
lines.note: μάγοι (magois) is transliterated; πολυΐδμοσι = “of many wiles/very resourceful.” κεῖθι (“there”) points back to Assyria; the line implies gifts/bribes to the magoi.

lines.gr: εἰ δ' ἄγε δέχνυσο μῦθον· ἐγὼ δ' ἐδάην, τά κε λέξω.
lines.en: But come, show forth the tale; I for my part have learned what I shall tell.
lines.note: εἰ δ’ ἄγε is an epic transitional formula (“come now”). δέχνυσο is an epic/middle imperative of δείκνυμι “show, display” used with μῦθον “tale”; some editors compare the common epic formula δέξο μῦθον (“receive the word”). ἐδάην is the epic aorist “I learned.” τά κε with the modal particle κε functions like “what(ever),” here best rendered simply as “what”; λέξω is the future of λέγω (“I shall tell”).

lines.gr: - Πρῶτα μὲν οὖν σπένδοντας ἀναιμάκτων ἐπὶ βωμῶν
lines.en: First, then, while pouring libations upon bloodless altars,
lines.note: “Bloodless altars” (anaimaktōn bomōn) signals Orphic practice: libations/incense rather than animal sacrifice; spendein = “pour libations.”

lines.gr: ‑ οὐ γὰρ ἄγειν θέμις ἐστὶ θυηλὴν ἐμψύχοιο ‑
lines.en: — for it is not lawful to bring a burnt-offering of a living creature —
lines.note: Thyēlē here = “burnt-offering/sacrificial burning,” with empsychou (“ensouled, living [creature]”); agein in sacrificial diction = “bring/lead [to sacrifice].” The line states the Orphic ban on animal sacrifice.

lines.gr: Ἥλιον εὐρύοπα κλῄζειν ὕμνοισιν ἄνωγα,
lines.en: I bid you to invoke wide-seeing Helios with hymns,
lines.note: Euryopa (“wide‑seeing”) is a traditional epic epithet (elsewhere of Zeus), apt for Helios; klēizein = “invoke/celebrate with hymns.”

lines.gr: καὶ χθόνα πίειραν πάντων τροφὸν οὐθατόεσσαν.
lines.en: and the fertile Earth, nurse of all, rich‑uddered.
lines.note: The transmitted outhatoessan is likely a corruption for outhartoessan (“rich‑uddered”), from outhar (“udder,” by extension “rich yield”), a common poetic metaphor for Earth’s fertility; hence the rendering “rich‑uddered.”

lines.gr: δεύτερον αὖτ' αἴθωνος ὑπὲρ λίθον Ἡφαίστοιο
lines.en: Secondly again, over the stone of fiery Hephaistos,
lines.note: αἴθωνος Ἡφαίστοιο (“of fiery Hephaistos”) is an epithet phrase; “the stone of Hephaistos” denotes the hearth/brazier. Ὑπὲρ λίθον here means “over/upon the stone,” i.e., on the fire.

lines.gr: τήκειν ἡδείῃ ταναοὺς θέλγοντα δράκοντας
lines.en: melt a substance that, with sweet fragrance, beguiles the long serpents;
lines.note: τήκειν is an imperative infinitive in didactic style, ‘melt’ in the sense ‘burn (on coals)’ an aromatic; the direct object is understood and characterized by the participle θέλγοντα (“bewitching, charming”). δράκων = ‘serpent’ (not a mythic dragon).

lines.gr: ὀδμῇ, τὴν ἄρα κεῖνοι ἀνερχομένην ἐσορῶντες
lines.en: the scent which, when they behold it rising,
lines.note: τὴν refers to ὀδμή (‘scent’), and κεῖνοι to the serpents; ἀνερχομένην ἐσορῶντες = ‘seeing it as it rises’ (of the smoke/aroma).

lines.gr: σπερχόμενοι ποτὶ βωμὸν ἀολλέες ἐκπρομολόντες
lines.en: hastening toward the altar, all in a throng, having come forth from the cleft,
lines.note: ἀολλέες = ‘in a body/in a mass’; ἐκπρομολόντες = ‘coming forth’; χηραμόθεν (‘from a cleft/fissure’) is a rare word for a crack or hole in the ground/wall.

lines.gr: χηραμόθεν ῥώονται ἐφερπύζοντες ἅπαντες.
lines.en: they rush, every one of them, creeping up.
lines.note: ῥώονται (middle) = ‘rush, dart’; ἐφερπύζοντες is ἐπ- + ἑρπύζω, ‘creeping up toward’—apt for serpentine movement.

lines.gr: αὐτὰρ ἔπειτα λίνοιο νεόπλυτα φάρεα κοῦροι
lines.en: But then let the youths don freshly washed linen garments,
lines.note: “Freshly washed linen” signals ritual purity before the rite; φάρεα (garments) of λίνον (linen) suits cultic instruction.

lines.gr: ἑσσάμενοι τρεῖς, ὀξὺ φέρων ἄμφηκες ἕκαστος
lines.en: three in number, each bearing a sharp, double‑edged
lines.note: ἄμφηκες ἆορ is a standard epic collocation for a “double‑edged sword”; the phrasing is enjambed across the verse break.

lines.gr: ἆορ, ἀναρπάζων ὄφιν αἰόλον, ὅς κε μάλιστα
lines.en: sword, snatching up a mottled serpent, the one that most
lines.note: αἰόλος is “variegated, mottled”; ἀναρπάζων (snatching up) describes the ritual seizure of the snake by each youth.

lines.gr: κνίσσης ἱμείρων πυρὸς ἐγγύθι δινεύῃσι·
lines.en: whirls near the fire, yearning for the savour of the grease‑smoke;
lines.note: κνίση is the sacrificial “grease‑smoke” or savour; δινεύειν “to whirl” vividly depicts the serpent’s motion near the fire.

lines.gr: τοῦ δὲ διαμελεϊστὶ δαΐζειν ἐννέα μοίρας·
lines.en: and him cut joint by joint into nine portions:
lines.note: διαμελεϊστί (lit. “limb‑by‑limb”) is a rare adverb; δαΐζειν “to cut/rend” here = dismember into nine ritual portions (μοῖραι).

lines.gr: τρεῖς μὲν ἐπὶ κλῆσιν πανδερκέος ἠελίοιο,
lines.en: three for the calling upon of all‑seeing Helios,
lines.note: κλῆσις is “invocation”; πανδερκής ἠέλιος is “all‑seeing Helios,” a formal cultic epithet.

lines.gr: τρεῖς δ' ἑτέρας γαίης ἐριβώλου λαοβοτείρης,
lines.en: and three others for Gaia, rich‑soiled, folk‑sustaining,
lines.note: ἐριβῶλος (“rich‑soiled”) and λαοβοτείρη (“people‑sustaining”) are traditional epithets of Gaia.

lines.gr: τρεῖς δὲ θεοπροπίης πολυΐδμονος ἀψεύστοιο·
lines.en: and three for the much‑wise, unerring oracle;
lines.note: θεοπροπία (“oracle, prophecy”) with epithets πολυΐδμονος (“much‑wise”) and ἀψευστου (“unerring”) probably alludes to Apollo’s truthful oracle, though no theonym is named.

lines.gr: τὰς δὲ λέβης κεράμοιο τετυγμένος αἱματοέσσας
lines.en: and let a cauldron wrought of clay receive them, the blood‑stained portions;
lines.note: Λέβης κεράμοιο τετυγμένος = an earthenware cauldron; αἱματοέσσας (“blood‑stained”) modifies the (implicit) μοίρας “portions.”

lines.gr: δεξάσθω· καὶ δῶρον ἐλάϊον Ἀτρυτώνης,
lines.en: and the gift, the oil of Atrytonē,
lines.note: δῶρον ἐλαῖον Ἀτρυτώνης = “the gift, the oil of Atrytonē,” i.e., Athena’s olive‑oil; the infinitive “to pour” is supplied in the next line.

lines.gr: ἠδὲ μέθυ Βρομίοιο καλεσσιχόρου καταχεύειν,
lines.en: and to pour down the wine of Bromios, summoner of the chorus,
lines.note: Βρομίος (“Roaring One”) is Dionysos; καλεσσιχόρου = “chorus‑summoning, caller of the dance,” an epithet highlighting his festive rites.

lines.gr: ἐν δ' ἅλας ἀργεννοὺς βαλέειν θεράποντας ἐδωδῆς·
lines.en: and into them let the attendants of the meal cast white salt;
lines.note: θεράποντες ἐδωδῆς = “attendants of the meal,” i.e., cooks/servers; ἅλας ἀργεννούς is “white/bright salt.”

lines.gr: ἐν δέ σφιν καὶ δριμὺν ἐπήλυδα κόκκον ἄνωγα
lines.en: and among them too the pungent foreign berry I bid
lines.note: δριμὺς (“pungent”) and ἐπήλυδος (“foreign/imported”) suggest an exotic spice; κόκκος (“berry/seed”) may refer to peppercorns or mustard seed.

lines.gr: μῖξαι ῥυσοχίτωνα, μελαγχροίην, ἐρίτιμον·
lines.en: to mix—yellow‑clad, dark‑skinned, most precious;
lines.note: The adjectives likely describe varieties or qualities of the same “berry/seed”: “yellow‑clad” and “dark‑skinned” suit yellow and black types; ἐρίτιμον = “most precious.” (Some editors read ἐρύσιμον “hedge‑mustard,” but the given text has ἐρίτιμον.)

lines.gr: ἐν δὲ καὶ ὅσσα περ ἄλλα μετ' ἀλλήλοισι μιγέντα
lines.en: and besides, whatever other things, when mingled together,
lines.note: Generalizing addition of further seasonings; μετ’ ἀλλήλοισι μιγέντα underscores compounding for flavor.

lines.gr: ἵμερον ἐσπέμπουσιν ἐδητύος ἀνθρώποισιν.
lines.en: send to mortals a longing for the meal.
lines.note: ἵμερος (“desire, longing”) + ἐδητύς (“cooked fare, meal”) expresses inducing appetite; ἐσπέμπουσιν “send in” is a poetic idiom for imparting.

lines.gr: ὄφρα δ' ἐνὶ τρίποδος κρέα γαστέρι δάμνατ' ἐόντα,
lines.en: While in the belly of the tripod the meat is being cooked,
lines.note: “Belly of the tripod” (gaster of the tripod) refers to the cauldron set on a sacrificial tripod; δάμνημι (‘subdue’) is a common idiom for ‘cook’ meat in epic diction.

lines.gr: τόφρα δὲ κικλήσκειν μακάρων ἄρρηκτον ἕκαστον
lines.en: meanwhile invoke the unbreakable name of each of the Blessed Ones;
lines.note: κικλήσκειν is an imperatival infinitive in ritual instruction (‘to invoke’ = ‘invoke’). ἄρρηκτον ὄνομα (‘unbreakable name’) is magical-ritual diction meaning inviolable/efficacious name; μάκαρες (‘the Blessed Ones’) denotes the gods.

lines.gr: οὔνομα· τέρπονται γάρ, ἐπεί κέ τις ἐν τελετῇσι
lines.en: for they take delight whenever someone, in the rites,
lines.note: τελεταί are initiatory or mystery rites; the line frames the invocation within formal ritual performance.

lines.gr: μυστικὸν ἀείδῃσιν ἐπώνυμον οὐρανιώνων.
lines.en: chants the mystic proper name of the Heaven-dwellers.
lines.note: μυστικόν (‘mystic/secret’) and ἐπώνυμον (‘proper/true name’ or ‘name-bearing epithet’) mark specialized ritual nomenclature; οὐρανιῶνες (‘Heaven-dwellers’) is a poetic periphrasis for the celestial gods.

lines.gr: ἀρᾶσθαι δὲ Μέγαιραν ἀπόπροθι παφλάζοντος
lines.en: and to pray that Megaira rush far away from the seething
lines.note: Enjambment: παφλάζοντος … τρίποδος (“seething … tripod”). ἀρᾶσθαι with accusative (Μέγαιραν) = ‘to invoke/call upon’ the Fury; παφλάζειν used of boiling liquid supported by the tripod (cauldron/oracular apparatus).

lines.gr: σευέμεναι τρίποδος κακομήχανον· ἐς δ' ἄρα τούς γε
lines.en: tripod, the evil-contriving one;
lines.note: σευέμεναι is the Homeric middle infinitive ‘to rush, dart.’ κακομήχανον is best taken as an epithet of Megaira (“evil-contriving”), not of the tripod.

lines.gr: πνεῦμα διϊπετὲς ἔνδον ἄγειν ἱερὰς ἐπὶ μοίρας.
lines.en: and to bring the Zeus-sent breath within into those men, unto holy destinies.
lines.note: πνεῦμα διϊπετές = ‘Zeus-sent breath,’ suggestive of oracular/inspiratory pneuma; ἐς δ’ ἄρα τοὺς γε (‘into those men indeed’) likely refers to the intended targets of the rite; ἱερὰς ἐπὶ μοίρας = ‘unto holy destinies/fates.’

lines.gr: ὁππότε δ' ἑψομένοισιν ἐπὶ κρεάεσσιν ἵκηται,
lines.en: and whenever it comes upon the meats as they boil,
lines.note: Subject of “it comes” is supplied from the prior context (the power invited to the boiling cauldron); ἑψομένοιςιν is “as they are being boiled” and ἐπὶ κρεάεσσιν “over/at the meats.”

lines.gr: δαίνυσθαι τότ' ἔπειτα κορέννυσθαι μεμαῶτας
lines.en: then feast, and thereafter, eager to be sated,
lines.note: δαίνυσθαι … κορέννυσθαι are infinitives used as directives; μεμαῶτας (“eager”) modifies the implied subject (you).

lines.gr: αὐτόθεν ἐκ τρίποδος· τὰ δὲ λείψανα γαῖα καλύπτοι·
lines.en: straight from the tripod; and let the earth cover the leavings;
lines.note: αὐτόθεν ἐκ τρίποδος refers to the cauldron set on a tripod; λείψανα “leavings” are to be buried (chthonic practice).

lines.gr: καί σφιν ἐπισπεῖσαι λευκὸν γάλα καὶ μέθυ ἡδὺ
lines.en: and pour for them white milk and sweet wine,
lines.note: σφιν = “for them,” i.e., the recipients of the rite; μέθυ = wine; ἐπισπεῖσαι is “to pour/libate upon.”

lines.gr: καὶ λίπ' ἐπήρατον ἠδὲ μελίσσης ἄνθιμον εἶδαρ,
lines.en: and lovely oil and the bee’s flowery food,
lines.note: μέλισσης ἄνθιμον εἶδαρ is the traditional periphrasis for honeycomb; λίπ’ = oil (olive oil).

lines.gr: καὶ στέψαι πλέξαντας ἀκρόδρυα καρποφόροιο
lines.en: and, having plaited them, wreathe with the tree-fruits,
lines.note: ἀκρόδρυα = “tree-borne fruits” (here effectively olives); πλέκειν implies twining a garland for wreathing.

lines.gr: παρθενικῆς ἀφελόντας ἐλαίης· ἀμφὶ δὲ κόρσαις
lines.en: plucked from the fruit-bearing maiden olive; and about your own temples
lines.note: παρθενικῆς ἐλαίης “maiden olive” is a cultic epithet (cf. Athena’s sacred olive); the object of “wreathe” is your head, understood.

lines.gr: σφωϊτέραις πέπλους ἑλέειν οἶκόνδε κιόντας·
lines.en: take up veils as you go home;
lines.note: κόρσαις = “temples (of the head)”; πέπλους ἑλέειν “take up garments/veils,” i.e., veil the head on returning.

lines.gr: μηδὲ μεταστρωφᾶσθαι, ἐπεί κ' ἀπονόσφι τράπησθε,
lines.en: and do not turn back, once you have turned away apart,
lines.note: μεταστρωφᾶσθαι = “turn back/look back”; ἀπονόσφι = “apart, away,” marking ritual separation after the rite.

lines.gr: ἀλλ' αἰεὶ προτέρην ἐς ἀταρπιτὸν ὄσσε φέροντας
lines.en: but always bearing your eyes toward the forward path
lines.note: ἀταρπιτός = “(foot)path, track”; προτέρην … ὄσσε φέροντας = “keeping the eyes straight ahead.”

lines.gr: ἔρχεσθ' ἐς μέγαρον, μηδὲ προτιμυθήσασθαι,
lines.en: go to the hall, and do not begin conversing,
lines.note: προτιμυθήσασθαι = “to address, enter into talk/greet”; μέγαρον = the main hall of the house.

lines.gr: εἴ κέν τις ξύμβληται ὁδίτης, ἔστ' ἂν ἵκησθε
lines.en: if some wayfarer meets you, until you reach the house;
lines.note: ὁδίτης = “wayfarer”; ἔστ’ ἄν = “until such time as.”

lines.gr: ἐς δόμον· ἔνθα δ' ἔπειτα θυηλὰς ἀθανάτοισιν
lines.en: and there thereafter again perform burnt-offerings for the Deathless Ones,
lines.note: θυηλάς = smoke/burnt-offerings (esp. of incense) for the gods (the Deathless Ones). “Again” (ἐξαῦτις) signals repetition after arrival home.

lines.gr: ἐξαῦτις ῥέζοντας ἀρώματα ποικίλα καίειν.
lines.en: burning variegated aromatics.
lines.note: ἀρώματα ποικίλα = “variegated aromatics,” i.e., mixed incense/spices to be burned as fumigation.

lines.gr: - Ταῦτ' ἐγὼ ἐκτελέσας, ὅσα τ' ἔσσεται, ὅσσα τε κοῦφοι
lines.en: These things having been accomplished—what shall be, and all that the light birds cry—
lines.note: ἐκτελέσας suggests ritual or task completion; ὅσα τ’ ἔσσεται = “what shall be.” κοῦφοι ὄρνιθες literally “light” birds (nimble, swift), here of augural cries. The main verb ἐπίσταμαι (“I know”) comes in the next line and governs the whole series.

lines.gr: ὄρνιθες κλάζουσιν, ἐπίσταμαι, ὅσσα τε θῆρες
lines.en: I know, and all that the wild beasts
lines.note: κλάζουσιν is the sharp cry typical of cranes/geese, used generically of birds. The placement of ἐπίσταμαι is parenthetic and syntactically governs both preceding and following relative clauses, marking a seer-like boast of knowledge.

lines.gr: ὠμησταὶ τετράπεζοι ἐνί σφισιν ὠρύονται.
lines.en: flesh-eating, four-footed, howl among themselves.
lines.note: ὠμησταί = “raw-eating,” i.e., carnivorous; rendered “flesh-eating” for idiom. τετράπεζοι = “four-footed” (poetic for quadrupeds). ἐνί σφισιν = “among themselves.” ὠρύονται describes the roaring/howling of beasts.

lines.gr: - Ἔνθεν ἐγὼν ἐδάην καὶ Βακχικὰ νεβρίταο
lines.en: Thence I also learned the Bacchic gifts of Nebrites,
lines.note: “Nebrites” (nebritēs) is the name of a stone; its name evokes the Bacchic fawn-skin (nebris). ἐδάην (“I learned”) is the epic aorist of δάω, here marking a didactic disclosure.

lines.gr: δῶρα λίθου Βρομίῳ κεχαρισμένα· τόν περ ἔχοντες
lines.en: the gifts of the stone, pleasing to Bromios;
lines.note: Bromios is an epithet of Dionysos. κεχαρισμένα “pleasing/acceptable” suggests cultic favor.

lines.gr: ἄνθρωποι θύοιτε καὶ ἀράων ἀΐουσιν
lines.en: which, when men possess it, let them offer sacrifice, and the Ouranidai hear their prayers.
lines.note: Θύοιτε is an exhortative/subjunctive-like optative: “let them offer sacrifice.” Οὐρανίδαι (“Ouranidai”) = the heavenly gods; ἀρῶν can mean prayers or imprecations; in this ritual context, “prayers.”

lines.gr: Οὐρανίδαι. γυμνῷ δὲ ῥάχιν πόδα πευκεδανοῖο
lines.en: and upon the bare ridge of the foot,
lines.note: ῥάχις here is best taken as “ridge/instep” of the foot. The construction is enjambed with the next line; see note ad 757 on the difficult syntax.

lines.gr: εἴ κέν τις θλίψας ὄφιος διὰ σάρκας ἀκάνθῃ
lines.en: if someone, having crushed it, with a pine-wood thorn of a serpent should lacerate his own flesh through the flesh,
lines.note: This verse is textually and syntactically vexed. πευκεδανός = “of pine(-wood),” naturally goes with ἀκάνthē (“thorn”) to yield “pine-thorn” (a common cause of foot wounds). ὄφιος is puzzling; many take it as an epic/genitival form of ὄφις (“of a serpent”), yielding the sense of a bite (by its “thorn” = fang), while others regard it as corrupt or a gloss. I translate so as to include both elements, but the practical sense is that a poultice of the stone soothes a foot wound from a thorn (and, by extension, a bite). θλίψας (“having crushed”) implies making a poultice.

lines.gr: δῃώσῃ σφετέρας, ὀδυνήφατος ἔσσεται αὐτῷ
lines.en: Nebrites will be pain-banishing for him;
lines.note: ὀδυνήφατος = “pain-banishing, analgesic.” The line states the stone’s medical efficacy once applied.

lines.gr: νεβρίτης. ἔρδει δ' ἀλόχῳ πόσιν ἱμερόεντα.
lines.en: and it effects for a wife a desirable husband.
lines.note: ἔρδει (“effects, accomplishes”) marks efficacy; ἱμερόεντα (“desirable, charming”) with πόσιν suggests a love-charm: the stone promotes conjugal affection, “a desirable husband for the wife.”

lines.gr: - Ἔνθεν καὶ κατένωπα κελαινῆς ἀσπίδος ἔγνων
lines.en: Thence too I came to know the aspects of the dusky jasper,
lines.note: The transmitted ἀσπίδος (“of a shield”) is likely a corruption; most editors read ἰάσπιδος (“of jasper”), fitting the following mention of πράσος/prāsius. κατένωπα (neut. pl.) is rare; here taken as “faces/aspects,” i.e., the visible features or surface-marks of the stone.

lines.gr: καρτερὰ φάρμακα σεῖο, βροτοσσόε θέσκελε πέτρη,
lines.en: your potent charms, O man-terrifying, wondrous stone,
lines.note: φάρμακα in the Lithica are “charms/spells,” i.e., magical properties, not merely “drugs.” βροτοσσόε = “terrifying to mortals,” an epic/vocative epithet.

lines.gr: τῆς ὄνομα χροιή τε πέλει χλοεροῖο πράσοιο.
lines.en: whose very name and hue are that of the green leek.
lines.note: χλοεροῖο πράσοιο (“of the green leek”) explains the gem-name πράσιος (prase), a leek-green variety of jasper; hence “name and hue” both derive from the leek.

lines.gr: - Ἔνθεν καὶ σέο, δῖε χαλάζιε, πειρηθῆναι
lines.en: Thence too, O divine Chalazios, to make trial of you
lines.note: Ἔνθεν (“thence”) points back to the preceding trials of stones. πειρηθῆναι is the (deponent) aorist infinitive “to make trial (of),” governing the genitive σέο (“of you”). δῖε is the epic epithet “divine.” χαλάζιε is the vocative of χαλάζιος, the “hail-stone” gem (usually rock crystal), addressed anthropopathically, as is common in the Lithica.

lines.gr: ἐν θυμῷ βαλόμην, καί σευ μένος εὗρον ἄριστον.
lines.en: I cast in my heart, and I found your might the best.
lines.note: ἐν θυμῷ βαλόμην is a Homeric idiom meaning “I put/cast in my heart,” i.e., “I resolved.” σευ is the epic genitive of σύ (“of you”). μένος denotes “might/power,” here the efficacy of the stone; ἄριστον = “best, preeminent.”

lines.gr: ἄμφω γάρ, καὶ νοῦσον ἀναψύχεις πυρόεσσαν,
lines.en: For you do both: you cool the fiery sickness,
lines.note: ἀναψύχεις “cool, refresh”; πυρόεσσαν “fiery,” here likely referring to a feverish illness.

lines.gr: καί μοι σκορπιόθεν βεβολημένῳ ἦρα κομίζεις.
lines.en: and for me, scorpion‑struck, you bring remedies.
lines.note: σκορπιόθεν is a poetic -θεν form meaning “by/from a scorpion”; βεβολημένῳ is the perfect passive participle “having been struck/wounded”; ἦρα (Homeric) denotes “helps, remedies, reliefs.”

lines.gr: - Λητοΐδαο μάλα χρησμοῖς, Ποιάντιος ἥρως,
lines.en: By the oracles of the son of Leto, O Poïantian hero,
lines.note: Λητοΐδαο (“son of Leto”) = Apollo; Ποιάντιος ἥρως is a vocative, “Poïantian hero,” i.e., Philoctetes, son of Poias.

lines.gr: ἑσπόμενον τάδε πάντα μ' ἀμήχανά φημι πιφαύσκειν.
lines.en: I declare that, in following them, I make manifest all these things as beyond contrivance.
lines.note: ἑσπόμενον (acc. masc. sg. ptc.) agrees with μ’ (“me”): “as I follow [sc. the oracles].” φημί governs an acc.-inf. construction with πιφαύσκειν (“to make manifest, declare”); τάδε πάντα is the object, with ἀμήχανα predicative (“beyond contrivance, impossible”), a heightened didactic/mirabilia nuance.

lines.gr: αὐτοκασιγνήτην κεχολωμένος Ἀργυρότοξος
lines.en: Angered at his own sister, Argyrotoxos,
lines.note: αὐτοκασιγνήτην (acc. sg. fem.) is taken with Κασσάνδρην in the next line (“his own sister Kassandra”), while κεχολωμένος is used intransitively (“being angered”). The designation of Kassandra as Apollo’s “own sister” is mythographically irregular; many take it as rhetorical/proximate (priestly intimacy) or a poetic slip; it nonetheless frames the familiar curse-motif of Apollo and Kassandra.

lines.gr: Κασσάνδρην ἐκέλευσεν ἀκουόντεσσιν ἄπιστα
lines.en: ordered Kassandra to prophesy to the hearers things not to be believed,
lines.note: ἀκούοντεσσιν ἄπιστα = “unbelievable to those who hear,” i.e., the essence of Apollo’s curse: her true prophecies would not be believed.

lines.gr: θεσπίζειν Τρώεσσιν ἐτήτυμά περ φρονέουσαν·
lines.en: to prophesy to the Trojans, though she knew what is true;
lines.note: ἐτήτυμά περ φρονέουσαν: περ is concessive (“although”), φρονέω here “to be mindful of/know.”

lines.gr: αὐτὰρ ἐγὼ καὶ πρόσθεν ἀπώμοσα καρτερὸν ὅρκον,
lines.en: but I too earlier swore a mighty oath,
lines.note: ἀπώμοσα καρτερὸν ὅρκον is a formal didactic self-guarantee (“I swore a mighty oath”).

lines.gr: ψευδέα μήποτε μῦθον ἐνισπεῖν ἀνθρώποισι·
lines.en: never at any time to utter a lying word to human beings;
lines.note: ἐνισπεῖν = “to utter, speak forth” in epic diction; ψευδέα μῦθον is a marked phrase for falsehood.

lines.gr: καὶ νῦν ἀτρεκέως μάλα τοι λέξαντος ἕκαστα
lines.en: and now too, since I have set out each thing very exactly,
lines.note: ἀτρεκέως “precisely, exactly” suits didactic register; τοι is an enclitic particle here (“indeed”), not 2nd-person dative.

lines.gr: ἡμετέροις, ἥρως ἑκατηβόλε, πείθεο μύθοις.
lines.en: be persuaded by my words, hero Hekatēbole.
lines.note: ἥρως ἑκατηβόλε is a vocative; ἑκατηβόλος is typically Apollo’s epithet (“far-shooter”), but here the address “hero, Hekatēbole” likely marks the poem’s addressee in elevated style; theonymic epithet is preserved by transliteration as requested.

lines.gr: - Ὣς ἄρ' ἔφη Πριάμοιο διοτρεφέος φίλος υἱὸς
lines.en: Thus then he spoke, the dear son of Priam, Zeus‑nurtured,
lines.note: διοτρεφέος (“Zeus‑nurtured”) is a Homeric epithet regularly applied to kings like Priam; the whole line adopts formulaic epic diction (Ὣς ἄρ’ ἔφη).

lines.gr: ἀτρέστου θεράποντι φέρων χάριν Ἡρακλῆος·
lines.en: rendering thanks to the fearless attendant of Herakles;
lines.note: θεράπων (“attendant, henchman, squire”) is the standard epic term for a warrior’s close companion; here, the “attendant of Herakles” evokes Iolaos. ἀτρεστοῦ (“undaunted, fearless”) modifies θεράποντι. φέρειν χάριν is the idiom “to render thanks/repay a favor.”

lines.gr: νῶϊ δὲ ποιήεσσαν ἐς ἀκρώρειαν ἰοῦσι
lines.en: and for the two of us, as we were going toward the grassy ridge,
lines.note: νῶϊ is the epic dual “we two.” ποιήεσσαν (“grassy”) is a poetic epithet (from ποίη/πόα, “grass”). ἀκρώρεια denotes a mountain ridge or height.

lines.gr: τρηχεῖαν μάλα μῦθοι ἀταρπιτὸν ἐπρήϋναν.
lines.en: the words greatly smoothed the rough, trackless way.
lines.note: μῦθοι … ἐπρήυναν (“words soothed/smoothed”) uses a common epic metaphor of speech easing toil. ἀτάρπιτος is a rare adjective meaning “pathless, impassable,” here with τρηχεῖαν (“rugged, rough”). The dative νῶϊ from the previous line is the dative of advantage: the words “smoothed [it] for us two.”
